title: 9  Linkage and re-identification
text:
9.1 Why this matters
A hospital removes names from discharge records but retains postcode, date of birth, sex and diagnosis. A voter roll lists names with the same quasi-identifiers. Joining the tables can identify many records. This is a linkage attack; identifying a person in a supposedly de-identified record is re-identification.
Estimate linkage risk by measuring identifying information in bits. Each bit halves the candidate set, so \(\log_2 n\) bits can distinguish one person among \(n\). For the 1990 United States, this is 27.9 bits. When known attributes carry slightly more information, many people have unique combinations that can be linked.

title: 9  Linkage and re-identification
text:
9.2 Quasi-identifiers and the linkage attack
Direct identifiers, such as names or email addresses, identify a person on their own. Sensitive attributes, such as diagnoses, are the subject of the release. Quasi-identifiers do not identify people individually but can do so in combination; they also appear beside names in other datasets.
To assess a release, group its \(n\) records into equivalence classes, each containing records with identical quasi-identifiers. Let \(J\) be the number of classes. Suppose an adversary knows the target’s quasi-identifiers and knows that the target is in the release. If the target’s class contains \(k\) records, the adversary identifies the target with probability \(1/k\). Each class contributes one expected correct identification across its \(k\) records. Thus, across all \(n\) targets, the success probability is \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac{J}{n}, \tag{9.1}\] No adversary using only quasi-identifiers can do better. This is the prosecutor model, a worst-case assumption in which the adversary knows that the target is in the release.
The script practitioner_table_risk.py measures uniqueness on Adult, a dataset of 48,842 people from the 1994 US Current Population Survey in the UCI repository. Because Adult lacks ZIP codes and birth dates, the script starts with age, sex and race, then adds quasi-identifiers one at a time. For each set, it prints the unique-record share, the share in classes smaller than 5, the minimum class size and \(J/n\).
n = df.height
for qis in QI_SETS:
    # One row per equivalence class (records that agree on every quasi-identifier), with its size.
    sizes = df.group_by(qis).len()
    unique = sizes.filter(pl.col("len") == 1).height / n  # share of records alone in their class
    small = sizes.filter(pl.col("len") < 5)["len"].sum() / n  # share in classes smaller than 5
    min_k = sizes["len"].min()  # the table is k-anonymous for this k
    print(
        f"{' + '.join(qis)}: unique={unique:.2%}  in classes <5={small:.2%}  "
        f"min k={min_k}  J/n={sizes.height / n:.3f}"
    )
Run it with uv run python code/part02-attacks/practitioner_table_risk.py, which prints:
age + sex + race: unique=0.12%  in classes <5=0.75%  min k=1  J/n=0.012
age + sex + race + native-country: unique=3.07%  in classes <5=7.83%  min k=1  J/n=0.060
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status: unique=5.88%  in classes <5=11.99%  min k=1  J/n=0.100
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status + education: unique=14.64%  in classes <5=26.83%  min k=1  J/n=0.227
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status + education + hours-per-week: unique=36.55%  in classes <5=57.05%  min k=1  J/n=0.480
Three columns leave 0.12% of records unique; six leave 14.64%. Adding hours worked per week, which is not usually treated as an identifier, raises the unique share to 36.55%. Test every column an adversary could know, adding them one at a time. Every set here contains single-record classes, despite the common minimum class-size rule of 5.

title: 9  Linkage and re-identification
text:
9.3 Pseudonyms and hashed identifiers
Many releases replace identifiers with pseudonyms, codes that remain constant across one person’s records. These codes can fail in two ways. First, an adversary can reverse an unkeyed hash such as MD5 when the possible identifiers can be enumerated: hash each candidate and look for a match. New York City used this approach for taxi-driver licenses in its 2013 trip release. The set contained about 2 million possible licenses; in 2014, Vijay Pandurangan hashed them all and identified the drivers.
The second risk remains even with a key. A pseudonym links one person’s records, so identifying one record reveals the others. In the taxi data, a passenger who knows a trip’s pickup time and place can identify the driver; the driver’s pseudonym then links all their trips. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) therefore still treats pseudonymized data as personal data.
If a join key is necessary, generate it with a keyed hash, such as a hash-based message authentication code (HMAC), and store the key separately from the data.
import hashlib
import hmac
import secrets

licence = "482913"  # a six-digit licence number, the identifier being pseudonymized
pseudonym = hashlib.md5(licence.encode()).hexdigest()  # what an unkeyed release prints

# Dictionary attack: hash all 10**6 possible licences once, then look the pseudonym up.
lookup = {hashlib.md5(f"{i:06d}".encode()).hexdigest(): f"{i:06d}" for i in range(10**6)}
print(lookup[pseudonym])  # 482913

# A keyed hash still gives one code per person, but without the key nobody can build the table.
key = secrets.token_bytes(32)  # store it apart from the data; draw a new one for each release
keyed = hmac.new(key, licence.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
print(keyed in lookup)  # False
The key prevents dictionary attacks but does not prevent linkage through a person’s record history. Reusing the key across releases enables cross-release linkage, so generate a new key for each release.

title: 9  Linkage and re-identification
text:
9.4 How many people are unique?
Before the table exists, estimate uniqueness by summing information across attributes. An attribute with \(v\) equally likely values carries \(\log_2 v\) bits; independent attributes’ bits add. Attributes with \(b\) total bits divide the population into \(2^b\) cells. If each person is assigned uniformly at random to a cell, the expected fraction of \(n\) people alone in their cell is approximately \[\frac{\text{unique people}}{n} \approx \exp\big(-2^{\log_2 n - b}\big). \tag{9.2}\] The fraction depends on the number of bits above \(\log_2 n\) and increases rapidly with that excess. Half the people are unique at 0.53 bits above \(\log_2 n\).
ZIP code, birth date and sex carry 31.1 bits, slightly more than the 27.9 bits needed to single out one American. The formula predicts that 0.899 of Americans are unique, close to Latanya Sweeney’s 87% estimate from the 1990 census. Real attributes are skewed and correlated, which usually lowers uniqueness; the uniform-cell estimate is therefore cautious.

title: 9  Linkage and re-identification
text:
9.5 Sparse data: the Netflix attack
Ratings, purchases and locations can identify people without quasi-identifier columns. In 2006, Netflix released about 100 million movie ratings with random identifiers instead of subscriber names. Narayanan and Shmatikov (2008) matched these records to public reviews. Their score sums agreement with known items, weighting rare items more heavily than popular ones. Eight ratings with dates known within 14 days identified 99% of records, even when two ratings were incorrect.
The highest score always identifies some record, even when the target is absent. The eccentricity test declares a match only when the highest score exceeds the second-highest by a specified margin, measured in standard deviations of all scores. Calibrate this margin using people known to be outside the release. In the full edition’s simulated ratings, the original attack’s margin also matched 26.3% of outsiders. Report attack success at a specified false positive rate (Hypothesis testing).

title: 9  Linkage and re-identification
text:
9.6 Does releasing a sample protect?
Agencies often release samples, as with Adult, because a record unique in the sample may match someone outside it. Let \(q\) be the sampling rate, the fraction of the population in the release. Suppose the adversary finds exactly one matching record, and let \(\lambda\) be the expected number of other people in the population who share the target’s cell. A look-alike can account for the match only if the target was not sampled, with probability \(1-q\). For a rare cell, the probability \(\kappa\) that the match is correct is approximately \[\kappa \approx \frac{1}{1 + \lambda(1 - q)}. \tag{9.3}\]
For a cell with \(\lambda = 0.1\) expected other people, a match is correct with probability 0.910 even in a 1% sample. Since \(1-q\) cannot exceed 1, the probability of a correct match is at least \(1/(1+\lambda)\). Reducing the sample size therefore offers little protection for rare cells. Sampling mainly helps when cells are already crowded.
The Adult figures above measure sample uniqueness, which is exact under the assumption that the target is in the release. Population uniqueness is lower but remains close for rare cells. Estimate it with a model; ARX and sdcMicro provide such estimates, and Rocher, Hendrickx and de Montjoye (2019) model attribute correlations.

title: 9  Linkage and re-identification
text:
9.7 A pre-release risk check
List every field an adversary could find beside a name in another source, such as a date, location or rare event. No tool can identify all available auxiliary data. Reduce risk by first coarsening geography and dates, which often carry many bits, then suppressing records that remain unique (Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks). For analyses that require fine-grained or sparse data, release differentially private outputs instead (Release statistics with a library). Pre-release privacy risk assessment applies thresholds set before examining the counts.

title: 10  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
10.1 Why this matters
Linkage and re-identification showed that removing names does not make a table anonymous. Combinations of age, postcode and sex can still identify people. A common response is to generalize the table until each person belongs to a group. These definitions are syntactic because they can be checked directly from the released table. Statistics offices and tools such as ARX and sdcMicro still use them. Each definition applies to one table and assumes fixed adversarial knowledge; additional information or another release can defeat it.
crumbs: 10  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 10  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
section: 10.2 What the adversary believes about a class
text:
10.2 What the adversary believes about a class
To anonymize a table, the custodian—the organization holding the data—applies generalization, such as replacing an age with a range or a postcode with a prefix. Records with identical generalized quasi-identifiers form an equivalence class. An adversary who knows the target’s quasi-identifiers can identify the target’s class \(E\) but cannot distinguish its records. The adversary’s posterior for a sensitive value is therefore the fraction of the class with that value. Let \(\lvert E\rvert\) be the class size and \(n_E(v)\) the number of records in it with sensitive value \(v\). The posterior that the target’s sensitive value \(S_{\text{target}}\) equals \(v\) is
\[\Pr[S_{\text{target}} = v \mid \text{release}] = \frac{n_E(v)}{\lvert E\rvert}. \tag{10.1}\] An adversary can use background knowledge to eliminate values, then recompute the posterior over the remaining records. The attacks in this chapter use this calculation.
crumbs: 10  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 10  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
10.3 k-anonymity and what it costs
k-anonymity (Sweeney and Samarati, 1998) requires each class to contain at least \(k\) records, where the custodian chooses \(k\). Generalization and suppression—deleting records that remain distinguishable—can enforce the requirement. In the previous chapter, an adversary who knows the target is in the release links it with probability \(J/n\), where \(J\) is the number of classes and \(n\) the number of records. If each class contains at least \(k\) records, there are at most \(n/k\) classes, so \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac{J}{n} \le \frac1k. \tag{10.2}\] This bound concerns linkage and assumes the adversary knows only the quasi-identifiers. The choice of \(k\) is a policy decision; 5 is a common minimum.
Anonymizers such as Mondrian search for a low-cost generalization. Alternatively, generalize the table manually and recheck it. The script practitioner_table_risk.py uses the Adult census extract and six quasi-identifiers from the previous chapter. It groups age into 10-year bands, native country into US or other, and education into four levels. It then counts records alone in their class and the distinct occupations in each class, treating occupation as the sensitive attribute. The script uses Polars because no maintained Python package computes k-anonymity or distinct \(\ell\).
general = df.with_columns(
    (pl.col("age") // 10 * 10).alias("age"),  # 10-year bands: 30 stands for 30-39
    pl.when(pl.col("native-country") == "United-States")
    .then(pl.lit("US"))
    .otherwise(pl.lit("other"))
    .alias("native-country"),
    # education-num runs from 1 (preschool) to 16 (doctorate); 9 is high-school graduate.
    pl.col("education-num")
    .cut([8, 9, 12], labels=["no diploma", "HS-grad", "some college", "bachelor+"])
    .alias("education"),
)
# Recheck, and count the occupations in each class (distinct l).
classes = general.group_by(QIS).agg(pl.len(), pl.col("occupation").n_unique().alias("l"))
unique = classes.filter(pl.col("len") == 1).height / general.height
one_job = classes.filter(pl.col("l") == 1)["len"].sum() / general.height
print(f"after generalizing: unique={unique:.2%}  in a class with one occupation={one_job:.2%}")
Run it with uv run python code/part02-attacks/practitioner_table_risk.py. Its first two output lines use the six generalized quasi-identifiers, and the third adds the raw hours worked per week.
after generalizing: unique=0.94%  in a class with one occupation=1.20%
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status + education: unique=0.94%  in classes <5=3.31%  min k=1  J/n=0.032
age + sex + race + native-country + marital-status + education + hours-per-week: unique=10.09%  in classes <5=21.78%  min k=1  J/n=0.175
  records in classes of size >=5 with l=1: 0.03%
Generalization reduced the unique share from 14.64% to 0.94%, but the smallest class still contains one record. Suppress the 3.31% of records in classes smaller than 5 or use broader bands. The result remains fragile: an adversary who also knows hours worked finds 10.09% of records unique.
crumbs: 10  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 10  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
10.4 Homogeneity, background knowledge and l-diversity
k-anonymity obscures record identity but not sensitive values (Machanavajjhala et al., 2006). In a homogeneity attack, all three records in Alice’s class report heart disease, so her posterior probability of heart disease is 1. In a background knowledge attack, Bob’s class contains two cancer records and one flu record. A neighbour who knows Bob did not have flu can eliminate that record and infer cancer.
l-diversity requires each class to contain enough distinct sensitive values. Its distinct version requires at least \(\ell\) values but does not limit the most common value’s share; a class can be 3-diverse even if one value dominates. The recursive version also caps that share using a custodian-selected constant \(c\). If an adversary rules out \(\ell-2\) values, the posterior is below \(c/(1+c)\). At \(c=1\), this bound is one half, so the guarantee prevents certainty but not a high posterior.
Suppressing small classes also removes most homogeneous classes. In Adult, 1.20% of generalized records are in a class where every record has the same occupation; only 0.03% are in such a class of at least 5 records. In the full edition’s synthetic hospital table, distinct 3-diversity removed certain disclosures at little cost. The recursive version required some classes to grow to 641 patients.
crumbs: 10  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 10  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
10.5 Measuring what a release teaches
Compare each posterior with the imputation baseline from Attribute inference and model inversion, the best population-only prediction of a sensitive value. Only improvement over this baseline reflects information about an individual. On the hospital table, age alone predicts each patient’s diagnosis correctly for 53.6% of patients; a 5-anonymous release raises this to 59.3%. Most of the increase reflects the age-diagnosis association that the study reports. The additional 5.7 percentage points are leakage.
crumbs: 10  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 10  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
10.6 Skewness, similarity and t-closeness
l-diversity does not prevent two attacks (Li, Li and Venkatasubramanian, 2007). In a skewness attack, a class that is half HIV-positive is 2-diverse, but if 1% of the full table is HIV-positive, membership in the class raises the posterior fifty-fold. In a similarity attack, a class containing three distinct stomach diseases is 3-diverse but still reveals that the person has a stomach disease.
t-closeness addresses both attacks by requiring the sensitive-value distribution in every class \(E\) to be within distance \(t\) of the full table’s distribution. Let \(P_E(A)\) and \(P(A)\) be the probabilities that a value drawn from the class or full table lies in set \(A\). Under total variation (TV) distance, no such probability—and therefore no posterior belief—changes by more than \(t\): \[\lvert P_E(A) - P(A)\rvert \le t. \tag{10.3}\] The bound controls an absolute difference, not a ratio, so it gives weak protection for rare values. At \(t = 0.15\), a value present in 1% of the table may reach 16% in a class. To address similarity attacks, Li and colleagues used earth mover’s distance, which accounts for distances between values.
t-closeness reduces utility. At \(t = 0.15\), a guess of diagnoses from the hospital release was correct for 22.2% of patients, below the 53.6% accuracy from age alone. The release therefore provided less information than age alone.
crumbs: 10  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 10  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
10.7 The composition attack
Ganta, Kasiviswanathan and Smith (2008) asked what happens when two hospitals each publish a k-anonymous or l-diverse table. A patient treated at both sits in a class \(E_A\) of one release and a class \(E_B\) of the other. The adversary keeps only the diagnoses that appear in both classes, \[\{v : n_{E_A}(v) > 0\} \cap \{v : n_{E_B}(v) > 0\}. \tag{10.4}\] When one candidate is left, the diagnosis is pinned down.
In the full edition’s simulation, two hospitals share 6,649 patients. Together, their two 5-anonymous releases pin down the diagnosis of 9.9% of them, over three times what either pins alone. With distinct 3-diversity, neither release pins anyone, yet together they pin 18.
A single-table definition cannot prevent this attack because neither custodian checks the intersection of two releases. A robust definition must compose across releases, hold under arbitrary adversarial knowledge and bound belief ratios to protect rare values. The definition of differential privacy has these properties; statistical agencies such as the US Census Bureau have adopted it (Reconstruction attacks).
crumbs: 10  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 10  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
10.8 Choosing and running an anonymization
Start with the quasi-identifiers described in Linkage and re-identification; an incomplete list is a common failure. Use k-anonymity to limit linkage. Add distinct l-diversity when a class containing one sensitive value is a disclosure. Use t-closeness when the sensitive attribute is skewed or contains similar values, because it can reduce utility substantially.
Audit the anonymizer’s output in Polars as the excerpt does, or use pycanon, which reports \(k\), \(\ell\) and \(t\) for a pandas table. Pre-release privacy risk assessment uses these results to inform the release decision. Use differential privacy when other releases of the same people exist, the sensitive attribute is rare or the data are sparse. For counts and sums, Release statistics with a library provides an end-to-end workflow.
crumbs: 10  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks

title: 11  Reconstruction attacks
text:
11.1 What it is
A reconstruction attack recovers records from published aggregates because each count is a linear equation in the values of the people counted. Suppose each of \(n\) people has a secret bit, represented in vector \(d\). A subset-sum query counts the people in a set whose bit is 1. The attacker’s \(m\) queries form a binary matrix \(A\), one query per row. The curator publishes the true answers plus an error vector \(e\): \[a = Ad + e. \tag{11.1}\]
Least squares finds real-valued records whose query answers are closest to the published answers, then rounds each value to 0 or 1. Suppose each query includes each person with probability one half and the noise is normal with standard deviation \(\sigma\). Least squares then recovers approximately the following fraction \[\Phi\left(\frac{\sqrt{m - n}}{4\sigma}\right) \tag{11.2}\] of the bits, where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function. The baseline is the majority guess, which assigns the more common value to every person and is correct on half of balanced bits. With several times more queries than people, noise well below \(\sqrt n\) can reveal the data. If the curator answers all \(2^n\) subset sums, only error of order \(n\) prevents reconstruction (Dinur and Nissim 2003).
These results form the Fundamental Law of Information Recovery: too many accurate answers can destroy privacy. Preventing reconstruction alone does not establish privacy. A curator could answer queries using a secret random half of the population, preventing reconstruction while revealing that half exactly. Membership inference also requires far fewer statistics (Lower bounds).

title: 11  Reconstruction attacks
text:
11.2 When you meet it
Every published count, cross-tabulation, dashboard cell and query answer contributes an equation. The Census Bureau attacked its 2010 publications and reconstructed a record for every person. About 46% of records matched a real person exactly on block, sex, age, race and ethnicity. Commercial data confirmed the identities of about 17% of the population, motivating the 2020 Census to adopt differential privacy. Query systems are also vulnerable: because Diffix noise did not increase with query count, Cohen and Nissim (2020) averaged it away.

title: 11  Reconstruction attacks
text:
11.3 How to use it
To audit an aggregate release, count its equations. If the cells or allowed queries outnumber the people, protection depends on the noise. Substitute the noise level and query count into Equation 11.2. If predicted recovery exceeds the majority baseline substantially, run the attack. The snippet uses OpenDP’s Gaussian mechanism and least squares. Because OpenDP noise cannot be seeded, the snippet checks whether the recovered share is within tolerance of the prediction rather than printing that share.
from statistics import NormalDist

import numpy as np
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, m = 500, 2000  # people with a secret bit each, and random subset-sum queries
sigma = 0.25 * np.sqrt(n)  # noise sd added to each answer
secret = rng.integers(0, 2, n)
queries = rng.integers(0, 2, (m, n))
space = dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False)), dp.l2_distance(T=float)
gaussian = dp.m.make_gaussian(*space, scale=sigma)  # OpenDP's Gaussian mechanism on all m answers
answers = np.array(gaussian((queries @ secret).astype(float).tolist()))
estimate = np.linalg.lstsq(queries, answers, rcond=None)[0]  # the textbook attack: least squares
recovered = np.mean(np.clip(estimate, 0, 1).round() == secret)
predicted = NormalDist().cdf(np.sqrt(m - n) / (4 * sigma))
print(f"predicted {predicted:.4f}")  # predicted 0.9584
print(f"recovered within 0.04 of it: {abs(recovered - predicted) < 0.04}")  # recovered within 0.04 of it: True
Query count matters as much as noise. In the full edition’s simulation, noise of twice \(\sqrt n\) and four queries per person recovered 0.5875 of the bits. At the same noise level, Equation 11.2 predicts that 106.1 queries per person recover 90%. Fixed noise therefore becomes insufficient as the query count grows; differential privacy scales noise with the number of answers.
For nonrandom queries, use Dinur and Nissim’s linear-programming decoder, which constrains unknowns to \([0,1]\) with scipy.optimize.linprog. For published tables, express each cell as a constraint on integer unknowns and solve with scipy.optimize.milp. Count the feasible solutions: one solution is enough to reconstruct records. The release fails if either decoder outperforms the majority baseline.

title: 11  Reconstruction attacks
text:
11.4 What goes wrong
Rounding, household swapping and small-cell suppression do not provide noise. Rounding hides nothing because an attacker can round candidate answers in the same way. Swapping leaves most constraints exact. A suppressed cell adds a constraint that its count is below the threshold. Sticky noise—returning the same answer to a repeated query—prevents only duplicate queries, which reconstruction does not require.
Test the union of all releases, not each table separately. Least squares alone is insufficient because adversarially chosen errors affect it more than random noise. Before publication, apply both decoders to the release and record the results in Pre-release privacy risk assessment.

title: 11  Reconstruction attacks
text:
11.5 References

Cohen & Nissim, “Linear Program Reconstruction in Practice” (Journal of Privacy and Confidentiality, 2020): the attack on Diffix.
Garfinkel, Abowd & Martindale, “Understanding Database Reconstruction Attacks on Public Data” (2019): a census block rebuilt with a solver.

Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 12  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
text:
12.1 Why this matters
Before release, assess whether a model or table exposes information about individuals. This chapter evaluates three artefacts: a classifier behind a scoring API, a language model whose weights are shared with a partner, and a census extract. It compares attack results from earlier chapters with fixed thresholds and records the decision.
Specify blocking thresholds before running attacks to prevent choosing thresholds that fit the results. A failed attack establishes only that the tested attack failed, so report its strength as well.
The three scripts below produce the results on this page. The first two run in seconds on public data. The third is from Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA and takes a few minutes on an idle CPU.

title: 12  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
text:
uv run python code/part02-attacks/practitioner_lira.py
uv run python code/part02-attacks/practitioner_table_risk.py
uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/practitioner_lora.py

title: 12  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
section: 12.2 Fix the threat model and the thresholds first
text:
12.2 Fix the threat model and the thresholds first
Complete the worksheet in Threat models and privacy games for each artefact because releases can expose the same data differently. By default, use the person as the privacy unit and assume the adversary sees model scores, as many services return them.
Record the blocking rules in Table 12.1. The membership rule uses two rates: the true positive rate (TPR), the fraction of members flagged, and the false positive rate (FPR), the fraction of non-members incorrectly flagged. At FPR \(10^{-3}\), block release if the lower end of the TPR’s 95% confidence interval exceeds ten times the FPR. Using the lower bound reduces sensitivity to a lucky run. The factor of ten is a policy choice; it allows some advantage over chance.
Several remedies use differential privacy (DP), which bounds information any attack can learn about one person at privacy level \(\varepsilon\) (Part 3). One method is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipped per-record gradients and added noise, called DP-SGD.

A canary within 3 bits of maximum exposure ranks among the 8 most likely possible secrets. The rule uses one-copy canaries because a deduplicated corpus contains each secret once. For a corpus that is not deduplicated, apply it at the largest observed repeat count.
The four middle rows block release when an attack exceeds its baseline. Attribute inference, property inference, reconstruction attacks and gradient inversion specify these baselines. title: 12  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
text:
12.3 Classifier: the free check
First compare model accuracy on training and held-out data. The classifier is logistic regression trained on scikit-learn’s 1,797 handwritten-digit images, as in Membership inference. Across 64 models, the mean gap is 0.0422. The rule “member if correctly classified” therefore has advantage 0.0422, a lower bound on leakage.
This check cannot clear a model because the average gap does not identify exposed records. For example, the loss attack flags records with low loss. At FPR \(10^{-3}\), its TPR is 0.0009, no better than random guessing. Failure of a weak attack provides little evidence. A large gap motivates regularization; a small gap requires further testing.

title: 12  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
text:
12.4 Classifier: LiRA with shadow models
The release decision uses the likelihood ratio attack (LiRA) from Membership inference. It compares each target output with those of shadow models, trained with and without that record. Fix attack strength before testing; a weaker attack may pass a model that a stronger attack blocks. Follow the defaults in Running LiRA on your model: use online LiRA with 64 shadows when feasible. With at most 16 shadows, fit one variance for all records. Include each record in each model by a fair coin, and evaluate each model in turn as the target.
With these defaults, the digits experiment has 57,704 member pairs and 57,304 non-member pairs of a model and an image. Reading the result reports the attack’s hits. Online LiRA has TPR 0.0318 at FPR 0.00099. Its 95% interval has lower bound 0.0303, above the 0.01 threshold, so the classifier fails Table 12.1. Offline LiRA and the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox shadow-model attack would pass it. Base the decision on the strongest affordable attack.
Report the FPR interval as well. At \(10^{-3}\), the non-member pairs yield about 57 false positives, giving an interval from 0.00075 to 0.00129. The script sets and evaluates thresholds on the same pairs, which slightly inflates attack performance. Inspect the ten highest-scoring records; they are often rare or mislabeled.

title: 12  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
section: 12.5 Fine-tuned language model: canaries and extraction
text:
12.5 Fine-tuned language model: canaries and extraction
A language model may reproduce a secret, which membership tests do not measure. This assessment inserts canaries, random secrets with a fixed format, and measures how strongly the trained model memorizes them. Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA runs this audit using the scoring method in Memorization and training-data extraction. It adapts Pythia-14m to 1,024 Tiny Shakespeare sequences, once without privacy and once with DP at \(\varepsilon = 8\) per sequence. Canaries with 1 to 64 copies and uninserted controls receive two scores each. Exposure, in bits, ranks the secret by the sum of its tokens’ log-probabilities, not their mean. Extraction checks whether greedy decoding with the partner’s settings outputs the secret.
Apply the exposure rule to the extrapolated values, not the measured column. Ranking against 2,000 random candidates caps measured exposure at 10.97 bits, while the full secret space allows 16.61 bits. The measured value therefore cannot approach within 3 bits of the maximum. First check the controls: a random rank has mean exposure \(\log_2 e = 1.44\) bits, and the controls’ 1.4 bits are consistent with that value.
The non-private model fails Table 12.1. Its one-copy canaries have exposure of 2.0 bits, below the threshold, but greedy decoding outputs all three 64-copy secrets. Do not share this model. The DP run extracts no canaries, but its most repeated canaries still average about 4 bits, compared with 2.2 bits for its controls. The guarantee applies to one sequence, while a repeated secret spans multiple sequences. Deduplicate the training data before training.

title: 12  Pre-release privacy risk assessment
text:
12.6 Table: re-identification on quasi-identifiers
Quasi-identifiers are the columns an adversary can find elsewhere, such as age, sex and country in a register. Records that agree on all of them form an equivalence class, and a record alone in its class can be linked to a name. The table is Adult, a census extract of 48,842 records, and the agreed quasi-identifiers are six columns, from age to education.
Linkage and re-identification measures uniqueness. The agreed six columns make 14.64% of records unique, so the table fails. Adding hours per week raises this to 36.55%. List every column an adversary might know, and test uncertain columns as well.
Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks generalizes age, country and education, then repeats the check. Generalization reduces the unique share to 0.94%, but the smallest class still has one record, so the table fails. Suppressing classes smaller than 5 removes 3.31% of records. This result applies only to the tested columns: adding raw hours per week makes 10.09% of records unique. In addition, 1.20% of records are in a class with one occupation, a distinct \(\ell\) of 1 (Syntactic anonymity). Such a class reveals occupation even without identifying a record.
These shares measure uniqueness within the sample, matching the prosecutor model in which the adversary knows the target is in the table. Otherwise, estimate population uniqueness (Linkage and re-identification). A table that passes after suppression may still be vulnerable to intersection with another release of the same people (Syntactic anonymity). If the table cannot remain useful after anonymization, release differentially private statistics as in Release statistics with a library. Accurate aggregates are not a safe fallback; they can enable reconstruction (Reconstruction attacks).

Compare each result with its threshold and record it in the release memo (Table 12.2). Include an interval for each estimated rate so that a reviewer can verify the decision.

title: Differential privacy foundations
text:
Part 2 showed that anonymization and access control do not prevent leakage. This part introduces differential privacy (DP), a property of a release process rather than a dataset. If one person’s data changes, the probability of each output changes by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), with additive slack \(\delta\). A DP claim must state \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\) and the unit of privacy, such as a record or a user. This guarantee limits the attacks covered in Part 2.



Table 1: Notation used throughout Part 3.









Symbol
Meaning




\(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\)
Privacy level and slack


\(\Delta_1f\), \(\Delta_2f\)
Sensitivity, the most one record moves the answer


\(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\), \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\)
Laplace noise of scale \(b\), normal noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\)






The workflow has three steps. First, specify the unit of privacy and neighbouring relation (the definition of differential privacy). Next, bound each person’s contribution and calibrate a mechanism to that bound (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). Finally, account for every release; only post-processing is free (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). Release statistics with a library applies these steps to a shop’s invoices using OpenDP.
The full chapters cover common tasks. Selection chooses the best of several options or a private median; Query release publishes multiple counts. Trust models compares settings where no central party can hold raw data, and Private mean estimation calculates the sample size required for a private mean. Four reference pages cover advanced composition and sensitivity, discrete noise mechanisms and accuracy lower bounds.
Part 4 then replaces hand composition with accountants, and Part 5 uses all of it to train models. At the end of the part, you can release a count, sum, median or table with error bars and a privacy guarantee.

title: 13  The definition of differential privacy
text:
13.1 Why this matters
Attacks in Threat models and attacks compare outputs from datasets that differ in one person. Differential privacy (DP) bounds how much the output distribution changes between these datasets, including for tests not yet developed. DP is a property of the algorithm, not the data, so it can be checked before data access.
crumbs: 13  The definition of differential privacy

title: 13  The definition of differential privacy
text:
13.2 Neighbouring datasets
The neighbouring relation defines what it means for datasets to differ in one record. Under add/remove, neighbours differ by one record, so the guarantee hides whether a person is included. Under replace, neighbours have the same size but one record has a different value, so the guarantee hides the record’s value. A replacement can be represented as a removal followed by an addition. Each step costs privacy level \(\varepsilon\) from Section 13.3, so \[\varepsilon\text{-DP under add/remove} \implies 2\varepsilon\text{-DP under replace}. \tag{13.1}\] The reverse fails, because replace never compares datasets of different sizes.
Specify the unit of privacy, the entity represented by one record. At the example level, the unit is one training record or event. At the user level, it is all data from one person. A user with 200 messages is a group of 200 records under example-level DP, with a guarantee that scales to \(200\varepsilon\) (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). Confirm that the stated unit matches the intended protection. The guarantee must hold for every record allowed by the data format, including an age of 900 that could strongly affect an average. Private algorithms therefore clip each input to a fixed range before adding noise.
crumbs: 13  The definition of differential privacy

title: 13  The definition of differential privacy
text:
13.3 The definition
A mechanism \(M\) is a randomized algorithm that takes a dataset and returns an output. Write \(D\) for a dataset and \(D'\) for one of its neighbours. The definition asks that no set of outputs becomes more than a factor \(e^\varepsilon\) more likely when one record changes, up to a small additive slack \(\delta\). Here \(\varepsilon\) is not negative. A mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differentially private if every pair of neighbours and every set \(S\) of outputs satisfy \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\,\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta. \tag{13.2}\] The probabilities come only from the randomness of the mechanism, and the data stay fixed.
When \(\delta = 0\), the guarantee is pure DP; otherwise, it is approximate DP. A deterministic mechanism that returns different answers on neighbouring datasets assigns probability 1 to an answer on one dataset and 0 on the other. No finite factor \(e^\varepsilon\) can bound this change. Rounding, aggregation and suppression of small cells therefore provide no guarantee by themselves.
crumbs: 13  The definition of differential privacy

title: 13  The definition of differential privacy
text:
13.4 The privacy loss and δ
For output \(y\), let \(p_{M(D)}(y)\) be its probability or density when the mechanism runs on \(D\). The privacy loss of \(y\) is the log-likelihood ratio between \(D\) and \(D'\): \[L(y) = \ln\frac{p_{M(D)}(y)}{p_{M(D')}(y)}. \tag{13.3}\] Independent outputs multiply their likelihood ratios, so their privacy losses add. Part 4’s accountants use this property. Pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP holds exactly when every output has privacy loss between \(-\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon\). Laplace noise meets this condition; Gaussian noise has unbounded privacy loss in the tail (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms).
Under approximate DP, \(\delta\) bounds the probability mass where privacy loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\). It counts only the probability on \(D\) above \(e^\varepsilon\) times the corresponding probability on \(D'\). Thus, \(\delta\) is not the probability that privacy loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\); the exact quantity is the hockey-stick divergence (Divergences). Each \(\varepsilon\) has a smallest corresponding \(\delta\), and the function \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the mechanism’s privacy curve. Report the noise parameters with the guarantee so that others can reproduce the curve (Numerical accounting).
crumbs: 13  The definition of differential privacy

title: 13  The definition of differential privacy
text:
13.5 Randomized response
In randomized response, each survey respondent tells the truth with probability \(t\) and otherwise lies. A respondent who answers truthfully on the first coin toss and uses a second toss on tails answers truthfully with probability \(\frac34\). The true answer is then three times as likely as the false answer, giving pure DP at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\). In general, randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\) tells the truth with probability \[t = \frac{e^\varepsilon}{1 + e^\varepsilon}. \tag{13.4}\]
With independent randomization, the guarantee is \(\varepsilon\) per person for any number of respondents. It holds only under replace: under add/remove, the number of reports reveals who participated. Let \(\bar y\) be the fraction of “yes” reports among \(n\) people. Correcting for false answers gives an estimate of the true fraction \(\pi\) and its standard deviation: \[\hat\pi = \frac{\bar y - (1 - t)}{2t - 1}, \qquad \operatorname{sd}(\hat\pi) = \frac{e^{\varepsilon/2}}{(e^\varepsilon - 1)\sqrt n}. \tag{13.5}\] For 1,000 people, the two-coin scheme has a standard deviation of 0.0274. When the true fraction is 0.3, that is about twice the sampling error of 0.0145 that the survey already has. This increase is the cost of the local model, in which no party sees a true answer (Local, shuffle and distributed trust models).
OpenDP builds the mechanism from its truth probability, 0.75 for the two coins, and map turns one changed answer into its \(\varepsilon\), \(\ln 3\). The contrib feature turns on mechanisms that are not yet formally vetted.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
rr = dp.m.make_randomized_response_bool(prob=0.75)
print(f"{rr.map(1):.4f}")  # 1.0986
crumbs: 13  The definition of differential privacy

title: 13  The definition of differential privacy
section: 13.6 What ε means for an attacker
text:
13.6 What ε means for an attacker
A membership attacker observes the output and predicts whether the target was included in the data (Hypothesis testing). Its false positive rate (FPR) is the fraction of non-members it flags; its true positive rate (TPR) is the fraction of members it flags. The flagged outputs form a set bounded by the definition, so under add/remove every attack satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta. \tag{13.6}\]
This form matches Part 2’s evaluation of attacks by TPR at low FPR. For \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), the default in Section 13.7 for 10,000 people, an attack at FPR \(10^{-3}\) has TPR at most \(e \cdot 10^{-3} + 10^{-5} = 0.002728\). As FPR approaches 0, the bound depends almost entirely on \(\delta\).
Rearranging the cap gives a lower bound on \(\varepsilon\) from a measured attack: \[\varepsilon \ge \ln\frac{\mathrm{TPR} - \delta}{\mathrm{FPR}}. \tag{13.7}\] Suppose a model is claimed to be \((2, 10^{-5})\)-DP, and an attack has TPR 0.05 at FPR 0.001. If these rates were exact, then \(\varepsilon\) would be at least \(\ln 50 = 3.91\), contradicting the claim. A real audit uses confidence bounds on the rates and a canary, a record designed to be easy to detect (Auditing).
Two summaries aid interpretation. The membership advantage is TPR minus FPR, the attack’s improvement over random guessing. Under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, it is at most \[\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} \le \frac{e^\varepsilon - 1 + 2\delta}{e^\varepsilon + 1}. \tag{13.8}\]
The second summary bounds posterior belief. Under pure DP, one output can multiply the adversary’s odds between two neighbouring datasets by at most \(e^\varepsilon\). A prior probability \(p\) that the data are \(D\) can therefore rise at most to \[\Pr[D \mid y] \le \frac{e^\varepsilon p}{e^\varepsilon p + 1 - p}. \tag{13.9}\] Table 13.1 turns a claimed \(\varepsilon\) into both numbers.

Above 10, the bounds provide little protection, so include an audit (Choosing ε). For statistics, specify acceptable error and solve for \(\varepsilon\) (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). The table assumes pure DP; for an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantee, report both the advantage bound and TPR cap, which include \(\delta\).
crumbs: 13  The definition of differential privacy

title: 13  The definition of differential privacy
text:
13.7 How small δ must be
A small \(\delta\) has little effect on the advantage bound, but an average can hide severe harm to a few people. Consider a mechanism that independently publishes each record in full with probability \(\delta\). It is \((0, \delta)\)-DP under add/remove because a record changes the output only when its own random draw publishes it. Across \(n\) records, the probability of publishing at least one is \[1 - (1 - \delta)^n \approx 1 - e^{-n\delta}. \tag{13.10}\] With 10,000 records and \(\delta = 1/n\), that is \(1 - e^{-1} = 0.6321\).
Treat \(\delta\) as a per-person budget for catastrophic failures such as full record publication. Following Ponomareva et al. (2023), this book’s default keeps \(n\delta\), the expected number of people exposed this way, well below 1. Let \(n\) count people, not records, and choose \[\delta \le \frac{1}{n^{1.1}}, \tag{13.11}\] rounded down to a power of ten. For 10,000 people, the rule gives \(10^{-5}\). The publishing mechanism then has \(n\delta = 0.1\), and it exposes someone with probability only 0.0952.
crumbs: 13  The definition of differential privacy

title: 13  The definition of differential privacy
section: 13.8 What differential privacy does not protect
text:
13.8 What differential privacy does not protect
DP compares datasets with and without a record, so it does not prevent conclusions that hold in both datasets. A study that never used Alice’s record may still show that smokers have a high cancer rate. This can affect beliefs about Alice, but the study is 0-DP with respect to her. A harm violates DP only if the inference would materially change without her record. Correlated records create a second limitation: a household of five whose members’ records always change together is a group of five unless the household is the privacy unit. Implementation errors create a third limitation (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms).
crumbs: 13  The definition of differential privacy

title: 13  The definition of differential privacy
text:
13.9 Writing the guarantee down
A reviewer can check only a fully specified claim. State the privacy unit and neighbouring relation, and report \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\) for the whole release, not per query. Also name the mechanism, library version, trust model and data treated as public; DP does not protect public data. This example uses the central model, in which a trusted curator holds the raw data and adds noise:

This release satisfies \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP for adding or removing one customer and all their invoice lines, at most 100 per customer, under the central model, with Gaussian noise from OpenDP 0.16.0. The market list was fixed in advance.

Release statistics with a library and Release and governance print such statements from the code that made the release.

title: 14  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
14.1 Why this matters
A private mechanism is one component of a system. Its output may be rounded or used to fit a model; one person may contribute multiple records; and an analyst may ask multiple questions. Three properties of differential privacy (DP) address these cases: post-processing, group privacy and composition. They allow separate analysis of each mechanism and tracking of the total privacy budget.
crumbs: 14  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 14  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
14.2 Post-processing
Let \(M\) be a mechanism that is DP with privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and slack \(\delta\). Apply a function \(f\) to its output. The function may use additional randomness but must not access the data. The processed release remains equally private: \[f(M(D)) \text{ is } (\varepsilon, \delta)\text{-DP}. \tag{14.1}\]
Rounding a noisy count, clamping it at zero or reconciling noisy subtotals with their total therefore costs no additional privacy. A system can add noise to counts or gradients, then treat subsequent computations as post-processing. The rule also applies to attacks: membership inference is a function of the output, so the definition’s limit on attack success applies to future attacks.
The condition is that \(f\) never accesses the data. For example, selecting the noisy top category and then reporting its exact count violates post-processing because the second step is a new, non-private mechanism.
crumbs: 14  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 14  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
14.3 Group privacy
The definition protects one record, but an online-shop customer may have dozens of invoice lines. For a person with \(k\) records, the guarantee must cover datasets that differ in \(k\) records. Transforming one dataset into the other requires \(k\) single-record changes, each costing \(\varepsilon\). Under pure DP, where \(\delta = 0\), per-record \(\varepsilon\)-DP therefore becomes group-level \(k\varepsilon\)-DP. Under approximate DP, the slack can grow faster than \(k\). For a group of \(k\) records, an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism is \[\Big(k\varepsilon,\ \delta_k\Big)\text{-DP}, \qquad \delta_k = \delta\,\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1} \le k\,e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\delta. \tag{14.2}\]
The right-hand form is simpler but looser. At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) per record, a person with 10 records has slack \(2.272\times10^{-3}\). This exceeds the book’s default, which sets \(\delta\) far below one divided by the number of people (How small δ must be).
OpenDP calculates group guarantees from the mechanism itself. A measurement’s map(d_in=k) gives its guarantee when neighbouring datasets differ in \(k\) records, here for a Laplace count and a Gaussian count.
count = dp.t.make_count(dp.vector_domain(dp.atom_domain(T=int)), dp.symmetric_distance())
laplace = count >> dp.m.then_laplace(scale=2.0)  # epsilon = 0.5 per record
print(f"Laplace count: epsilon {laplace.map(d_in=1):.1f} per record, {laplace.map(d_in=10):.1f} for 10")

def gaussian(scale: float) -> dp.Measurement:  # a Gaussian count, as a privacy curve
    return dp.c.make_zCDP_to_approxDP(count >> dp.m.then_gaussian(scale=scale))

def at_1e5(scale: float) -> dp.Measurement:
    return dp.c.make_fix_delta(gaussian(scale), delta=1e-5)

scale = dp.binary_search_param(at_1e5, d_in=1, d_out=(0.5, 1e-5))  # (0.5, 1e-5) per record
curve = gaussian(scale).map(d_in=10)  # the privacy curve for a group of 10 records
print(f"Gaussian count, group of 10: epsilon {curve.epsilon(1e-5):.2f} at delta 1e-5")
# delta_k is the slack that the group-privacy formula gives the group
print(f"Gaussian count, group of 10: epsilon {curve.epsilon(delta_k):.2f} at delta {delta_k:.3e}")
Laplace count: epsilon 0.5 per record, 5.0 for 10
Gaussian count, group of 10: epsilon 6.43 at delta 1e-5
Gaussian count, group of 10: epsilon 4.57 at delta 2.272e-03
For the Laplace count, map(d_in=10) gives \(k\varepsilon = 5.0\), matching the formula. The Gaussian count, calibrated to \((0.5, 10^{-5})\) per record, gives a tighter group bound because OpenDP uses the mechanism’s full privacy curve. At the formula’s slack of \(2.272\times10^{-3}\), the group has \(\varepsilon = 4.57\), below the formula’s 5.0. Use the library’s group mapping when available; otherwise use the formula.
Prefer the person as the privacy unit, so neighbouring datasets differ in all of one person’s records. Bound each person’s contribution before adding noise, as in Release statistics with a library. Use group privacy when a person-level guarantee is unavailable or when records from different people reveal information about each other, such as shared household address and income.
crumbs: 14  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 14  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
14.4 Sequential composition
Suppose an analyst asks several queries of the same data, each with fresh noise, and an adversary sees all answers. For \(k\) mechanisms with budgets \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\), the release of all outputs is \[\Big(\sum_{i=1}^k\varepsilon_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\delta_i\Big)\text{-DP}. \tag{14.3}\] This is basic composition. It needs every mechanism to draw fresh noise and to use the same neighbouring relation, add/remove or replace.
The rule also covers adaptive composition, where each query depends on earlier answers, provided every query’s budget is fixed in advance. If the budget depends on the answers—for example, continuing until an estimate meets a target—a privacy filter must determine when to stop (Adaptive composition).
For many releases, basic composition can be loose. Ten Gaussian counts at \((0.5, 10^{-5})\) each cost \((5, 10^{-4})\) under basic composition, but their exact \(\varepsilon\) at that slack is 1.504. For multiple releases, use an accountant that composes the mechanisms themselves (Advanced and optimal composition, Part 4).
crumbs: 14  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 14  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
14.5 Parallel composition
Statistics by region use disjoint data subsets. If each person has one record, each record belongs to one region, so each region can use the full budget. The partition must follow a public rule fixed in advance that assigns every possible record to exactly one part. Run a mechanism \(M_i\) with independent noise on each part. If each \(M_i\) is \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\)-DP under add/remove, the full release is \[\big(\max_i\varepsilon_i,\ \max_i\delta_i\big)\text{-DP under add/remove}. \tag{14.4}\]
A histogram with Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) on each bin is therefore \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any number of bins. Under replace, a record can move between two bins, doubling the cost to \(2\varepsilon\). The rule also fails when a person contributes records to multiple bins. Charge each bin as a separate query or bound the number of bins each person can affect.
The fixed-partition condition is easy to violate. A split into “the top 10% of earners and the rest” changes its boundary when one high earner is added, so both parts change. A partition based on observed keys also fails: a key present in only one person’s record identifies that person. Use fixed bins or a public key list. If the keys are not public, release only keys whose noisy counts exceed a threshold, using partition selection (Release statistics with a library).
crumbs: 14  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 14  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
14.6 Keeping a budget
Set a total budget before the first release and charge every release against it. In diffprivlib, a BudgetAccountant tracks the total, and each function charges its \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\). A call that would exceed the total raises BudgetError and returns no answer. The script practitioner_adult_statistics.py uses it on Adult, a dataset with 48,842 people and one row per person. The default slack is \(10^{-6}\). The script spends the budget on two queries, then attempts a third count.
age = adult["age"].to_numpy()
acc = BudgetAccountant(epsilon=1.0, delta=1e-6)  # the total, fixed in advance
mean_age = tools.mean(age, epsilon=0.5, bounds=(17, 90), accountant=acc, random_state=seed)
over_50 = tools.count_nonzero(age > 50, epsilon=0.5, accountant=acc, random_state=seed)
print(f"private mean age: {mean_age:.2f}  private count over 50: {over_50:,}")
print(f"spent: {acc.total()}")
try:
    tools.count_nonzero(age > 60, epsilon=0.1, accountant=acc, random_state=seed)
except BudgetError as err:
    print(f"refused: {err}")
Run it with uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/practitioner_adult_statistics.py. With random_state=0 it prints the following.
private mean age: 38.64  private count over 50: 9,813
spent: (epsilon=1.0, delta=0.0)
refused: Privacy spend of (0.1,0) not permissible; will exceed remaining privacy budget. Use BudgetAccountant.remaining() to check remaining budget.
The true values are 38.64 and 9,808. Laplace noise uses no \(\delta\), leaving \(10^{-6}\) available for a Gaussian query. The ledger has two limitations. First, it applies basic composition to each call, overcharging calls on disjoint data subsets. Second, it trusts each call’s guarantee. diffprivlib’s mean divides by the exact row count, which is public only when neighbouring datasets have equal size. The ledger therefore holds only under replace neighbours.
Most composition failures violate a condition of one of these properties, often invalidating the guarantee (Table 14.1).

Shared noise violates the fresh-randomness condition. Suppose a release gives the number of smokers and the number of smokers aged 40 or more, using the same Laplace draw of scale 1 for both. Each release alone is 1-DP, but subtracting them cancels the noise and reveals the exact number of smokers under 40. The pair is not DP. Code can reuse noise through a shared random seed, cached value or shard-level draw. A fixed seed such as random_state=0 makes examples reproducible, but in production it makes the noise known and removable. Releasing the same noisy answer to an identical query is safe because it is post-processing of one release.

title: 15  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
15.1 Why this matters
Suppose a hospital wants to publish the number of patients with diabetes under differential privacy (DP). Most private releases use one of the two mechanisms in this chapter. Private training also uses them to add noise to gradients. Each mechanism computes a query \(f\) on dataset \(D\), adds fresh noise \(Z\) and publishes \[M(D) = f(D) + Z. \tag{15.1}\] Three choices determine the mechanism. Calibrate noise to the query’s sensitivity, the largest change one record can cause. Choose Laplace noise for pure DP or Gaussian noise with slack \(\delta\). Then apply a calibration formula to obtain the noise required for target \(\varepsilon\). The formulas follow from privacy loss in the definition of differential privacy.
crumbs: 15  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 15  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
15.2 Sensitivity
Sensitivity measures the largest change one record can cause. For a vector query with \(d\) outputs, such as a histogram, the change needs a norm. Laplace noise uses the \(\ell_1\) norm, the sum of absolute changes; Gaussian noise uses the \(\ell_2\) norm, the square root of the sum of squared changes. For neighbouring datasets \(D \sim D'\), the query’s \(\ell_p\) sensitivity is the largest change between their answers: \[\Delta_pf = \max_{D \sim D'}\big\|f(D) - f(D')\big\|_p, \qquad p \in \{1, 2\}. \tag{15.2}\] The two are equal when one record moves a single coordinate. When it moves all \(d\) of them, \(\Delta_1f\) can be \(\sqrt d\) times \(\Delta_2f\).
The sensitivity also depends on the neighbouring relation. Under add/remove, one dataset has one record more than the other. Under replace, one record changes into another, so the size \(n\) is public. With \(B\) for the largest value of a record after clipping, Table 15.1 gives the standard queries.

Calculate sensitivity from the domain before examining the data. A data-dependent bound, such as the observed maximum, can leak information (Beyond global sensitivity). Unbounded data have infinite sensitivity, so clip each value to a fixed range. If ages are clipped at 100, the mean age of 1,000 patients has sensitivity \(B/n = 0.1\) under replace.
crumbs: 15  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 15  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
15.3 The Laplace mechanism
The Laplace mechanism adds independent noise from the Laplace distribution, a two-sided exponential distribution centred at 0, to each coordinate. Write \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) for Laplace noise with scale \(b\). For an \(\varepsilon\)-DP guarantee, set the scale to sensitivity divided by \(\varepsilon\): \[b = \frac{\Delta_1f}{\varepsilon}. \tag{15.3}\]
The mechanism’s error is its noise. Each coordinate’s mean absolute error is \(b\), and its probability of exceeding distance \(t\) is \(e^{-t/b}\). To keep the failure probability across all \(d\) coordinates at most \(\beta\), allocate \(\beta/d\) to each coordinate. The simultaneous error bound is \[\Pr\Big[\max_i|Z_i| > b\ln\frac d\beta\Big] \le \beta. \tag{15.4}\] Publish this width with the release. In reverse, the width gives an error budget, because for a single number you can fix a target width \(t\) and solve for the privacy level, \[\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta_1f\,\ln(1/\beta)}{t}. \tag{15.5}\] A count required to be within 10 of its true value with probability 0.95 needs \(\varepsilon = \ln(20)/10 = 0.2996\). For \(d\) outputs, use failure probability \(\beta/d\) for each and add their privacy levels by composition.
At the hospital, 1,234 of the 10,000 patients have diabetes. A count has sensitivity 1 under add/remove, so at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) the noise is \(\mathrm{Lap}(10)\). Its 95% error bar is \(10\ln 20 = 29.96\), or 2.43% of the count.
The noise scale does not depend on dataset size, so relative error for a count of size \(n\) is about \(1/(n\varepsilon)\). Sensitivity must include every output a record can change. If one record affects all 10 released counts, calibrating each count separately makes the release \(10\varepsilon\)-DP, not \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
crumbs: 15  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 15  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
15.4 The Gaussian mechanism
The Gaussian mechanism adds independent normal noise with mean 0 and standard deviation \(\sigma\) to each coordinate. Its privacy loss is unbounded in the tail, so its guarantee requires \(\delta\). Gaussian noise uses \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, which may be much smaller than \(\ell_1\) sensitivity. Let \(\mu = \Delta_2f/\sigma\) be the neighbour-output distance in noise standard deviations, and let \(\Phi\) be the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF). The mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when \(\delta\) is at least \[\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big). \tag{15.6}\]
Calibrate the mechanism using this formula. As \(\mu\) increases, exact \(\delta\) increases from 0 to 1, so a unique value \(\mu^*\) gives the target. The minimum noise scale is \[\sigma^* = \frac{\Delta_2f}{\mu^*}, \qquad \text{where } \delta_{\mu^*}(\varepsilon) = \delta, \tag{15.7}\] and libraries solve for \(\mu^*\) (Section 15.7). For 10,000 patients, the book’s default slack is \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\), this analytic calibration then gives \(\sigma^* = 3.7306\,\Delta_2f\).
Many papers and libraries still use the classic calibration of Dwork and Roth (2014), proved only for \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\) between 0 and 1: \[\sigma = \frac{\Delta_2f\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}. \tag{15.8}\] At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), it gives \(4.8448\,\Delta_2f\), 30% more noise than the analytic \(3.7306\,\Delta_2f\). Above \(\varepsilon = 8.42\), it gives insufficient noise for its claimed guarantee. Use analytic calibration instead.
A Gaussian mechanism has a privacy curve, with a value of \(\delta\) for each \(\varepsilon\). Accountants in Part 4 compose these curves. Report \(\sigma/\Delta_2f\) and the selected \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) for each Gaussian release.
At the hospital, Gaussian noise for the diabetes count at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) gives a 95% error bar of 60.27, which is 1.96 standard deviations. Laplace noise gave 29.96 with no \(\delta\), so for a single count Laplace noise is better in error and in guarantee.
crumbs: 15  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 15  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
15.5 Laplace or Gaussian?
Choose a mechanism based on how one record’s change is distributed across coordinates. Compare the root-mean-square error (RMSE) per released value at the same \(\varepsilon\). Laplace noise with scale \(b = \Delta_1f/\varepsilon\) has standard deviation \(\sqrt2\,b\). Let \(\sigma_1\) be the analytic Gaussian noise scale at unit \(\ell_2\) sensitivity. The per-coordinate errors are \[\text{Laplace: } \frac{\sqrt2\,\Delta_1f}{\varepsilon}, \qquad \text{Gaussian: } \Delta_2f\,\sigma_1. \tag{15.9}\]
In a sparse query, such as a histogram under add/remove, one record moves one coordinate, so the two sensitivities are equal. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and the default \(\delta\), \(\sigma_1 = 3.7306\). So Laplace noise is better at every \(d\), because \(\sqrt2 = 1.4142\) is smaller. In a dense query, such as the threshold counts, one record moves every coordinate. Then the Laplace error grows like \(d\) and the Gaussian error only like \(\sqrt d\). So Laplace noise is more accurate only while \[d < \frac{(\varepsilon\sigma_1)^2}2, \tag{15.10}\] so with \(\sigma_1 = 3.7306\), Gaussian noise is better for 7 or more threshold counts.
Gaussian noise is also better for many releases, because several Gaussian releases compose exactly into one Gaussian mechanism. Private training has dense queries and many releases, because one record’s gradient moves every coordinate of a model at every step. So it clips the \(\ell_2\) norm of each gradient and calibrates Gaussian noise to that clip.
crumbs: 15  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 15  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
15.6 Calibrating a release
Every noisy release has five steps.

Fix the neighbouring relation and the unit of privacy, usually one person under add/remove.
Clip every value to a range fixed in advance. Then take the sensitivity from Table 15.1, or calculate it from the worst record.
Use Laplace noise for one number or a sparse vector, and Gaussian noise for a dense vector.
Set the scale with Equation 15.3 or Equation 15.6. Charge it to your budget (Post-processing, group privacy and composition).
Draw the noise with a library that experts have checked. Publish the error bar and the noise parameters with the result.

A mean under add/remove has no simple sensitivity because its denominator changes. Release a noisy sum and a noisy count, splitting the budget between them, then divide; this division is post-processing. To obtain a 95% interval for the mean, use 97.5% intervals for both quantities. The mean is at least the sum’s lower bound divided by the count’s upper bound, and at most the sum’s upper bound divided by the count’s lower bound when both lower bounds are positive.
OpenDP’s .dp.mean uses the same split, and summarize(alpha=0.025) reports both 97.5% intervals. If the clipping range is unknown, Private mean estimation describes how to estimate it privately. Use numpy.random.laplace only for prototypes: floating-point samplers can leak through low-order output bits (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms). For a complete release with clipping, grouping and one budget, see Release statistics with a library.
crumbs: 15  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms

title: 15  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
15.7 Code
The snippet checks the hospital’s values and analytic \(\sigma^*\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\). In OpenDP, a mechanism’s map converts sensitivity to privacy cost. Accuracy helpers convert between noise scale and a 95% error bound. For a count with sensitivity 1, the reciprocal of the Laplace scale is the privacy level. IBM’s diffprivlib calibrates the analytic Gaussian mechanism.
import math

import opendp.prelude as dp
from diffprivlib.mechanisms import GaussianAnalytic

dp.enable_features("contrib")
laplace = dp.m.make_laplace(dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False), dp.absolute_distance(T=float), scale=10.0)
print(laplace.map(1.0))  # 0.1
print(f"{dp.laplacian_scale_to_accuracy(10.0, alpha=0.05):.2f}")  # 29.96
print(f"{1 / dp.accuracy_to_laplacian_scale(10.0, alpha=0.05):.4f}")  # 0.2996
gauss = GaussianAnalytic(epsilon=1.0, delta=1e-5, sensitivity=1.0)
print(f"{math.sqrt(gauss.variance(0.0)):.4f}")  # 3.7306
Apply the mechanism to the value to add noise, as in laplace(1234.0).

title: 16  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
16.1 What it is
A dashboard may refresh a hundred counts, and a training run may take thousands of noisy steps. Both require one differential privacy (DP) guarantee for the full release. Each step has privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and slack \(\delta\) (The definition of differential privacy). Basic composition adds these values, so \(k\) steps cost \(k\varepsilon\) and \(k\delta\) (Post-processing, group privacy and composition).
This total is valid but can be loose. Each step’s privacy loss depends on the noise and may be negative, so the sum rarely reaches the worst-case value \(k\varepsilon\).
Advanced composition (Dwork, Rothblum & Vadhan 2010) accounts for these cancellations. With an additional slack \(\delta'\) for the run, the steps together satisfy \((\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}, k\delta + \delta')\)-DP, with \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}} = \varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2). \tag{16.1}\] The first term is the spread of total privacy loss, which grows like \(\sqrt k\). The second term is its mean, or drift.
Optimal composition (Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath 2015) gives the tightest total guarantee when each step is known only by its pair \((\varepsilon,\delta)\). For 100 counts on 10,000 people, each with \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) and no slack, basic composition gives total \(\varepsilon=10\). Advanced and optimal composition use slack \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\), the book’s default for 10,000 people, and give totals 5.30 and 4.31.

title: 16  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
16.2 When you meet it
These rules appear in papers, privacy reviews and libraries that report one total \(\varepsilon\) for multiple steps (Table 16.1).

Optimal composition is tight only when each step is represented by one privacy pair. A mechanism’s full privacy curve contains a \(\delta\) for each \(\varepsilon\), and reducing it to one pair discards information. For example, 1,000 Gaussian steps with noise standard deviation 20 on a query of sensitivity 1 have an exact curve of \((7.51, 10^{-5})\)-DP. Composing the best single pair for each step gives 62.7, about eight times larger. When the mechanism is known, compose its curve with an accountant (Privacy accounting).

title: 16  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
16.3 How to use it
To allocate total budget \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}\) across \(k\) steps, invert advanced composition. When \(\varepsilon\sqrt k\) is small, the drift term in Equation 16.1 is negligible, so each step can use approximately \[\varepsilon \approx \frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}}{\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}}. \tag{16.2}\] When \(\varepsilon\sqrt k\) approaches 1, the drift is no longer negligible and this approximation overestimates the per-step budget.
For a known mechanism, report the accountant’s result at the run’s total \(\delta\). Otherwise, report optimal composition. The snippet allocates a total budget of \((1, 10^{-5})\) across 100 counts, placing all slack in \(\delta'\). It then accounts for 1,000 Gaussian steps with Google’s dp_accounting using privacy loss distribution (PLD) and Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountants.
import math

import dp_accounting

print(f"{1.0 / math.sqrt(2 * 100 * math.log(1e5)):.4f}")  # 0.0208
step = dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(noise_multiplier=20.0)
run = dp_accounting.SelfComposedDpEvent(step, 1000)
pld = dp_accounting.pld.PLDAccountant()
pld.compose(run)
print(f"{pld.get_epsilon(target_delta=1e-5):.2f}")  # 7.51
rdp = dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant()
rdp.compose(run)
print(f"{rdp.get_epsilon(target_delta=1e-5):.2f}")  # 8.08
Each count receives 0.0208, twice the \(1/100\) under basic composition. The PLD accountant returns 7.51; the RDP accountant returns the valid but larger value 8.08 (Choosing an accountant).

title: 16  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
16.4 What goes wrong
For a small number of steps, advanced composition may give a larger bound than basic composition; use the smaller bound. Every rule also composes the per-step slacks, so include each \(\delta\).
These rules allow each query to depend on earlier answers, provided each query’s budget is fixed before the run. If budgets depend on the answers, use a privacy filter (Adaptive composition). Stopping rules also matter. A rule based only on noisy answers is post-processing, so the run costs no more than its planned length. A rule that stops when a true group count exceeds a threshold reveals information through the run length. In that case, each answer may be \(\varepsilon\)-DP while the full run has no finite DP guarantee.
In a review, a total below the optimal-composition bound is a warning unless an accountant derived it from the mechanism’s full privacy curve.
Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 17  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
17.1 Why this matters
Many analyses select an item, such as the best model on a validation set, a median or the first statistic above a threshold. Publishing every candidate score with Laplace noise spends budget on every score. The mechanisms in this chapter release the selected position, not the scores. Under differential privacy (DP), selecting one item costs one query regardless of the number of candidates; the candidate count affects accuracy through its logarithm.
crumbs: 17  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
