title: 17  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
17.3 The exponential mechanism
Let \(\mathcal R\) be a fixed candidate set. Each candidate \(r\) has a score \(u(D,r)\) on dataset \(D\), such as the number of validation records a model classifies correctly. The exponential mechanism of McSherry and Talwar (2007) samples candidates with probability proportional to an exponential of their scores. With privacy budget \(\varepsilon\), it outputs candidate \(r\) with probability \[\Pr[M_E(D) = r] = \frac{\exp\big(\varepsilon\,u(D, r)/(2\Delta u)\big)}{\sum_s\exp\big(\varepsilon\,u(D, s)/(2\Delta u)\big)}. \tag{17.1}\] It is \(\varepsilon\)-DP because one record changes each weight, and also their sum, by at most a factor \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\), which makes \(e^\varepsilon\) for their ratio.
Two conditions determine whether the mechanism is valid. First, fix the candidate list independently of the private data; a data-derived list may itself reveal records, such as a word used by one person. Second, remove the factor 2 in the exponent only for monotone scores, where one record changes all scores in the same direction. Counts under add/remove are monotone. A histogram under replace is not: replacing a record lowers one count and raises another, doubling the privacy cost if the factor 2 is omitted.
crumbs: 17  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 17  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
section: 17.4 Accuracy, and the cost of many candidates
text:
17.4 Accuracy, and the cost of many candidates
The number of candidates \(|\mathcal R|\) does not affect privacy but can reduce accuracy by increasing the number of low-scoring choices. Define the gap as the best score minus the selected score. Its expected value is at most \[\frac{2\Delta u}{\varepsilon}(\ln|\mathcal R| + 1), \tag{17.2}\] so doubling the candidate count adds only \(\ln 2\) to the bracket.
Suppose 50 models are evaluated on a private validation set of 1,000 records. Model \(r\), numbered from 1, correctly classifies \(900-r\) records, so model 1 is best. A single record changes this count by at most 1, giving \(\Delta u = 1\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\), the mechanism selects the best model 39% of the time but loses only 1.54 correct predictions on average, or 0.15% accuracy, because errors are mostly near-ties. Hyperparameter tuning uses this method.
crumbs: 17  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 17  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
section: 17.5 A private quantile or clipping norm
text:
17.5 A private quantile or clipping norm
A median or clipping norm computed directly from private data can leak information. Use the exponential mechanism and fix the candidate range before accessing the data, then clip records to that range. Score each candidate by how closely the fraction of records below it matches the target quantile; for the median, the target is one half. Adding or removing one record changes each score by at most 1. Scores are constant between adjacent sorted records, so the mechanism selects one such interval, called a piece, and returns a uniform point within it. Longer pieces near the target quantile receive higher probability.
diffprivlib’s tools.quantile and tools.median accept epsilon and a bounds range. OpenDP’s .dp.quantile and .dp.median operate on Polars data frames and select from a finite candidate list. The script practitioner_adult_statistics.py estimates the median age in Adult, a census dataset with 48,842 people and one row per person, at \(\varepsilon = 1\). The survey documentation supplies the range 17 to 90.
age = adult["age"].to_numpy()
private = tools.median(age, epsilon=1.0, bounds=(17, 90), random_state=seed)
print(f"true median age: {np.median(age):.1f}  diffprivlib median: {private:.2f}")
With random_state=0, it prints a true median of 37.0 and a private median of 37.72. Ages are integers, so points between 37 and 38 have the same score; the mechanism samples a point from that piece. OpenDP requires a public upper bound on row count, specified by a Margin. Choose a bound from public information that is at least the true row count; a larger bound has little cost.
context = dp.Context.compositor(
    data=adult.lazy(),
    privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=1),  # one row per person
    privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=1.0),
    split_evenly_over=1,
    margins=[dp.polars.Margin(max_length=100_000)],  # a public bound on the number of rows
)
age_col: Any = pl.col("age")  # OpenDP adds .dp to Polars expressions when it is imported
query = context.query().select(age_col.dp.median(candidates=list(range(17, 91))))
print(query.summarize(alpha=0.05))
released = query.release().collect()  # changes on every run: OpenDP's noise has no seed
The summary reports ExponentialMin with scale 2.0 because OpenDP 0.16 adds exponential noise to each candidate score and selects the best. This is permute-and-flip (McKenna & Sheldon 2020), which has the exponential mechanism’s guarantee and no larger expected error. Accuracy is null because OpenDP does not provide a quantile error bar. The noise is unseeded, so the released value changes each time uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/practitioner_adult_statistics.py runs.
The error bound concerns rank, not value. With probability \(1 - \beta\), the exponential-mechanism gap is at most \((2\Delta u/\varepsilon)(\ln|\mathcal R| + \ln(1/\beta))\), the tail bound corresponding to Equation 17.2. For a median with \(\Delta u = 1\), the gap is the number of records between the output and the middle rank. At \(\beta = 0.05\), this gives a 95% rank interval. A value interval requires the number of records near the median, which the release does not reveal. A dashboard needing value accuracy can spend budget on noisy counts below selected candidates. A wide range adds little cost because the gap depends on the logarithm of the candidate count.
Two limitations matter in practice. If data are sparse near the quantile, the best piece is long, so a small rank error may produce a large value error. The range and candidates must also be independent of private data. Setting the upper bound to the observed maximum reintroduces leakage. diffprivlib raises a PrivacyLeakWarning when bounds is omitted (Sensitivity).
crumbs: 17  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 17  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
17.6 Report-noisy-max and Gumbel noise
Report-noisy-max adds independent Laplace noise to the score of each candidate and outputs the candidate with the largest noisy score. It is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any number of candidates when the noise has scale \(2\Delta u/\varepsilon\), or \(\Delta u/\varepsilon\) when one record pushes all scores the same way. Release only the index of the winner, and pay for a fresh noisy answer if you need its score.
Gumbel noise of scale \(2\Delta u/\varepsilon\) in place of the Laplace noise gives exactly the exponential mechanism. Libraries sample it with this Gumbel-max trick, because the exponential of a score in the thousands overflows, but noisy scores do not. The \(c\) largest scores with Gumbel noise give the top \(c\) at once (Durfee & Rogers 2019).
crumbs: 17  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

title: 17  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
17.7 The sparse vector technique
Sometimes queries come one at a time, and you want the first one that is high enough. The sparse vector technique (Dwork et al. 2009) compares each query with one noisy threshold and pays only for the query that fires. Its basic form, AboveThreshold, takes a threshold \(\tau\) and a stream of queries \(f\), all with the same sensitivity \(\Delta f\). It divides the budget into \(\varepsilon_1\) for the threshold and \(\varepsilon_2\) for the queries.

Draw one threshold noise, written \(\nu\), from \(\mathrm{Lap}(\Delta f/\varepsilon_1)\) for the whole run.
For each query, draw a fresh noise from \(\mathrm{Lap}(2\Delta f/\varepsilon_2)\) and add it to the answer of the query. If the result is at least \(\tau + \nu\), output “above” and stop. If not, output “below” and continue.

AboveThreshold is \((\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2)\)-DP for any number of “below” answers, even when each query is chosen after the earlier answers. All the “below” answers together pay \(\varepsilon_1\), through the one threshold noise, and the single “above” pays \(\varepsilon_2\).
But the accuracy depends on the stream length \(k\), which you must fix before the run. Write \(\beta\) for the chance that the accuracy guarantee fails. With an equal split, \(\varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_2 = \varepsilon/2\), every query gets the correct answer unless its true value is within a margin \[\alpha = \frac{8\Delta f\big(\ln k + \ln(2/\beta)\big)}{\varepsilon} \tag{17.3}\] of the threshold. Monitor 1,000 counts, each with \(\Delta f = 1\), against a threshold of 500 at \(\varepsilon = 1\). At \(\beta = 0.05\), the margin is 84.77. So with probability 0.95, only a count that near the threshold can get the wrong answer.
To find the first \(c\) queries above the threshold, start AboveThreshold again after each “above”, with fresh threshold noise and \(\varepsilon/c\) per run. Stop after the \(c\)-th. The margin then grows with \(c\), so ask for as few alarms as you can. Lyu, Su and Li keep one threshold for all \(c\) alarms and multiply the query noise by \(c\).
crumbs: 17  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector

text:
17.8 When the sparse vector technique goes wrong
Several published variants do not have the privacy they claim (Table 17.2).



Table 17.2: Variants of the sparse vector technique and their actual privacy, from Lyu, Su & Li (2017).










Variant (as numbered by Lyu, Su & Li)
What it changes
Actual privacy




Algorithm 3
Outputs the noisy value of each “above”
\(\infty\)


Algorithm 4
Query noise does not grow with \(c\)
\(\frac{1 + 6c}{4}\varepsilon\)


Algorithm 5
No noise on the queries
\(\infty\)


Algorithm 6
Never halts
\(\infty\)






The variant that never stops is the one to remember. It adds exactly as much noise per query as AboveThreshold, so a reviewer who checks noise scales does not find it. But at \(\varepsilon = 1\), its privacy loss gets to 18.1246 on 80 queries.
So review the accounting, not only the noise. Draw one threshold noise per run. If you draw the threshold again for each query, every “below” answer costs budget that nobody counted. Draw fresh noise for every query, because one noise draw for all of them is the same as Algorithm 5. Stop after the permitted number of “above” answers. Never publish the noisy values that you compared.

title: 18  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
18.1 Why this matters
Analysts may request every two-way table over several columns or a synthetic dataset that supports repeated queries. Both require differential privacy (DP). These tables are marginal tables: each counts records for combinations of attribute values, and each count is a cell.
Add noise to each table and calibrate it to the maximum change one person can make to that table. With one record per person, one person affects one cell, so a table costs about as much as one count. Subsequent computation on noisy tables is post-processing. If there are too many queries to noise every cell, fit synthetic data to a selected set of noisy tables.
crumbs: 18  Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 18  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
18.2 Which method to use
Choose a method based on query count, record count and the number of attributes per record (Table 18.1).



Table 18.1: Which query-release method to use.





Situation
Use




A few marginal tables, with a public list of cells
Noisy counts on every cell, one budget share per table


Hundreds of tables or thousands of cells
Gaussian noise on every cell, scaled to the whole set of tables


A table whose list of values is not public
Noisy counts, keeping only cells that clear a noisy threshold (Release statistics with a library)


Far more queries than records, or queries not known in advance
Synthetic data from AIM or MST


Queries that arrive one at a time, perhaps adaptively
Online private multiplicative weights






Each person can affect every table, so the combined query is dense. The dense-query rule in the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms identifies when Gaussian noise becomes more accurate. At privacy level \(\varepsilon = 1\) and slack \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), Gaussian noise is better for seven or more tables.
crumbs: 18  Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 18  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
18.3 Noise on every cell
Under add/remove neighbours, one record changes one cell of a marginal table by 1, so the table’s sensitivity is 1. Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) on each cell makes the table \(\varepsilon\)-DP by parallel composition. Under replace neighbours, a record can move between cells, changing two cells and doubling sensitivity.
Releasing several tables of the same records composes their costs. With Laplace noise, splitting the budget across tables makes per-cell error grow in proportion to table count. Gaussian noise scales with the square root of the sum of squared sensitivities. If each person affects \(m\) tables, Gaussian error grows as \(\sqrt m\).
For example, a table of 10,000 records has eight yes/no attributes, so \(2^8 = 256\) possible records. The release is every cell of the marginal table of every set of attributes, 6,560 cells in all. Each cell is a fraction of the records, under replace neighbours. A uniform guess, which ignores the data, has a largest error of 0.232 on these cells. At \(\varepsilon = 1\), Laplace noise on every cell is worse, with 0.497. Gaussian noise at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) is much better, with 0.037.
Two errors are common. Calibrating each cell as a separate query spends \(\varepsilon\) once per table. Applying basic composition to thousands of cells also wastes budget. Calibrate noise to the complete set of tables.
crumbs: 18  Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 18  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
18.4 Releasing a marginal with OpenDP
The script practitioner_adult_statistics.py releases an education-by-income table from Adult at \(\varepsilon = 1\). Adult contains 48,842 people with one row each. The survey documentation lists 16 education levels and two income classes, making the 32 table keys public. Release empty cells as well; omitting one would reveal that its count is zero. Map missing values to a listed key such as “Unknown”, because OpenDP drops rows with keys outside the list. In OpenDP, Margin(invariant="keys") declares the cell list public, and with_keys restricts the release to that list.
keys = pl.LazyFrame({"education": EDUCATION}).join(pl.LazyFrame({"income": INCOME}), how="cross")
context = dp.Context.compositor(
    data=adult.lazy(),
    privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=1),
    privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(epsilon=1.0),
    split_evenly_over=1,
    margins=[dp.polars.Margin(by=["education", "income"], invariant="keys")],  # the cells are public
)
query = context.query().group_by("education", "income").agg(dp.len(signed=True)).with_keys(keys)
print(query.summarize(alpha=0.05))
released = query.release().collect()  # all 32 cells, zeros included; changes on every run
Run uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/practitioner_adult_statistics.py to print the deterministic summary.
shape: (1, 5)
┌────────┬──────────────┬─────────────────┬───────┬──────────┐
│ column ┆ aggregate    ┆ distribution    ┆ scale ┆ accuracy │
│ ---    ┆ ---          ┆ ---             ┆ ---   ┆ ---      │
│ str    ┆ str          ┆ str             ┆ f64   ┆ f64      │
╞════════╪══════════════╪═════════════════╪═══════╪══════════╡
│ len    ┆ Frame Length ┆ Integer Laplace ┆ 1.0   ┆ 3.375618 │
└────────┴──────────────┴─────────────────┴───────┴──────────┘
Each cell receives integer Laplace noise with scale 1 (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms). The 95% accuracy of 3.38 means each noisy count is within 3.38 of the true count with 95% probability. Report this error bar with every cell; it covers noise but not sampling error or data errors. OpenDP noise is unseeded, so the following values are from one run, alongside the true counts.
  Doctorate >50K: 432  true 431  accuracy 3.38
  HS-grad <=50K: 13281  true 13281  accuracy 3.38
  Preschool <=50K: 82  true 82  accuracy 3.38
  Preschool >50K: 0  true 1  accuracy 3.38
Noise has little effect on large cells. The smallest true cell—one person with preschool education and high income—is smaller than the noise. Merge rare categories in advance if small counts matter. With signed=True, a noisy count may be negative, preserving unbiasedness. Clamping at zero, rounding and scaling cells to a released total are post-processing and cost no additional privacy.
Three implementation details matter. First, deriving cell keys from private data—for example, calling unique() on a private column—may reveal rare values. Use partition selection when no public codebook exists (Release statistics with a library). Second, each additional table over the same people needs a budget share; set split_evenly_over to the table count. Third, for many tables, specify dp.loss_of(rho=...) with a \(\rho\) that converts to the desired \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) (Release statistics with a library). OpenDP then uses Gaussian noise and accounts in zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), which composes more tightly (Concentrated differential privacy).
crumbs: 18  Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 18  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
18.5 Synthetic data
When the query set is too large to noise every cell, or queries are not known in advance, release synthetic data using four steps.

Select a set of marginal tables to measure, from domain knowledge or privately with the exponential mechanism, scoring each table by how badly the current model fits it.
Measure each whole table with Gaussian noise, scaled to the whole set.
Generate a compact graphical model that fits the noisy tables.
Sample synthetic rows from the model.

All steps after measurement are post-processing, so synthetic rows can be queried and shared without further privacy cost. MST and AIM are standard methods developed by McKenna and coauthors; AIM selects tables adaptively. SmartNoise Synth, the snsynth package, provides both methods through one interface. It is not installed in this book’s environment, so the example below was not run.
# smartnoise-synth 1.0.8: not installed in this book's environment, not run
from snsynth import Synthesizer

synth = Synthesizer.create("aim", epsilon=1.0, delta=1e-6)
synth.fit(adult_pandas, categorical_columns=["education", "sex", "race", "occupation", "income"])
rows = synth.sample(48_842)
A synthetic table fits the measured tables by construction. Evaluate it on additional queries, but account for privacy when evaluation uses private data. Selecting the best of several runs based on private data is also a private query, and each run spends the generator’s budget again. Evaluate settings on public data with the same structure or charge comparisons to the budget. Synthetic data from a generator without DP are not anonymized.
crumbs: 18  Query release and private multiplicative weights

title: 18  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
18.6 Private multiplicative weights
The synthetic-data tools use the select-measure-update loop of the multiplicative weights exponential mechanism (MWEM) (Hardt, Ligett and McSherry 2012). MWEM maintains a guessed histogram with one weight per possible record—256 in the eight-attribute example. In a fixed number of rounds, it selects a poorly answered query using the exponential mechanism, measures it with fresh Laplace noise and updates the histogram toward that measurement. The correction count is bounded independently of the query count, so error grows logarithmically with the number of queries.
MWEM is useful for large query sets. In the eight-attribute example at privacy level 1, 38 rounds give a maximum error of 0.078. This is better than Laplace noise but about twice the Gaussian-noise error. Runtime grows with the number of possible records, limiting MWEM to a few attributes.
Fix the round count from the error bound before accessing private data; the bound uses only public quantities. Measure each query with fresh noise because exact selection scores could leak information. Release the average of the guesses, not the last one, because the accuracy guarantee applies only to the average. For sequential queries, an online variant pays only for its corrections (Adaptive data analysis).

title: 19  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
19.1 What it is
The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms calibrate noise to global sensitivity, the maximum change one record can cause across all neighbouring datasets. For ages bounded between 0 and 100, the median’s global sensitivity is 100. Under differential privacy (DP) at \(\varepsilon = 1\), the Laplace mechanism’s median error is \(100\ln 2 = 69.31\) years. On a simulated sample of 1,001 ages, however, one person changes the median by only 0.1386 years. This smaller dataset-specific value is local sensitivity, the largest change one record can cause to answer \(f\) on dataset \(D\): \[\mathrm{LS}_f(D) = \max_{D' \text{ a neighbour of } D}|f(D) - f(D')|. \tag{19.1}\]
These techniques use the data’s local scale under one condition: a noise scale, bound or threshold computed from private data is itself a statistic and must also be private. This chapter assumes fixed-size datasets and replace-one-record neighbours.

title: 19  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
19.2 When you meet it
Use these techniques when a statistic has no useful worst-case sensitivity (Table 19.1).



Table 19.1: Which technique releases what, and where you meet it.










You release
Technique
Where you meet it




A sum, mean or gradient of unbounded values
Clipping to a bound fixed in advance
Every library’s bounds, and the clipping norm of private training


A median or quantile
Inverse sensitivity
diffprivlib.tools.quantile, OpenDP’s dp.quantile


A discrete answer with a clear winner
Stability-based release
The threshold of private partition selection


A black-box model or estimator
Subsample-and-aggregate
Teacher ensembles for private prediction






A stability-based release publishes a discrete answer, such as the most common value, when a noisy test shows that it exceeds the runner-up by about \(2\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) records for slack \(\delta\). Otherwise, it returns no answer; downstream steps must handle refusals. The same test selects keys for a group-by (Release statistics with a library).
Subsample-and-aggregate runs an estimator on disjoint blocks, clips their answers and releases a noisy average. Private aggregation of teacher ensembles (PATE) uses this method for voting (Private prediction).
Propose-test-release proposes a local-sensitivity bound and refuses to release unless a noisy test shows that the data are sufficiently far from the bound. Smooth sensitivity scales heavy-tailed noise to a bound that changes gradually between neighbours. PATE uses smooth sensitivity to calibrate its voting mechanism, but on the 1,001-age example it is about twelve times less accurate than inverse sensitivity.

title: 19  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
19.3 How to use it
For unbounded inputs, use clipping. Replace each value \(x\) by \(\min(x,C)\), where clip bound \(C\) is fixed independently of the data. If values are nonnegative, one record changes the mean of \(n\) records by at most \(C/n\). Laplace noise with scale \(C/(n\varepsilon)\) therefore gives \(\varepsilon\)-DP for the clipped mean. A larger \(C\) reduces clipping bias but increases noise.
Choose \(C\) from public domain information, such as a legal maximum or sensor range. Otherwise, spend part of the budget on a private high quantile, account for it by composition, and clip at that quantile. Without a bound, diffprivlib uses the data to calculate one and raises PrivacyLeakWarning. Convert the warning to an error with warnings.simplefilter("error", PrivacyLeakWarning), as in practitioner_adult_statistics.py.
For a median or quantile, use inverse sensitivity. This exponential mechanism favours candidate outputs that require fewer record changes to become the median. Set bounds or a candidate grid in advance. On the 1,001-age sample at \(\varepsilon = 1\), median error is 0.0783 years, below the local sensitivity of 0.1386.

title: 19  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
19.4 What goes wrong
Noise calibrated to local sensitivity alone is not private. The five ages \((0, 0, 0, 0, 100)\) have median 0, and no single change moves it, so the mechanism adds no noise. A neighbouring dataset \((0, 0, 0, 100, 100)\) receives continuous noise and never outputs exactly 0; therefore, output 0 identifies the first dataset. Similar leaks arise from a clip bound based on the observed maximum, a candidate grid derived from private data or keys read from private data. During review, search for max(), quantile() and unique() calls on private data that set parameters.
Upper clipping biases a mean downward. Two-sided clipping removes that bias only when the range is centred on the data (Private mean estimation). If neighbouring datasets differ by adding or removing a record, \(n\) is not public. Release a noisy clipped sum and noisy count, then divide them.
Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 20  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
20.1 What it is
The proof of the Laplace mechanism assumes densities on the real line, but computers sample from a finite set of floating-point numbers with uneven spacing. The textbook sampler adds \(\pm b\ln(1/U)\) to the true answer, where \(b\) is the noise scale and \(U\) is uniform. Mironov (2012) showed that this sampler leaks the true answer through low-order bits in double precision. Floating-point values are dense near 0 and sparse at large magnitudes. Some outputs can therefore occur for a true answer of 0 or 1 but not for intermediate values, identifying the input exactly.
Differential privacy (DP) does not hide this implementation leak. DP limits how much one record can change an output probability. The privacy level \(\varepsilon\) bounds the multiplicative change, and the slack \(\delta\) allows an additive failure probability (The definition of differential privacy).
Let dataset \(D\) denote the data and let \(S\) denote a set of possible outputs. Suppose \(D\) can produce outputs in \(S\), but a neighbouring dataset cannot. The neighbour assigns probability zero to \(S\), so multiplying that probability by \(e^\varepsilon\) still gives zero. The mechanism therefore requires slack at least \[\delta \ge \Pr[M(D) \in S]. \tag{20.1}\] In a toy sampler with 12-bit floats, these outputs have probability 0.4791. Using more bits does not reduce this probability.
DP applies to the output distribution that the code actually produces. One repair is the snapping mechanism: clamp the answer, add noise, round to a coarse power-of-two grid, then clamp again. Another repair is to make the query integer-valued and add exact discrete Laplace or discrete Gaussian noise.

title: 20  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
20.2 When you meet it
This issue arises when reviewing code that samples noise directly, such as x + np.random.laplace(0, b), or when choosing a library. OpenDP provides exact samplers, including discrete Laplace and discrete Gaussian noise for integer data. diffprivlib provides mechanisms.Geometric, mechanisms.GaussianDiscrete and mechanisms.Snapping. Its continuous Laplace mechanism, used by its tools functions, reduces this risk but is not exact. It draws four uniform variates (Holohan & Braghin 2021). Secure aggregation also requires integer noise (Local, shuffle and distributed trust models).
Opacus adds continuous Gaussian noise in floating point during private training, so the proof of Private stochastic gradient descent applies to idealized code. Its secure_mode=True uses a cryptographic generator, making these attacks harder. Verify that released models use this mode and state which idealized mechanism their guarantee assumes.

title: 20  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
20.3 How to use it
Use a library to add noise to integer data. Discrete Laplace noise assigns a noise value \(z\) probability proportional to \(e^{-|z|/b}\) and uses the same calibration as continuous Laplace noise. Let \(\Delta f\) denote the sensitivity of the integer-valued query \(f\). Its privacy level is \(\varepsilon = \Delta f/b\). At \(b = 1\), a count is exact with probability 0.4621.
Discrete Gaussian noise assigns each integer \(x\) probability proportional to \(e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), where \(\sigma\) is the noise width. Its exact privacy curve is slightly weaker than the continuous Gaussian’s. For sensitivity 1 and noise width 1, the discrete mechanism has privacy level \(\varepsilon = 1\) with slack \(\delta = 0.1414\). The corresponding slack for continuous noise is 0.1269. Report the discrete curve or use OpenDP’s accounting in zero-concentrated DP. Under that accounting, both Gaussian mechanisms have the same budget \(\rho\), where \(\rho = (\Delta f)^2/(2\sigma^2)\). In the snippet, map(1) returns each guarantee at sensitivity 1.
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
integers, distance = dp.atom_domain(T=int), dp.absolute_distance(T=int)
laplace = dp.m.make_laplace(integers, distance, scale=1.0)
print(laplace.map(1))  # 1.0
gauss = dp.m.make_gaussian(integers, distance, scale=2.0)
print(gauss.map(1))  # 0.125
print(gauss.output_measure)  # ZeroConcentratedDivergence
To integerize a real-valued query, such as a sum of clipped values, divide by a step much smaller than the noise scale. Round up with probability equal to the fractional part and down otherwise; this preserves the expectation. Recompute sensitivity in these units because rounding can increase the distance between neighbours. Then add discrete noise and multiply by the step.

title: 20  Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms
text:
20.4 What goes wrong
Check each implementation against the following conditions.

Is every sensitivity computed from bounds fixed in advance, with no max(), quantile() or unique() on the private data (Beyond global sensitivity)?
Does a vetted library draw the noise, or an exact sampler with no floating-point exp, log or random() inside? Search for np.random, random., scipy.stats, default_rng, .laplace( and .normal(.
Does integer data get integer noise, and is every floating-point output snapped and clamped to a fixed range?
Does each release draw fresh noise from a cryptographic source, such as secrets.SystemRandom(), rather than a fixed seed that makes it removable?
Is the running time fixed or padded? The rounds of a rejection sampler depend on the value it draws, and Jin et al. (2022) use that time as a leak.
Does the stated guarantee match the mechanism, including the discrete Gaussian’s own curve and the sensitivity after rounding?

Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 21  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
21.1 Why this matters
Earlier mechanisms in this part assume a trusted curator who holds raw data and releases only the mechanism’s output. In this central model, differential privacy (DP) protects released outputs, not data exposed by a breach, employee or court order. A browser vendor collecting usage statistics may not be able to rely on a trusted curator.
Three models reduce reliance on a curator, with different protections. In the local model, each person randomizes their record on-device, so no central party sees the raw record. In the shuffle model, a shuffler breaks the link between each report and its sender. In the distributed model, cryptography and enough honest participants allow a server to reveal only a sum. Each model reduces trust in intermediaries but increases noise.
crumbs: 21  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 21  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
21.2 Choosing a trust model
Reduced trust generally increases noise. For a private count, central-model noise remains fixed as the population grows, while local-model noise grows with the square root of population size. Shuffle and distributed models narrow this gap.
Use the central model when a curator may hold raw data, as in Release statistics with a library. Use the local model when no party may see raw records and the population is large enough, based on the standard deviation in Section 21.3. Report the trust model with the privacy parameters: the same \(\varepsilon\) protects against different adversaries in different models.
crumbs: 21  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 21  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
21.3 Central and local differential privacy
In the local model, each person sends a report, the output of a local randomizer \(R\) applied to their record. Let \(\varepsilon_0\) denote the privacy level of one report. The randomizer is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP if changing a record increases the probability of any report set by at most \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\). Write \(x\) and \(x'\) for two possible records. Let \(S\) denote a set of reports. The guarantee is \[\Pr[R(x) \in S] \le e^{\varepsilon_0}\Pr[R(x') \in S]. \tag{21.1}\] Changing one person’s record changes only that person’s report, so the report collection is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP under replace-one-record neighbours. This guarantee protects the randomized value, not identifying metadata. For example, a network address stored with a report may identify its sender.
The basic local randomizer applies randomized response to one bit. Let \(p\) be the probability that a report is truthful: \(p = e^{\varepsilon_0}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0})\). Each person reports the true bit with probability \(p\) and its complement otherwise. To correct for flips, the analyst subtracts \(1-p\) from the fraction of reported ones and divides by \(2p-1\). If \(n\) is the number of people, the estimate’s standard deviation is \[\operatorname{sd}(\hat\pi) = \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0/2}}{(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)\sqrt n}. \tag{21.2}\]
The script practitioner_adult_statistics.py compares the models on Adult, a census dataset of 48,842 people. It uses \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\) for local randomization. Each bit indicates whether a person’s income exceeds $50K. The local model uses diffprivlib’s Binary mechanism, so the analyst receives only randomized reports.
answers = (adult["income"] == ">50K").cast(pl.Int8).cast(pl.String).to_list()  # "1" or "0"
n, eps = len(answers), log(3)
coin = Binary(epsilon=eps, value0="0", value1="1", random_state=seed)
reports = [coin.randomise(a) for a in answers]  # each person randomizes their own answer
p = exp(eps) / (1 + exp(eps))  # chance a report is truthful: 0.75
reported = reports.count("1") / n
local = (reported - (1 - p)) / (2 * p - 1)  # undo the expected flips
local_sd = math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n) / (2 * p - 1)  # the randomization noise alone
print(f"true share over 50K: {answers.count('1') / n:.4f}")
print(f"local estimate: {local:.4f}  sd {local_sd:.4f}")
For the central-model estimate, a trusted curator applies diffprivlib’s tools.count_nonzero to the true bits at the same privacy level. The call adds Laplace noise with standard deviation \(\sqrt2/\varepsilon\) to the count.
rich = (adult["income"] == ">50K").to_numpy()
central = tools.count_nonzero(rich, epsilon=log(3), random_state=seed) / len(rich)
central_sd = math.sqrt(Laplace(epsilon=log(3), sensitivity=1).variance(0)) / len(rich)  # the count's noise
print(f"central estimate: {central:.4f}  sd {central_sd:.6f}")
Running uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/practitioner_adult_statistics.py with seed 0 gives:
true share over 50K: 0.2393
local estimate: 0.2359  sd 0.0039
central estimate: 0.2393  sd 0.000026
local sd / central sd: 149
At the same guarantee, local noise is 149 times larger, and the ratio grows with the square root of population size. This cost is inherent to local DP, not specific to randomized response: no local protocol estimates a fraction with error below order \(1/((e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)\sqrt n)\), and randomized response achieves that order. Apple, Google and Microsoft therefore use local DP mainly to estimate frequent items across very large populations.

title: 21  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
section: 21.4 Frequency estimation: \(k\)-ary randomized response and unary encoding
text:
21.4 Frequency estimation: \(k\)-ary randomized response and unary encoding
Most deployed local-DP systems perform frequency estimation. Each person has a category, such as an emoji, from a known list; the analyst estimates each category’s share. Let \(v\) denote one category. A report votes for \(v\) with probability \(p_1\) when the person has that category and with smaller probability \(p_0\) otherwise. Let \(c_v\) count the reports for \(v\) among the \(n\) reports. Correcting for expected false votes gives the unbiased estimate \[\hat f_v = \frac{c_v/n - p_0}{p_1 - p_0}. \tag{21.3}\]
Two designs set \(p_1\) and \(p_0\) for a list of \(k\) values. In \(k\)-ary randomized response, a person reports the true value with probability \(e^{\varepsilon_0}/(e^{\varepsilon_0} + k - 1)\) and otherwise reports another value. Optimized unary encoding sends one bit per value, retains the bit for the person’s value about half the time and rarely flips a 0 to 1. Compare the designs’ variances for rare values, which determine the smallest detectable share. Use \(k\)-ary randomized response when \(k < 3e^{\varepsilon_0} + 2\); otherwise use unary encoding, which requires a \(k\)-bit report. The pure-ldp Python package implements both.
Consider a keyboard app estimating 128 emoji frequencies among one million users, at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\). For a rare emoji, unary encoding has standard deviation 0.0019; \(k\)-ary randomized response has 0.0066. A common detection rule requires an estimate to exceed zero by three standard deviations. Even the better design cannot reliably detect emoji used by fewer than about \(3 \times 0.0019\), or 0.6%, of users. Check the population size before collection. For larger lists, local hashing and heavy-hitter protocols reduce report length to a few bits (Wang et al. 2017; Bassily et al. 2017).
crumbs: 21  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 21  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
section: 21.5 Numbers in one bit: local mean estimation
text:
21.5 Numbers in one bit: local mean estimation
One bit per person can estimate a mean when each value lies in a known interval, such as app-use minutes (Ding, Kulkarni & Yekhanin 2017). The probability of reporting 1 increases linearly with the value. The analyst inverts this relation to estimate the mean without bias. With one million users and a bound of 1,440 minutes, the standard deviation is 1.420 minutes at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\). Set the bound before collection and clip values on-device. Otherwise, one person’s value could affect every user’s randomizer through the estimated bound.
crumbs: 21  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 21  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
21.6 Collecting every day: memoization
Telemetry asks the same question every day. If a value does not change, an analyst can average its daily reports to remove their fresh noise. Composition counts that leak as the sum of the \(\varepsilon_0\) of each report. Memoization prevents this averaging attack: the device draws one permanent randomized response per value and sends it each day. An unchanged value then costs only the level of that response, written \(\varepsilon_\infty\). RAPPOR, Google’s collection of the homepages of Chrome users, has \(\varepsilon_\infty = 2.043\).
Memoization fails when the value changes, because each new value costs another \(\varepsilon_\infty\). A user who changes their homepage every month gets to \(12 \times 2.043 = 24.5\) in a year.
crumbs: 21  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 21  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
section: 21.7 The shuffle model and amplification by shuffling
text:
21.7 The shuffle model and amplification by shuffling
In the shuffle model (Cheu et al. 2019), each person sends a local report to a shuffler. The shuffler removes identifiers and timing, then sends the reports in random order. Because each report is hidden among the others, the collection can satisfy central DP with privacy level \(\varepsilon\) far below the local level \(\varepsilon_0\). The guarantee also has slack \(\delta\) (Amplification by shuffling and by iteration). Feldman, McMillan & Talwar (2021) give a closed-form bound that requires enough people: \[\varepsilon_0 \le \ln\frac{n}{16\ln(2/\delta)}. \tag{21.4}\]
Fix the central target, then solve for the largest allowed \(\varepsilon_0\). The target here is privacy level 1 and slack \(10^{-6}\). At a population of 10,000, the bound allows \(\varepsilon_0 = 3.504\). At 1,000 people, it allows \(\varepsilon_0 = 1.460\). These targets use a \(\delta\) below the book’s default (How small δ must be). For 10,000 people, the closed-form bound overestimates the privacy level by a factor between 2.6 and 4.6. Use it for planning, but use the paper’s numerical bound for deployment.
Three conditions can remove amplification. If the shuffler colludes with the analyst, each report retains privacy level \(\varepsilon_0\). Choose a local level that is acceptable on its own under the definition. Fake senders provide no protection; therefore, count only honest participants in \(n\). Timing and message sizes may also leak information, so practical shufflers batch and pad traffic.
crumbs: 21  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 21  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
21.8 Distributed DP: splitting the noise
In the distributed model, each client adds a share of the central noise, and secure aggregation reveals only the sum to the server (Cryptography basics). Independent Gaussian variances add. If each of \(n\) clients adds normal noise with variance \(\sigma^2/n\), the sum has standard deviation \(\sigma\), matching the central Gaussian mechanism.
Small shares create a vulnerability: colluding clients can reveal their noise, and dropped clients add none. Let \(t\) be the number of clients that are unavailable or colluding. The remaining noise has standard deviation \[\sigma\sqrt{\frac{n - t}{n}}. \tag{21.5}\] Set in advance the largest fraction \(\rho\) of clients that may collude or drop out. Have each client add variance \(\sigma^2/(n(1 - \rho))\) so the remaining honest clients provide the required total noise.
For example, a server aggregates a histogram for about 100,000 users through 100 clients. The target is \((1, 10^{-6})\). Changing one user’s value decrements one count and increments another, giving \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\sqrt 2\). Analytic Gaussian calibration in the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms gives total standard deviation \(\sigma = 5.975\). This is \(5.975/\sqrt{100} = 0.597\) per client. If a fifth of the clients collude and noise is not over-provisioned, the guarantee weakens to \(\varepsilon = 1.128\) at the same \(\delta\).
Secure aggregation operates on integers, so clients add integer-valued noise, such as Skellam noise or the distributed discrete Gaussian in Discrete mechanisms. TensorFlow Federated provides tff.aggregators.DistributedDpSumFactory for this task. However, secure aggregation does not validate inputs, so a malicious client can still send an arbitrary vector.

title: 22  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
22.1 What it is
A lower bound states the best accuracy any mechanism satisfying differential privacy (DP) can achieve. It applies to all such mechanisms and provides a feasibility check. Accuracy has two parameters: error \(\alpha\), the maximum distance between output and true answer, and failure probability \(\beta\), the probability that the error exceeds \(\alpha\).
One common lower bound applies to a histogram with \(N\) bins under pure DP, at privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and with no slack. If every count is within \(\alpha\) records of its true value with probability at least \(1 - \beta\), then \[\alpha \ge \frac12\left(\frac{\ln\big(N(1 - \beta)\big)}{\varepsilon} - 1\right). \tag{22.1}\] The bound grows logarithmically with the number of bins and remains positive under pure DP. Under approximate DP with slack \(\delta\), it is about \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) records, independent of the number of bins.
crumbs: 22  Lower bounds: what privacy costs

title: 22  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
22.2 When you meet it
Use a lower bound to check whether a proposed accuracy is feasible. For example, consider a histogram of one million locations at \(\varepsilon = 1\), with no slack, that promises every bin within five records of its true count with 95% probability.
Determine whether one person affects one statistic, as in disjoint histogram cells, or many statistics, as in means of multiple attributes. The histogram bound applies to the first case; fingerprinting and reconstruction bounds apply to the second. If a target is below the lower bound, increase the data, coarsen the answer or weaken the guarantee. A mechanism near the bound is close to the best possible accuracy.
crumbs: 22  Lower bounds: what privacy costs

title: 22  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
22.3 How to use it
For one million locations, every pure-DP histogram has error of at least 6.38 records in some bin, so the five-record target is impossible. The Laplace histogram in the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms has error 16.79, about 2.6 times the lower bound. At \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), the bound is below about \(\ln(10^6) = 13.82\) records. A stability-based histogram that releases only non-empty bins has error independent of \(N\) (Beyond global sensitivity). For a large, mostly empty universe, approximate DP may therefore provide better utility.
The same bound gives a minimum dataset size: dividing count error by the record count \(n\) gives frequency error. A pure-DP histogram with all frequencies within \(\alpha\) requires \[n \ge \frac{\ln\big(N(1 - \beta)\big) - \varepsilon}{2\alpha\varepsilon}. \tag{22.2}\] If the data are sampled from a population, sampling error also requires records: about \(\ln(2N/\beta)/(2\alpha^2)\) by Hoeffding’s inequality. Use the larger of the privacy and sampling requirements. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 95% probability, a million cells with error 0.01 require at least 638 records for privacy but 87,522 for sampling. Sampling, not privacy, therefore limits the accuracy; no mechanism can remove that limit.
When one person affects many statistics, the cost increases. Under pure DP, estimating means of \(d\) yes/no attributes requires a number of records proportional to \(d\). Under approximate DP, the fingerprinting bound requires about \(\sqrt{d\ln(1/\delta)}/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) records. The Gaussian mechanism is within a factor \(\sqrt{\ln d}\) of this bound. Use approximate DP for high-dimensional outputs such as gradients. Once Gaussian noise is calibrated, adding records is more effective than seeking a substantially better mechanism. For about \(n\) counting queries on \(n\) records, the reconstruction attack of Dinur and Nissim gives a lower bound of order \(\sqrt n\) error per answer (Reconstruction attacks).
crumbs: 22  Lower bounds: what privacy costs

title: 22  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
22.4 What goes wrong
Aggregates do not prevent membership inference. The attack underlying the fingerprinting bound (Homer et al. 2008) identified participants in a genome study from published frequencies of genetic variants. It scores how much released means shift toward a target’s record and away from population means, attribute by attribute. Members tend to score higher because their records affect the means. For the means of 50 people over 2,000 attributes, the attack reaches true positive rate (TPR) 0.242 at false positive rate (FPR) 1%. A \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP Gaussian mechanism reduces TPR to 0.014.
Use this score to audit releases of many averages, estimating population means from a separate sample. Compare TPR at low FPR with the cap \(\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\) from the definition. An audit that exceeds the cap indicates a mechanism or accounting error. Passing does not establish privacy because an attack provides only a lower bound on \(\varepsilon\) (Auditing private training).
Each approximate-DP bound assumes a small \(\delta\), such as the book’s default (How small δ must be). A mechanism that publishes each record with probability \(\delta\) is \((0, \delta)\)-DP; if \(\delta\) is near \(1/n\), it can publish about one record in full.

title: 23  Private mean estimation
text:
23.1 Why this matters
Private machine learning uses means extensively: each private gradient-descent step averages clipped per-example gradients, and a survey share is the mean of binary answers. Before releasing a mean, determine the required sample size and choose a clipping range without inspecting private data.
Differential privacy (DP) must hold for every dataset, including datasets excluded by modelling assumptions (The definition of differential privacy). An assumption such as normally distributed records may improve accuracy, but does not enter the privacy proof. The mechanisms below therefore clip each record to a range. Noise increases with range width, but the range cannot be estimated directly from private data. Spend part of the budget to estimate the range privately, then clip to it.

title: 23  Private mean estimation
section: 23.2 Bounded data: privacy adds a lower-order term
text:
23.2 Bounded data: privacy adds a lower-order term
This chapter assumes fixed-size datasets of size \(n\), with neighbours differing in one replaced record. It measures estimation error by root-mean-square error (RMSE), the typical distance between the estimate and the population mean.
Suppose records lie in a known interval of width \(w\), such as binary answers coded 0 and 1, and let \(\sigma^2\) be their variance. Release the sample mean plus Laplace noise with scale \(w/(n\varepsilon)\). Since one record changes the mean by at most \(w/n\), this gives \(\varepsilon\)-DP (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). Laplace noise has variance twice the squared scale and is independent of sampling error, so the variances add: \[\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2}{n} + \frac{2w^2}{n^2\varepsilon^2}}. \tag{23.1}\] To plan a study, set RMSE to target error \(\alpha\) and solve for \(n\), as in the Code section. The required record count is at most \[\frac{\sigma^2}{\alpha^2} + \frac{\sqrt2\,w}{\alpha\varepsilon}. \tag{23.2}\]
Sampling alone requires about \(\sigma^2/\alpha^2\) records; privacy adds at most about \(w/(\alpha\varepsilon)\). For a binary survey with half the population answering yes, an RMSE of 0.05 requires 100 people, increasing to 108 at \(\varepsilon = 1\). The privacy term grows as \(1/\alpha\), compared with \(1/\alpha^2\) for sampling, so it matters most for coarse targets and small \(\varepsilon\). It also increases with interval width \(w\); subsequent sections reduce this width.
Libraries require a range. In diffprivlib, tools.mean(x, epsilon=..., bounds=(lower, upper)) clips values to the bounds and adds noise. Without bounds, it uses the observed minimum and maximum, which leaks them, and raises PrivacyLeakWarning.
Bounds that are too narrow clip valid records. The script practitioner_adult_statistics.py estimates mean weekly work hours in Adult, a census dataset with 48,842 people, at \(\varepsilon = 1\) using both loose and tight bounds.
hours = adult["hours-per-week"].to_numpy()
loose = tools.mean(hours, epsilon=1.0, bounds=(1, 99), random_state=seed)
tight = tools.mean(hours, epsilon=1.0, bounds=(20, 60), random_state=seed)
clipped = np.clip(hours, 20, 60).mean()  # what the tight bounds can at best recover
print(f"true mean hours: {hours.mean():.3f}")
print(f"bounds (1, 99): {loose:.3f}  bounds (20, 60): {tight:.3f}")
print(f"bias of (20, 60): {clipped - hours.mean():+.3f}")
The seed-0 run, uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/practitioner_adult_statistics.py, prints the following; the final two values come from code adjacent to the excerpt.
true mean hours: 40.422
bounds (1, 99): 40.421  bounds (20, 60): 40.361
bias of (20, 60): -0.061
people outside (20, 60): 8.7%
noise scale (1, 99): 0.0020  (20, 60): 0.0008
Tight bounds reduce the noise scale from 0.0020 to 0.0008 hours but clip 8.7% of people, shifting the mean by 0.061 hours—more than the noise reduction. Privacy budget cannot remove this bias. Report sampling error, clipping bias and noise separately. Choose bounds from the schema or public data, and measure the clipped share only on data available for inspection.
These formulas assume public \(n\), which holds for replace-one-record neighbours. If dataset size is private, release a noisy sum and noisy count, split the budget between them, then divide.

title: 23  Private mean estimation
section: 23.3 The cost of an unknown range
text:
23.3 The cost of an unknown range
Now suppose records are normal with variance 1 and their mean is known only to lie within distance \(R\) of zero. Let \(\tau\) be a radius that contains all records except with failure probability \(\beta\). For 1,000 records and \(\beta = 0.05\), \(\tau\) is 4.604.
The naive estimator clips records to the full possible range, from \(-(R+\tau)\) to \(R+\tau\), then adds Laplace noise calibrated to that width. Its error therefore grows linearly with \(R\). With 1,000 records at \(\varepsilon = 1\), RMSE is 2828.44 when \(R\) is one million. Lower bounds shows that an unknown range should require only about \(\ln R/\varepsilon\) additional records.
Coarse then fine (Karwa & Vadhan 2018) approaches this bound in two steps. The coarse step partitions the range into bins of width \(2\tau\) and uses budget \(\varepsilon_1\) with the exponential mechanism to select the fullest bin. Its record requirement grows logarithmically with the bin count. Because the data may span two bins, the fine step clips records to the selected bin and its two neighbours, then releases the mean with Laplace noise using the remaining budget. By composition, the combined procedure is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
Allocating one quarter of the budget to the coarse step gives RMSE 0.0609 for the same 1,000 records across \(R\) from 10 to one million. The fine step uses the remaining three quarters and a three-bin window, so the naive estimator performs better for small ranges, up to \(R = 13.81\). For larger ranges, use coarse then fine or estimate the range with a private quantile such as diffprivlib’s tools.quantile. Under approximate DP with slack \(\delta\), a stability-based histogram performs the coarse step with about \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) records, eliminating dependence on \(R\) (Beyond global sensitivity).
Two failures are possible. Choosing the budget split, bin width or \(\beta\) after inspecting private data leaks information. With too few records, the coarse step may select an empty bin and clip every record incorrectly.

title: 23  Private mean estimation
text:
23.4 Many dimensions: clip the norm
For \(d\)-dimensional vectors, such as embeddings or gradients, measure size with the \(\ell_2\) norm. Clip each record to radius \(C\), so one replacement changes the mean by at most \(2C/n\). Add Gaussian noise calibrated to this sensitivity (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). Private gradient descent uses this procedure; private training explains how to select its clipping norm.
The clipping radius determines the cost. With unit variance per coordinate, records lie about \(\sqrt d\) from their mean, so the radius must scale as \(\sqrt d\). Total noise across coordinates then grows as \(d\), compared with sampling error of order \(\sqrt d\). Privacy therefore dominates in high dimensions, as the fingerprinting lower bound confirms.
If the mean’s location is unknown, a grid of bins incurs a range cost in every dimension. CoinPress’s shrinking balls method (Biswas, Dong, Kamath & Ullman 2020) avoids a grid. Each round clips to a ball centred on a noisy mean estimate and reduces the radius. Fix the number of rounds and budget allocation before using private data.

title: 23  Private mean estimation
section: 23.5 Heavy tails: clip into the data
text:
23.5 Heavy tails: clip into the data
Incomes, session lengths and per-example gradient norms can have heavy-tailed distributions. If only the variance bound \(\sigma^2\) is known, a range that clips no records may be too wide for useful privacy. Clipping can reduce noise, but introduces bias.
Let \(\tau\) be the clipping half-width. A coarse step estimates a centre near the mean, then each record is clipped to within \(\tau\) of it. If the centre equals the mean, the bias is at most \(\sigma^2/\tau\), since only records beyond \(\tau\) change. Noise grows in proportion to \(\tau\). The resulting error bound is minimized at \[\tau_b = \sigma\sqrt{\frac{n\varepsilon}{2\sqrt2}}, \tag{23.3}\] This width depends only on \(n\), \(\varepsilon\) and the variance bound. At this width, error \(\alpha\) requires about \(\sigma^2/\alpha^2 + 8\sqrt2\,\sigma^2/(\alpha^2\varepsilon)\) records. Both terms scale as \(1/\alpha^2\), so privacy can cost as much as sampling.
Table 23.1 shows this trade-off for Pareto records scaled to variance 1. At the first width, 0.05 of records are clipped and noise dominates the error. The worst-case width \(\tau_b\) reduces error to 0.0607; a width tuned to this distribution reduces it further.

title: 23  Private mean estimation
text:
23.6 Code
The snippet computes the records that a bounded mean needs, checks its noise with OpenDP, and computes the default clipping width for heavy tails. The RMSE equal to \(\alpha\), times \(n^2\), is a quadratic in \(n\), and the first function rounds its positive root up.
from math import ceil, sqrt

import opendp.prelude as dp


def records_for_bounded_mean(alpha: float, sd: float, width: float, eps: float) -> int:
    """Smallest n with sd^2/n + 2 (width/(n eps))^2 <= alpha^2."""
    a, c = sd**2, 2 * (width / eps) ** 2
    return ceil((a + sqrt(a * a + 4 * c * alpha**2)) / (2 * alpha**2))


def heavy_tail_width(n: int, eps: float, sd: float) -> float:
    """The clipping half-width that balances the bias bound sd^2/tau against the noise."""
    return sd * sqrt(n * eps / (2 * sqrt(2)))


n = records_for_bounded_mean(0.05, 0.5, 1.0, 1.0)
print(n)  # 108
print(f"{dp.laplacian_scale_to_accuracy(1.0 / (n * 1.0), alpha=0.05):.4f}")  # 0.0277
print(f"{heavy_tail_width(1000, 1.0, 1.0):.2f}")  # 18.80
OpenDP gives accuracy as a half-width that holds the noise with a chosen probability. So laplacian_scale_to_accuracy changes the noise scale \(w/(n\varepsilon)\) of a range of width \(w\) at the planned 108 records into the half-width at 95%.

title: 24  Release statistics with a library
text:
24.1 Why this matters
An online shop wants a dashboard of purchase lines, revenue and typical sale, overall and by country, plus customer counts by product. Because these statistics describe customers, their release needs a differential privacy (DP) guarantee. A customer may contribute many rows, so a row-level guarantee would protect a purchase rather than the customer. This chapter uses OpenDP to build the release, define its privacy unit and state its guarantee.
The data are Online Retail from the University of California, Irvine (UCI) Machine Learning Repository: 541,909 invoice lines from a British online shop. Each line records a product, quantity, unit price, customer and country. The script practitioner_release_statistics.py runs every step in less than a minute with OpenDP 0.16.0 and Polars 1.36.1.
OpenDP uses an unseeded cryptographic generator, so released values vary between runs. This page quotes deterministic scales, error bars and thresholds, and marks one-run releases explicitly.

title: 24  Release statistics with a library
section: 24.3 Decide the unit and the budget
text:
24.3 Decide the unit and the budget
The unit of privacy is a customer. Neighbouring datasets differ by one customer and all their lines, added or removed (The definition of differential privacy). The script removes returns, zero-price lines and lines without a customer identifier. Each filter uses only the line itself, so adding or removing a customer affects only that customer’s lines.
raw = practitioner_datasets.online_retail()
lines, stats = clean(raw)
n_customers = stats.customers
delta = delta_for(n_customers)  # 1/n^1.1, rounded down to a power of ten
per_line = per_customer(lines)
print(f"customers: {n_customers:,}  purchase lines: {lines.height:,}")
print(f"delta: {delta:.0e}")
p50, p90, p99, top = quantiles(per_line, [0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 1.0])
print(f"lines per customer: p50={p50} p90={p90} p99={p99} max={top}")
customers: 4,372  purchase lines: 397,884
delta: 1e-05
lines per customer: p50=41 p90=208 p99=662 max=7847
The slack \(\delta\) follows the book’s default for \(n\) people (How small δ must be), giving \(10^{-5}\). OpenDP warns that \(\delta\) should be at most \(10^{-6}\), while this book sets it from the population size. The entire release has privacy level \(\varepsilon = 1\): all tables describe the same customers, and their costs compose (Post-processing, group privacy and composition).
Under a line-level guarantee, the largest customer represents 7,847 records, and group privacy multiplies \(\varepsilon\) by the group size. This maximum is reported only because the dataset is public.
crumbs: 24  Release statistics with a library

title: 24  Release statistics with a library
text:
24.4 Bound each customer’s contribution
Let \(k\) be the maximum number of lines retained per customer in each query. A smaller \(k\) reduces noise but discards more data; a larger \(k\) retains more data but requires more noise. The script measures this trade-off on the public dataset.
k=10: lines kept 10.2%  customers truncated 84.8%
k=25: lines kept 22.4%  customers truncated 64.6%
k=50: lines kept 36.9%  customers truncated 44.0%
k=100: lines kept 55.1%  customers truncated 24.9%
k=200: lines kept 72.7%  customers truncated 10.4%
k=500: lines kept 88.2%  customers truncated 1.8%
Choose \(k\) from a high percentile in public or historical data, never from the release data. If neither is available, spend a small part of the budget on a private high quantile over candidates fixed in advance (Selection). This chapter uses \(k = 100\), below the public-data 90th percentile of 208 because noise grows with \(k\). It retains 55.1% of lines and truncates about a quarter of customers.
Keeping the first \(k\) lines by date would bias statistics toward early purchases. The script instead samples \(k\) lines per customer. The filter below matches OpenDP’s truncate_per_group(k, keep="sample") while using a seed to keep validation values reproducible.
def sample_per_customer(k: int, seed: int, *by: str) -> pl.Expr:
    """True for at most k randomly chosen lines of each customer (within each value of `by`)."""
    return pl.int_range(pl.len()).shuffle(seed=seed).over("CustomerID", *by) < k
Bound each line value, defined as quantity times unit price. The script clips values to £0–£200. The lower bound follows from removing returns; the business sets the upper bound, which clips 1.02% of lines. Thus one customer can affect revenue by at most 100 lines of £200 each. Set value bounds from the domain, not the observed minimum or maximum (Beyond global sensitivity).
A grouped query may require two further bounds: \(L_0\), the number of groups one customer may affect, and \(L_\infty\), the number of lines they may contribute to one group. Country counts need neither because a customer’s \(k\) lines change the total counts by at most \(k\), already covered by the noise. Product partition selection requires both (Section 24.8).
crumbs: 24  Release statistics with a library

title: 24  Release statistics with a library
text:
24.5 Set up the context
OpenDP’s context stores the data, privacy unit, total budget and allocation across queries. Contexts require dp.enable_features("contrib"), which enables components that are not formally vetted. Reviewers who require vetted code must check each call against OpenDP’s documentation.
context = dp.Context.compositor(
    data=lines.lazy(),
    privacy_unit=dp.unit_of(contributions=1, identifier="CustomerID"),
    privacy_loss=dp.loss_of(rho=rho, delta=delta / 2),  # Gaussian noise; delta/2 for thresholds
    split_by_weights=WEIGHTS,  # scalars, countries, products
    margins=[dp.polars.Margin(by=[], max_length=MAX_LINES)],
)
The identifier column defines each customer as one privacy unit. Thus contributions=1 represents adding or removing one customer with all their lines; truncation bounds those lines. For replace-one neighbours, OpenDP instead takes changes=. The budget uses zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) (Concentrated differential privacy), represented by \(\rho\). Add \(\rho\) across queries, then convert the total to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\).
With a zCDP budget, the context adds Gaussian noise to each count and sum. This supports product counts, where one customer may affect many groups (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). The script’s rho_for selects \(\rho = 0.0284\), the largest value OpenDP converts to \(\varepsilon \le 1\) using half of \(\delta\). The remaining half pays for the threshold in Section 24.8. The margin supplies a public upper bound on line counts, which OpenDP needs before summing floating-point values.
The weights allocate one quarter of the budget to overall statistics, one quarter to countries and one half to products, which need the most. The script prints this allocation and converts the total budget back to the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) stated in the guarantee.
budget scalars: rho=0.0071 delta=1.25e-06
budget countries: rho=0.0071 delta=1.25e-06
budget products: rho=0.0142 delta=2.50e-06
whole release as (epsilon, delta): (1.0000, 1e-05)
OpenDP assigns a query its budget share when the query is built and spends that share on release. Each new query receives the next unspent share. Building all queries before releasing them can therefore assign each the first share; the product query would receive one quarter’s noise while costing half the budget. Build, inspect and release each query in sequence, as the script does.

title: 24  Release statistics with a library
section: 24.6 Release overall statistics with error bars
text:
24.6 Release overall statistics with error bars
The first query releases line count, revenue and median line value. Because the context stores the raw lines, each query applies its own truncation.
value = clipped_value()  # the line value, clipped to [low, high]
scalars = (
    context.query()
    .filter(sample_per_customer(K, seed))  # at most K lines per customer
    .select(
        dp.len(signed=True),
        value.dp.sum((low, high)).alias("revenue"),
        value.dp.median(candidates=MEDIAN_CANDIDATES).alias("median"),
    )
)
scalar_summary = scalars.summarize(alpha=0.05)
scalars_hat = scalars.release().collect()
signed=True retains negative noisy counts. Before release, summarize reports each statistic’s noise scale and 95% error bar.
scalars len: Frame Length, Integer Gaussian, scale=1,453.38 95% accuracy=2,850.0
scalars revenue: Sum, Float Gaussian, scale=290,804.33 95% accuracy=569,966.0
scalars median: 0.5-Quantile, GumbelMin, scale=1,453.38 95% accuracy=none
With probability 0.95, the released line count is within 2,850 of its true value and revenue is within £569,966. These error bars depend only on bounds and budget, so inspect them before release to assess whether the budget is sufficient.
The output also shows how OpenDP divides a query’s budget among its statistics. Each statistic receives the same noise scale relative to its sensitivity. The count and median therefore have scale 1,453.38, while revenue, with 200 times the count’s sensitivity, has about 200 times that scale. To allocate more budget to one statistic, place it in a separate weighted query. GumbelMin, an implementation of the exponential mechanism, selects the median from candidates spaced £0.50 apart. Its error is measured in ranks, so summarize provides no error bar (Selection).
The error bars cover noise, not bias from truncation and clipping, which together retain only 48.5% of revenue. The private statistic therefore estimates a truncated total, not the shop’s full takings. State this in the release. If coverage matters more than noise, increase \(k\).

title: 24  Release statistics with a library
section: 24.7 Group by a public key list
text:
24.7 Group by a public key list
The next query reports lines and revenue by country. Its key list must be fixed in advance because the distinct Country values reveal which countries occur in private data, and noise does not protect that list. The script uses 38 keys: the United Kingdom, 27 EU member states, four European Free Trade Association states, the United States, Canada, Australia, Japan, China and “Other”. A mapping standardizes three spellings, including EIRE to Ireland, and maps all remaining values to Other.
by_country = (
    context.query()
    .filter(sample_per_customer(K, seed))
    .group_by("Market")
    .agg(dp.len(signed=True), value.dp.sum((low, high)).alias("revenue"))
    .with_keys(pl.LazyFrame({"Market": MARKETS}))  # every key is released, zeros included
)
country_summary = by_country.summarize(alpha=0.05)
countries_hat = by_country.release().collect()
per country len: Frame Length, Integer Gaussian, scale=1,185.25 95% accuracy=2,324.0
per country revenue: Sum, Float Gaussian, scale=237,698.48 95% accuracy=465,880.5
The query releases every key, including 11 countries with no purchase lines; their counts contain only noise. Thus, the key list does not disclose which markets have customers. Each count has a 95% error bar of 2,324, and each revenue an error bar of about £466,000. Germany’s true count of 5,379 is informative, but its revenue of £131,902 is smaller than the error bar. Publish each cell’s error bar or combine small markets into Other before release.

title: 24  Release statistics with a library
section: 24.8 Group by unknown keys with partition selection
text:
24.8 Group by unknown keys with partition selection
The product list is private: a row for a product would reveal that at least one customer bought it. The release therefore uses partition selection to select products privately. It publishes only products whose noisy counts exceed a threshold, making products with few customers unlikely to appear. The threshold incurs \(\delta\) (Beyond global sensitivity).
To count customers rather than lines, the query first retains one line per customer-product pair, setting \(L_\infty\), the lines per customer in one group, to 1. It then retains at most \(m\) products per customer, setting \(L_0\), the groups per customer, to \(m\). The script evaluates this trade-off on public data.
m=1: pairs kept 1.6%  customers truncated 97.9%  scale=5.93  threshold=29  products above it: 1
m=5: pairs kept 7.9%  customers truncated 92.4%  scale=13.27  threshold=66  products above it: 9
m=10: pairs kept 15.1%  customers truncated 83.6%  scale=18.77  threshold=96  products above it: 19
m=20: pairs kept 27.5%  customers truncated 68.3%  scale=26.54  threshold=138  products above it: 30
m=50: pairs kept 52.7%  customers truncated 38.6%  scale=41.96  threshold=225  products above it: 50
The threshold rises from 29 to 225 as \(m\) increases because each customer can affect more groups. Product counts rise faster: the number of products whose true count exceeds the threshold grows from 1 to 50. The script uses \(m = 50\) (M in the code), selected using public data.
by_product = (
    context.query()
    .filter(sample_per_customer(1, seed, "StockCode"))  # one line per customer and product
    .filter(sample_per_customer(M, seed))  # at most M products per customer
    .group_by("StockCode")
    .agg(dp.len(signed=True).alias("customers"))
)
product_summary = by_product.summarize(alpha=0.05)
products_hat = by_product.release().collect()
per product customers: Frame Length, Integer Gaussian, scale=41.96 95% accuracy=83.0 threshold=225
The release shows a product only when its noisy count is at least 225; released counts have a 95% error bar of 83. Do not publish the number or identity of omitted products because both depend on private data. Positive noise can include a product just below the threshold. Treat counts near 225 as evidence of possible popularity, not as precise measurements.
In OpenDP 0.16.0, truncate_num_groups is intended to bound groups per customer but does not work. With default keep="sample", summarize accepts the query, but release fails after consuming its budget share. Test each query end to end on public data first. With keep="first", the function retains one fewer group than requested and biases counts. The filters above avoid both failures only because \(L_\infty = 1\) makes groups equivalent to lines. This book knows of no unbiased group bound for \(L_\infty > 1\) in this version.

title: 24  Release statistics with a library
text:
24.9 Check the release before publishing
To make sure that the code does what the plan says, the script compares the private values with the true values after the same truncation and clipping.
true lines after truncation: 219,291 (all purchase lines: 397,884)
true revenue after truncation and clipping: 4,318,947 (all lines, unclipped: 8,911,408)
true median line value after truncation: 15.00 (all lines: 11.80)
The release is random, and one run printed the following.
released (one run):
  lines 218,972  revenue 4,397,410  median 14.50
  United Kingdom: lines 196,311  revenue 3,927,959
  Germany: lines 7,151  revenue 643,094
  Spain: lines -546  revenue -37,048
  country line counts within their 95% accuracy: 34 of 38
  products released: 63
Compare it with the error bars, which must hold about 95% of the market counts. Negative values are noise on small markets, and you can round them up to zero, because post-processing costs no budget. Expect more than the 50 products whose true count is above the threshold, for the reason above. Compare the private median with the truncated £15.00, not with the £11.80 of all lines.
The check should fail when a value lies far outside its error bar, indicating incorrect sensitivity, or when substantially fewer or more than 95% of cells fall inside. It should also fail if a released product’s true count is far below the threshold. In production, do not use true values to decide what to publish; that decision would itself release private information. Run these checks during development on historical or public data, then release real data once with the validated code.

title: 24  Release statistics with a library
text:
24.10 Write the guarantee down
The script constructs the privacy statement from the variables that define bounds and budget, keeping the statement aligned with the implementation.
This release satisfies (epsilon = 1, delta = 1e-05)-differential privacy for adding or
removing one customer and all their invoice lines, with at most 100 lines per customer
(sampled at random), at most 50 random products per customer in the product counts, and
line values clipped to [0, 200] pounds, under the central model, using OpenDP 0.16.0 with
Gaussian noise (accounted as 0.0284-zCDP plus 5e-06 for thresholds, converted to epsilon
and delta). The market list was fixed in advance; the product list is not public.
The statement gives reviewers the information needed to recompute the guarantee (Writing the guarantee down). Also state what it excludes. Any further release about the same customers adds to the total budget. For a pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP release, add the two \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pairs. Alternatively, add its \(\rho = \varepsilon^2/2\) to this release’s \(\rho\), then convert the total; use the smaller result (Concentrated differential privacy). The dashboard must also state that its figures use truncated data. Release and governance connects this guarantee to data-protection law.

title: Privacy accounting
text:
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) trains a model through repeated updates. Differential privacy (DP) adds noise to each update; this method is DP-SGD. An accountant tracks each step’s privacy cost and converts the total to a guarantee \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) for the full run. Part 3’s composition theorems can give loose bounds.
In the running example, each of 10,000 DP-SGD steps samples records with probability 0.01 and adds noise with multiplier 1. At \(\delta=10^{-5}\), advanced composition gives \(\varepsilon=24{,}379.55\). Google’s privacy-loss-distribution accountant in dp_accounting gives 6.19. Report the accountant, sampler and neighbouring relation with each result; all three affect the bound.
Start with choosing an accountant, which matches accounting assumptions to an implementation, and calibrating a DP-SGD run, which selects noise for Part 5’s Adult-data training run. The full chapters on amplification by subsampling and Rényi differential privacy explain the two main tools: random sampling can reduce privacy cost, and Rényi differential privacy (RDP) provides a curve that many libraries track.
The reference pages cover RDP conversion, numerical accounting and Gaussian differential privacy, which interprets guarantees as limits on attacks. They also cover adaptive composition for budgets chosen during training, concentrated differential privacy for analytics ledgers and shuffling and iteration for other amplification methods. Code using Opacus and dp_accounting produces every number. By the end, you can calibrate a DP-SGD run, account for it with two libraries and report its privacy parameters.

title: 25  Choosing an accountant
text:
25.1 Why this matters
Report a model protected by differential privacy (DP), with privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and slack \(\delta\). The code computing \(\varepsilon\) is an accountant. Different accountants can give very different results for the same run: one reports 6.24, another 24,379.55. Table 25.1 compares advanced composition, Rényi differential privacy (RDP) and privacy loss distribution (PLD) accounting for one stochastic gradient descent (SGD) run with DP. Each record is sampled independently with probability \(q=0.01\), the sampling rate. The noise multiplier \(\sigma\) is the noise standard deviation relative to the clipping norm; here it is 1.
The true \(\varepsilon\) lies between the PLD bounds. Advanced composition gives a bound too loose to use here. RDP is tighter but still overstates \(\varepsilon\) by 14.6% for the shorter run and 7.6% for the longer one. Report the tightest upper bound whose assumptions match the implementation, with enough detail for independent recomputation.
