25.2 Which accountant
An accountant is tight only when its per-step model matches the mechanism. Choose it accordingly (Table 25.2).



Table 25.2: Which accountant to report for which mechanism.





Mechanism

Per-step composition

The central-limit approximation gives 1.6177 for 1,000 steps, but it is not a bound. This falls below the PLD’s certified lower bound of 1.8232, so it claims a guarantee the run does not satisfy. Opacus’s "gdp" accountant uses this approximation; do not report it. Opacus’s default PRV accountant is safe.

title: 25  Choosing an accountant
section: 25.3 The inverse problem: noise for a target ε
text:
25.3 The inverse problem: noise for a target ε
Usually, fix target privacy level \(\varepsilon\), batch size and epoch count, then solve for the smallest acceptable noise multiplier \(\sigma\). A looser accountant requires more noise to meet the same target. For a target \(\varepsilon=3\), RDP requires noise multiplier 1.662 on the 10,000-step run. PLD requires 1.584. Calibrate with the accountant used for reporting. Opacus’s get_noise_multiplier defaults to "rdp", so specify accountant="prv" when needed (Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run).

title: 25  Choosing an accountant
text:
25.4 Choosing δ
Let \(n\) denote the number of people in the protected unit. For user-level privacy, count users rather than records. Set \(\delta\) using the book’s rule: at most \(1/n^{1.1}\), rounded down to a power of ten (How small δ must be). The run in Table 25.1 has 10,000 steps. The sampling rate is 0.01, and the dataset has 50,000 records. Together, these settings give 100 epochs. The rule sets \(\delta=10^{-6}\), so the table’s \(10^{-5}\) is too large. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) recommends the stricter \(1/n^2\); also report \(\varepsilon\) at that value.
Publish the named accountant’s upper bound, rounded up; it does not certify the lower bound. Write the statement gives a complete privacy statement.

title: 25  Choosing an accountant
section: 25.5 Matching the accountant to the code
text:
25.5 Matching the accountant to the code
An accountant’s result is valid only if the code satisfies its assumptions. Many papers reported Poisson-sampling bounds but trained with fixed-size shuffled batches, a different algorithm (Ponomareva et al. 2023). Check the implementation against Table 25.3 before reporting.



Table 25.3: A checklist for matching the accountant to the training code.





Item
The accountant assumes
Check in the code
If it does not match




Sampler
Poisson sampling at rate \(q\)
Do batch sizes vary from step to step?
The sampler’s row of Subsampling: fixed-size batches at \(\sigma/2\); shuffle and partition unamplified, for zero-out neighbours


Neighbours
Add or remove one record
Which relation does the claim state?
Replace-one costs more per step; for Poisson sampling, compose the same steps in PLDAccountant(NeighboringRelation.REPLACE_ONE)


Unit
One record
Can one person give several records?
Clip and sample per user, or pay for the group (User-level DP)


Tuning, adaptivity and steps
Settings and steps fixed in advance
Tuning on private data, early stopping, restarts?
Account for the tuning runs (Hyperparameter tuning); report the planned maximum; keep the accountant’s state across restarts


Other data
Only the training rows are private
Pretraining, fitted preprocessing, validation rows?
Name them; preprocessing fitted on private rows needs its own budget






The sampler has the largest effect. At \(\delta=10^{-5}\), dp_accounting’s PLD gives 6.19 for Poisson sampling and 43.37 for fixed-size batches. Shuffle and partition give 91.82. The last bound applies only to zero-out neighbours (Subsampling).
Use the same checklist when reviewing another claim; Review someone else’s claim gives the review order.

title: 25  Choosing an accountant
text:
25.6 Checking an accountant
Test accountants against a known exact case. The sampling rate \(q\) is the probability that a record enters a batch; at \(q=1\), every record enters. Each step is then a full Gaussian mechanism, whose composition is exact (f-DP and Gaussian DP). Ten steps at noise multiplier 1 are \((17.8566,10^{-5})\)-DP. An upper bound must be at least 17.8566, and a PLD bracket must contain it. Also verify that \(\varepsilon\) does not decrease with more steps or increase with more noise.
Then compare two maintained libraries at pinned versions. This snippet recomputes Table 25.1 with Google’s dp_accounting.
import dp_accounting
from dp_accounting.pld import PLDAccountant
from dp_accounting.rdp import RdpAccountant

step = dp_accounting.PoissonSampledDpEvent(0.01, dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(1.0))
run = dp_accounting.SelfComposedDpEvent(step, 10_000)  # q = 0.01, sigma = 1, 10,000 steps
pld = PLDAccountant(value_discretization_interval=1e-4).compose(run)
rdp = RdpAccountant(orders=list(range(2, 65))).compose(run)  # integer orders only
print(f"{pld.get_epsilon(1e-5):.4f} {rdp.get_epsilon(1e-5):.4f}")  # 6.1877 6.7194
print(f"{pld.get_epsilon(1e-6):.4f} {rdp.get_epsilon(1e-6):.4f}")  # 6.9074 7.4869
Each PLD result falls inside the table’s bracket. RDP results are slightly higher because the table also evaluates fractional orders. When libraries disagree, compare their assumptions and calculations. RDP differences can result from using different orders; at order 10, that accounts for 0.3612 (RDP conversions). Non-overlapping PLD brackets may indicate a library bug. A factor-of-two difference often indicates different neighbouring relations.

title: 26  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
text:
26.1 Why this matters
An accountant maps settings for stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with differential privacy (DP) to privacy level \(\varepsilon\). Before training, it finds the noise needed for a target; afterward, it reports the run’s \(\varepsilon\). Both calculations can be wrong without an obvious training signal. Calibration and reporting may use different accountants, the loader may use a different sampler than assumed, or a restart may reset the step count. Any mismatch invalidates the claim without changing the loss curve.
This chapter accounts for DP-SGD on Adult from the UCI Machine Learning Repository; it does not train a model. The planned run uses 30,000 people, batches of 1,000, ten epochs and target \(\varepsilon = 4\). Train a model with DP-SGD performs the training.
The script practitioner_calibrate.py runs these steps in one to two minutes with Opacus 1.6.0 and dp-accounting 0.6.0. Defaults match Part 5. Options --n, --batch, --epochs and --epsilon configure another run, as shown for MNIST in the second command.

section: 26.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
text:
26.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
The guarantee protects one record, so define the record first. Each Adult row represents one person. If a person could have multiple rows, \(n\) must count people, as in User-level differential privacy.
Slack \(\delta\) bounds the probability of the guarantee’s exception. Set it using the book’s rule: at most \(1/n^{1.1}\), rounded down to a power of ten (How small δ must be).
def delta_for(n: int) -> float:
    """The book's default delta: at most 1/n^1.1, rounded down to a power of ten."""
    return 10.0 ** math.floor(math.log10(n**-1.1))
Adult rows: 48,842; Part 5's training split: n=30,000
delta_for(30,000) = 1e-05
delta_for(60,000) = 1e-06
delta_for(569) = 1e-04
Here, \(n\) counts people in the training split, not all Adult rows, so \(\delta\) is \(10^{-5}\). Set validation rows aside because the run neither trains on nor protects them. The other examples show that \(\delta\) must be recomputed for each dataset.

title: 26  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
text:
26.3 Choose the sampler
The accountants assume Poisson sampling: each record independently joins a batch with probability \(q\), so batch sizes vary. Other samplers can cost much more privacy (Section 26.6). For an expected batch size \(B\), the sampling rate is \(q = B/n\). A run of \(E\) epochs takes \(E/q\) steps, rounded down; the output calls this \(T\).
Poisson: B=1000, E=10: q=0.033333, T=300
Opacus DPDataLoader.from_data_loader: q=1/30=0.033333, 30 steps an epoch, 300 in 10 epochs
chosen run uses the loader's q and steps; get_noise_multiplier at that q counts int(E/q)=300: equal True
Training uses the Poisson DPDataLoader that Opacus creates from the input loader. Its rate is the reciprocal of the input loader’s batch count, \(\lceil n/B \rceil\), and it takes that many steps per epoch. Here, \(B\) divides \(n\), so both plans agree. Otherwise, the script reads \(q\) and \(T\) from the loader and checks that Opacus calibration counts the same steps.
This assumption fails if training uses a custom loader with shuffle=True and fixed batch_size; the logged batches will all have the same size (Amplification by subsampling).

title: 26  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
section: 26.5 Check ε with a second accountant
text:
26.5 Check ε with a second accountant
Train with the calibrated, unrounded \(\sigma\) as Part 5 does with Opacus’s 0.9729. If rounding is necessary, round up to the three decimals in the statement; lower noise increases \(\varepsilon\). Before training, compute the planned run’s \(\varepsilon\) with each available accountant. Include Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) in the comparison, but do not report it as a bound.
def crosscheck_epsilon(sigma: float, q: float, steps: int, delta: float) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Epsilon of one planned run by five accountants (GDP is the trap: it is not an upper bound)."""
    epsilons: dict[str, float] = {}
    for name, opacus_accountant in [("Opacus RDP", RDPAccountant()), ("Opacus PRV", PRVAccountant())]:
        opacus_accountant.history = [(sigma, q, steps)]  # what `steps` calls of .step() would record
        epsilons[name] = opacus_accountant.get_epsilon(delta)
    run = SelfComposedDpEvent(PoissonSampledDpEvent(q, GaussianDpEvent(sigma)), steps)
    epsilons["dp_accounting RDP"] = RdpAccountant().compose(run).get_epsilon(delta)
    epsilons["dp_accounting PLD"] = PLDAccountant().compose(run).get_epsilon(delta)
    gdp = GaussianAccountant()
    gdp.history = [(sigma, q, steps)]
    epsilons["Opacus GDP"] = gdp.get_epsilon(delta)
    return epsilons
chosen cell: Adult, B=1000, E=10, eps=4: sigma=0.972900 (Opacus PRV, as Part 5)
Opacus RDP         eps=4.50
Opacus PRV         eps=3.99
dp_accounting RDP  eps=4.50
dp_accounting PLD  eps=3.98
Opacus GDP         eps=3.34
PLD <= target: True; RDP >= PLD: True; |PRV - PLD|/PLD < 3%: True
crosscheck: pass
PLD bracket (grid 1e-4): lower 3.9656 (optimistic), upper 3.9806 (pessimistic); width 0.0150
The tight PRV and PLD accountants agree at 3.99 and 3.98, both meeting the target. The two RDP accountants agree at 4.50, a looser bound above target. GDP’s 3.34 is unsafe: it uses a central limit theorem (CLT) approximation rather than a bound and falls below certified results. Do not report it.
The pass line checks three conditions: PLD is at most the target, RDP is at least PLD within grid error, and PRV agrees with PLD within 3%. The PLD check fails if \(\sigma\) was rounded down or the step count differs from the plan. Any other failed comparison indicates mismatched accountant inputs.
The final line gives the PLD error interval. Rounding each step’s privacy loss up gives 3.9806; rounding down gives 3.9656. The true \(\varepsilon\) lies between them. Report the upper value and the lower value as its error bar (Which accountant). Longer runs widen the interval, so use a finer grid.

section: 26.6 If the loader is not Poisson
text:
26.6 If the loader is not Poisson
Some training loops use non-Poisson samplers with fixed batch sizes. Calculate their costs before training; the script evaluates four samplers from Amplification by subsampling.
Poisson (PLD)                              eps=3.98
fixed size, add/remove, sigma/2 (PLD)      eps=23.03
fixed size, replace-one (RDP)              eps=52.60
shuffle, zero-out, no amplification (PLD)  eps=18.51
PLDAccountant supports sampling without replacement: add/remove False, replace-one False
Fixed-size random batches cost more because an included record replaces another, allowing the clipped sum to move by twice the clipping norm \(C\). Under add/remove neighbours, account with a Poisson accountant at \(\sigma/2\); the cost rises from 3.98 to 23.03. For replace-one neighbours, only RDP supports the sampler, also at \(\sigma/2\) (last line). Its value 52.60 protects record values, not record presence, and is not comparable with add/remove values.
Shuffle-and-partition sampling has no amplification. The valid bound is one Gaussian step per epoch, 18.51 here, under zero-out neighbours, where one gradient is set to zero. State this relation explicitly. The sum changes by at most \(C\), as under add/remove, so the values are comparable. Shuffle-and-partition is cheaper than fixed-size random batches here, but the comparison reverses in the 100-epoch run of Matching the accountant to the code. Prefer Opacus’s Poisson loader when possible.

title: 26  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
text:
26.7 Train, stop early and resume
During training, Opacus’s optimizer calls accountant.step once per noisy update, or logical batch. This remains true when BatchMemoryManager divides it into smaller physical batches. The script simulates 300 calls and computes \(\varepsilon\) after each epoch.
def train_epochs(
    accountant: PRVAccountant, sigma: float, q: float, steps_per_epoch: int, epochs: int, delta: float
) -> list[float]:
    """Step the accountant once per logical batch for `epochs` epochs; epsilon at the end of each epoch."""
    epsilons: list[float] = []
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for _ in range(steps_per_epoch):
            accountant.step(noise_multiplier=sigma, sample_rate=q)  # what the optimizer's step does
        epsilons.append(float(accountant.get_epsilon(delta)))
    return epsilons
If validation loss stalls and training stops after six of ten epochs, the planned guarantee still covers this prefix. Report the planned maximum because stopping depends on released outputs; the realized six-epoch \(\varepsilon\) is not a valid claim. A privacy filter initialized at the first step could certify adaptive stopping (Adaptive composition). Log \(\varepsilon\) each epoch; it must not decrease. A decrease indicates an accountant reset.
Do not train beyond the planned maximum. Adding epochs after inspecting the model makes step count data-dependent. Create a new plan and account from the first step, or plan the longest run in advance and treat shorter runs as early stops.
When a job resumes, preserve accountant state. Save the accountant’s state_dict with the model and restore it before the next step. Opacus’s PrivacyEngine.save_checkpoint and load_checkpoint handle this.
state = accountant.state_dict()  # saved with the model; PrivacyEngine.save_checkpoint stores it too
# ... the job stops, and later restarts ...
restarted = PRVAccountant()
restarted.load_state_dict(state)  # without this, epsilon would restart from zero
resumed = train_epochs(restarted, sigma, q, steps_per_epoch, epochs - stop, delta)
steps_recorded = sum(steps for _, _, steps in restarted.history)
steps per epoch: 30; planned: 10 epochs = 300 steps
epoch  1: eps=1.70
epoch  2: eps=2.09
epoch  4: eps=2.69
epoch  6: eps=3.18
epsilon never decreases over 10 epochs: True
stopped early at epoch 6: eps=3.18; report the planned maximum: eps=3.99
after resuming at epoch 6: eps at epoch 10=3.99; uninterrupted run: eps=3.99; equal: True
steps recorded: 300; planned (the loader's 10 x 30): 300; equal: True
The resumed run ends at 3.99, like a run that never stopped, with all 300 steps in its history. A fresh accountant would have counted only the last four epochs and reported 2.69.

title: 26  Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run
text:
26.8 Write the statement
The last step writes the claim with every input that a reviewer needs to recompute it. The script fills the template from the run. It rounds up the PLD’s \(\varepsilon\) at two values of the slack, the rule’s \(\delta\) and \(1/n^2\), where \(n\) is still the number of training records.
def privacy_statement(
    unit: str, dataset: str, n: int, batch: int, epochs: int, sigma: float, clip: float, delta: float, calibration: str
) -> str:
    """The filled template of the reporting page: every input a reviewer needs to recompute epsilon."""
    q, _, steps = opacus_loader_plan(n, batch, epochs)  # the steps the Poisson loader runs
    run = SelfComposedDpEvent(PoissonSampledDpEvent(q, GaussianDpEvent(sigma)), steps)
    epsilon = round_up(PLDAccountant().compose(run).get_epsilon(delta))
    epsilon_tiny_delta = round_up(PLDAccountant().compose(run).get_epsilon(1 / n**2))
    return f"""\
Unit: one {unit} (a row of {dataset}); neighbouring datasets differ by adding or removing one {unit}
Data: n = {n:,}; Poisson sampling with q = {q:.6f} (B = {batch}); T = {steps:,} steps ({epochs} epochs)
Mechanism: DP-SGD, clipping norm C = {clip}, noise multiplier sigma = {sigma:.3f}
Accountant: PLD, dp-accounting {version("dp-accounting")}; {calibration}
Guarantee: (epsilon = {epsilon:.2f}, delta = {delta:.0e}); epsilon = {epsilon_tiny_delta:.2f} at delta = 1/n^2 = {1 / n**2:.1e}
Not covered: hyperparameter tuning runs (see Part 5), and any model released before this one"""
Unit: one person (a row of Adult); neighbouring datasets differ by adding or removing one person
Data: n = 30,000; Poisson sampling with q = 0.033333 (B = 1000); T = 300 steps (10 epochs)
Mechanism: DP-SGD, clipping norm C = 1.0, noise multiplier sigma = 0.973
Accountant: PLD, dp-accounting 0.6.0; calibrated with Opacus 1.6.0 (PRV)
Guarantee: (epsilon = 3.99, delta = 1e-05); epsilon = 6.30 at delta = 1/n^2 = 1.1e-09
Not covered: hyperparameter tuning runs (see Part 5), and any model released before this one
The guarantee reads 3.99 because the script rounds the PLD value up, while the cross-check above printed it to the nearest value, 3.98. The unit, the dataset and the clipping norm come from options, because the accountant never sees them. The last line matters most to a reviewer, because it names privacy spent outside this \(\varepsilon\). Examples are tuning on the private data (Hyperparameter tuning) and earlier models trained on the same people.
A published statement also gives what the script cannot know (Write the statement). That is the setting, the grid and bracket of the PLD, and the data outside the run, such as pretrained weights and the unprotected validation rows.

title: 27  Amplification by subsampling
text:
27.1 Why this matters
Private training often uses stochastic gradient descent (SGD) adapted to differential privacy (DP), called DP-SGD. Each step clips record gradients to a maximum length, the clipping norm, sums them and adds Gaussian noise. The noise standard deviation equals the clipping norm times the noise multiplier \(\sigma\). If every step used the full dataset, 10,000 steps at \(\sigma=1\) would cost \(\varepsilon=5425.5\) at \(\delta=10^{-5}\), providing no useful guarantee (Rényi DP).
DP-SGD reduces this cost by using a random batch at each step. Let \(q\) be the sampling rate, the probability that a record is included. Uncertainty about whether the record was sampled provides amplification by subsampling. The amplification depends on the sampling method, so the accountant must match the training sampler. A sampler mismatch causes larger accounting errors than the choice of accountant (Section 27.4).

title: 27  Amplification by subsampling
text:
27.2 One step under Poisson sampling
Under Poisson sampling, each record independently enters the batch with probability \(q\). This sampler pairs with add/remove neighbours, which differ by one extra record. Balle, Barthe and Gaboardi (2018) give the tightest one-step bound for this relation. If a full-dataset step is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP, where \(\delta\) is the slack defined in Part 3, then the same step on a Poisson sample is \((\varepsilon',\delta')\)-DP, with \[\varepsilon' = \ln\big(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\big), \qquad \delta' = q\delta. \tag{27.1}\]
The amplification depends on the step’s \(\varepsilon\). For small \(\varepsilon\), the cost is about \(q\varepsilon\): sampling 1% makes a 1-DP step cost 0.0170, about one hundred times less. For large \(\varepsilon\), the cost is approximately \[\varepsilon' \approx \varepsilon - \ln(1/q), \tag{27.2}\] so subsampling subtracts only a fixed amount; a 10-DP step on the same sample still costs 5.3993. The transition occurs near \(\varepsilon=\ln(1/q)\). Subsampling therefore helps most when each step is already fairly private, as in DP-SGD’s many small steps.
This result requires two conditions. Each record must be sampled independently with probability exactly \(q\), regardless of other batch members. The batch must also remain secret; an attacker who sees the sampled records, such as in a log, knows whether a step included the target.

title: 27  Amplification by subsampling
section: 27.3 Match the sampler to the accountant
text:
27.3 Match the sampler to the accountant
Most training code uses another sampler. Some implementations draw a new fixed-size batch of \(B\) from \(n\) records at every step. Others shuffle once per epoch and divide the data into consecutive batches, a method called shuffle and partition.
Each sampler requires accounting matched to its neighbouring relation. Under replace-one, datasets have the same size and differ in one record’s value. Under zero-out, the target’s gradient is set to zero. Table 27.1 lists the corresponding DP-SGD events in Google’s dp_accounting; a Rényi differential privacy (RDP) or privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant composes them.



Table 27.1: What to account for under each sampler and neighbouring relation in DP-SGD.











Sampler
Neighbours
What to account for

PoissonSampledDpEvent(q, GaussianDpEvent(σ))

The same event, at \(\sigma\), in a PLD accountant built with NeighboringRelation.REPLACE_ONE, which models the swap itself

The factor of two for fixed-size batches follows from the gradient sum. Under Poisson sampling, adding or removing one record changes the clipped sum by at most one clipping norm. A fixed-size batch has no extra slot, so a sampled record replaces another and the sum can change by twice as much (Lebeda et al. 2025). This is equivalent to halving the noise multiplier. Replace-one also swaps records and doubles the change; for fixed-size batches, only dp_accounting’s RDP accountant supports this relation.
Shuffle and partition provides no amplification because each record appears in exactly one batch per epoch. An attacker only needs to identify that batch. Chua et al. (2024) construct a dataset where the target gradient points against all others, making its batch distinguishable. At \(q=0.01\) and \(\sigma=1\), one shuffled epoch has \(\varepsilon\) at least 4.06, while a Poisson accountant reports at most 1.21. The valid bound is one full Gaussian release per epoch, as shown in the table, because each record is used once.
Inspect the data loader before accepting a reported \(\varepsilon\). A PyTorch DataLoader with shuffle=True and batch_size uses shuffle and partition. By default, Opacus replaces it with Poisson sampling: PrivacyEngine.make_private sets poisson_sampling=True. Its batch_sampler is a UniformWithReplacementSampler that independently samples each record, despite its name. Batch sizes therefore vary, which you can verify in the training log. If using another sampler, account for the matching row of Table 27.1 and report the sampler with \(\varepsilon\).

title: 27  Amplification by subsampling
text:
27.4 Accounting each sampler
Do not account for DP-SGD by applying Equation 27.1 separately to every step. This gives each step a very small share of \(\delta\), which raises its per-step \(\varepsilon\) and limits amplification. For 10,000 steps, advanced composition then gives 24379.55, worse than the 5425.5 bound without subsampling. An RDP accountant instead composes the Rényi curves and converts once, giving 6.71 (Rényi DP). A PLD accountant is tighter (Numerical accounting).
The snippet accounts for the run under four rows of Table 27.1, using 50,000 records and batches of 500 (\(q=0.01\)). It uses \(\delta=10^{-5}\) for comparison within this part, not the smaller reporting value (How small δ must be).
from dp_accounting import GaussianDpEvent, NeighboringRelation, PoissonSampledDpEvent
from dp_accounting import SampledWithoutReplacementDpEvent, SelfComposedDpEvent
from dp_accounting.pld import PLDAccountant
from dp_accounting.rdp import RdpAccountant

n, batch, sigma, steps, delta = 50_000, 500, 1.0, 10_000, 1e-5  # q = 0.01, 100 epochs
poisson = SelfComposedDpEvent(PoissonSampledDpEvent(batch / n, GaussianDpEvent(sigma)), steps)
fixed_size = SelfComposedDpEvent(PoissonSampledDpEvent(batch / n, GaussianDpEvent(sigma / 2)), steps)  # add/remove
shuffled = SelfComposedDpEvent(GaussianDpEvent(sigma), 100)  # one Gaussian release per epoch, no amplification
pld = [PLDAccountant(value_discretization_interval=1e-3).compose(e) for e in (poisson, fixed_size, shuffled)]  # 1e-3: the PLD's grid spacing
print(" ".join(f"{accountant.get_epsilon(delta):.2f}" for accountant in pld))  # 6.19 43.37 91.82
replace_one = RdpAccountant(neighboring_relation=NeighboringRelation.REPLACE_ONE)
swap = SampledWithoutReplacementDpEvent(n, batch, GaussianDpEvent(sigma / 2))  # replace-one: the sum moves by up to 2C
replace_one.compose(SelfComposedDpEvent(swap, steps))
print(f"{replace_one.get_epsilon(delta):.2f}")  # 118.73
Poisson sampling costs 6.19. With the same noise, fixed-size batches cost 43.37 under add/remove neighbours, about seven times more; shuffle and partition costs 91.82 under zero-out. The replace-one value, 118.73, protects a record’s value rather than its presence, so compare it only with other replace-one results. The sampler changes \(\varepsilon\) by at least sevenfold, while the accountant changes it by less than 10%: RDP gives 6.71 and PLD gives 6.19.
Before composing an unfamiliar event, check PLDAccountant().supports(event). For example, it returns False for SampledWithoutReplacementDpEvent.

title: 27  Amplification by subsampling
text:
27.5 Batch size, epochs and noise
Subsampling also affects run planning. Let \(E\) be the number of epochs; at sampling rate \(q\), the run takes \(E/q\) steps. For small \(q\) and a large noise multiplier, its Rényi cost at order \(\alpha\) is approximately \[\varepsilon(\alpha) \approx \frac{E\,q\,\alpha}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{27.3}\] At a fixed epoch count, a smaller sampling rate costs less privacy: each step costs about \(q^2\), while the step count grows as \(1/q\). Use this approximation only for planning. At high orders, the true curve rises substantially above it, beginning around order 9 for \(\sigma=1\) and \(q=0.01\).
Privacy is not the only cost: noise also affects the averaged gradient. If \(C\) is the clipping norm, noise on an average over \(B\) records has standard deviation \(\sigma C/B\). Compare plans using \(\sigma/B\), not \(\sigma\) alone. At the same \(\varepsilon\), a batch ten times larger needs a larger \(\sigma\), but its \(\sigma/B\) is six times smaller (Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run).
Plan in this order: choose batch size \(B\) and epochs \(E\) based on model accuracy. They determine \(q=B/n\) and the step count, where \(n\) is the filtered training-set size. Then use an accountant to find \(\sigma\). Specify the numerical accountant in Opacus’s get_noise_multiplier, whose default is RDP (Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run).

A Poisson number does not apply; better, switch the loader to Poisson sampling






Rules of thumb

Account for the sampler you run, check that its batches vary in size, and state the neighbouring relation next to \(\varepsilon\).

title: 28  Rényi differential privacy
text:
28.1 Why this matters
Model training may use thousands of private stochastic gradient descent (SGD) steps, but its report gives one differential privacy (DP) guarantee, \((\varepsilon,\delta)\). Part 3’s advanced composition can be too pessimistic (Composition). For example, 1,000 full-batch noisy gradient-descent steps, each with Gaussian noise 20 times the maximum per-record gradient change, give \(\varepsilon = 68.01\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) under advanced composition, nine times the exact value 7.51. Calibration to this loose bound adds unnecessary noise.
Rényi differential privacy (RDP) tracks a curve of privacy costs for each step. The curves compose without spending \(\delta\); convert the total to \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) once, after composition. Even Mironov’s original conversion (Section 28.6) gives 8.84 for this run, 18% above the exact value. Opacus and Google’s dp_accounting provide RDP accountants.

title: 28  Rényi differential privacy
text:
28.2 The RDP curve
A DP guarantee compares mechanism outputs on neighbouring datasets, which differ in one person’s record. RDP measures the distance between the output distributions using the Rényi divergence from Divergences. Its order \(\alpha > 1\) controls sensitivity to rare outputs: low orders emphasize typical outputs, while high orders give more weight to outputs much likelier on one dataset.
A mechanism is \((\alpha,\varepsilon)\)-RDP if its divergence is at most \(\varepsilon\) at order \(\alpha\) for every neighbouring pair. The smallest such value at each order defines its RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\); higher curves mean weaker privacy. The curve is nondecreasing. At infinite order it equals the largest output privacy loss, bounded by pure DP, where \(\delta=0\). Accountants use known curves for standard mechanisms on a grid of orders; you do not need to compute divergences directly.

title: 28  Rényi differential privacy
section: 28.3 RDP curves of the basic mechanisms
text:
28.3 RDP curves of the basic mechanisms
Accounting requires the mechanism’s RDP curve. The basic mechanisms have closed-form curves (Mironov 2017). For the Gaussian mechanism, let \(\sigma\) be its noise multiplier: the noise standard deviation divided by the query’s \(\ell_2\) sensitivity. Its curve is \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{28.1}\] Table 28.1 gives the curves of the Gaussian, Laplace and randomized-response mechanisms at a few orders, each at sensitivity 1.

The Gaussian curve has no finite limit, so the Gaussian mechanism is not pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any finite \(\varepsilon\). Its curve remains finite at each finite order, where accountants perform conversions. These curves describe full-dataset steps. For DP-SGD, each step uses a random batch, and libraries compute the smaller subsampled curves (Amplification by subsampling).

title: 28  Rényi differential privacy
text:
28.4 Composition adds curves
Training composes mechanisms sequentially, often adaptively: each gradient step depends on the current model. RDP adds their curves order by order. Let \(\varepsilon_i\) be the curve for step \(i\). A run of \(k\) steps has curve \(\varepsilon_M\) satisfying \[\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le \sum_{i=1}^k \varepsilon_i(\alpha) \qquad\text{for every order } \alpha. \tag{28.2}\] Different mechanisms can be mixed because composition adds their values at each common order.
The sum requires two conditions. All curves must use the same neighbouring relation, such as add/remove or replace-one, and the same privacy unit, such as one record or one user. Also, each step’s curve must be fixed before the run. Steps may depend on previous outputs, but data-dependent noise or stopping makes the curve data-dependent. Early stopping based on validation performance therefore requires Adaptive composition.
For Gaussian steps, each curve is the line \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\). Adding \(k\) such curves gives the cost of one step with noise multiplier \(\sigma/\sqrt k\). Thus, \(k\) full-dataset steps cost as much as one step with \(\sqrt k\) times less noise. For 10,000 steps at noise multiplier 1, this is equivalent to one step at multiplier \(1/\sqrt{10{,}000}=0.01\), whose \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta=10^{-5}\) is 5425.5. DP-SGD reduces this cost by using small random batches. The running example uses 10,000 steps at multiplier 1, each sampling 1% of the data.

title: 28  Rényi differential privacy
text:
28.5 Post-processing and group privacy
Post-processing is free in RDP: a computation on the output that does not access the data again cannot increase the curve. Releasing the trained model or its predictions therefore adds no cost beyond training.
The generic RDP group rule is loose. For Gaussian noise and a user with \(m\) records, use the group’s sensitivity, at most \(m\) times the per-record sensitivity. The curve is \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{group}}(\alpha) = \frac{m^2\alpha}{2\sigma^2}, \tag{28.3}\] This is \(m^2\) times the per-record curve; ten records per user therefore cost 100 times as much. Clip each user’s total contribution to one norm and account per user (User-level privacy).

title: 28  Rényi differential privacy
text:
28.6 Compose, then convert once
After composition, convert the curve to the reported \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) pair. Both libraries use the improved conversion (Balle et al. 2020; independently, Canonne, Kamath and Steinke 2020). Given curve value \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) at order \(\alpha\) and target \(\delta\), the conversion gives \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{28.4}\] Report the smallest \(\varepsilon'\) on the order grid, or 0 if it is negative. The minimizing order is the best order.
Older papers and code may use Mironov’s original conversion, which gives 7.43 rather than 6.71 for the DP-SGD example. The original paper’s moments accountant (Abadi et al. 2016) uses an RDP curve with that conversion. Its \(\varepsilon\) is looser but valid (From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests).

title: 28  Rényi differential privacy
text:
28.7 Check the order grid
A conversion can use only the orders on the grid of the accountant, so the grid must contain the best order. That order moves with the run, towards 1 for long runs with little noise and up for short runs with much noise. For the noisy gradient descent at the start of the chapter, it falls from 128 after one step to 4 after 1000.
The default grid of Opacus, RDPAccountant.DEFAULT_ALPHAS, stops at order 63, and that of dp_accounting, DEFAULT_RDP_ORDERS, at 1024. A best order at either end of the grid means that the true optimum is outside it, so give a longer list, with alphas=[...] in Opacus or orders=[...] in dp_accounting. Opacus warns you, but dp_accounting does not, so compare the returned order with the ends of the list yourself.

title: 28  Rényi differential privacy
text:
28.8 Accounting with a library
In practice, you describe each step to a library, and it composes and converts. In dp_accounting, a DP-SGD step is a GaussianDpEvent inside a PoissonSampledDpEvent, which samples each record independently, with probability 0.01 in the running example. This snippet composes the 10,000 steps and prints \(\varepsilon\) with the best order.
import dp_accounting

step = dp_accounting.PoissonSampledDpEvent(0.01, dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(1.0))
accountant = dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant()
accountant.compose(step, count=10_000)
eps, order = accountant.get_epsilon_and_optimal_order(1e-5)
print(f"{eps:.4f} {order:g}")  # 6.7128 4.1
In Opacus, the accountant is attached to the optimizer, which calls step after every noisy update. The same calls by hand give the same \(\varepsilon\) to the fourth decimal, at the same order, 4.1, which is well inside both grids.
from opacus.accountants import RDPAccountant

accountant = RDPAccountant()
for _ in range(10_000):  # what the optimizer does at each step of training
    accountant.step(noise_multiplier=1.0, sample_rate=0.01)
eps, order = accountant.get_privacy_spent(delta=1e-5)
print(f"{eps:.4f} {order:g}")  # 6.7127 4.1
Opacus’s defaults mix two accountants, so name the one that you want. In Opacus 1.6.0, PrivacyEngine uses "prv", a numerical accountant, by default, and accountant="rdp" selects this class. But get_noise_multiplier, which solves for the noise multiplier \(\sigma\), uses RDP by default. Both give valid upper bounds, but different ones, and the numerical accountant gives 6.19 for the running example.
Two more checks catch most mistakes. The event must match the sampler of your data loader, because shuffled batches of fixed size get none of the amplification of a Poisson event (Amplification by subsampling). And a manual call to step on top of the optimizer’s own call charges each update twice.

title: 29  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
29.1 What it is
An accountant that tracks Rényi differential privacy (RDP) returns a curve (Rényi differential privacy). At each order \(\alpha > 1\), it gives a privacy level \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\). A report needs a differential privacy (DP) guarantee \((\varepsilon',\delta)\). Conversion maps each point on the curve to such a pair; report the smallest resulting \(\varepsilon'\). These conversions are used to report the privacy cost of stochastic gradient descent (SGD).
Two conversions are in use. The original one, Mironov’s conversion (Mironov 2017), gives at each order \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{29.1}\] The improved conversion (Balle et al. 2020) gives \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{29.2}\] Both conversions are valid. At a fixed order, the improved conversion is always lower: by 0.3612 at order 10, and by more at smaller orders. Report 0 if the improved value is negative.
For example, one Gaussian release with noise multiplier 1 has the curve \(\alpha/2\). At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) its exact \(\varepsilon\) is 4.377, Mironov’s conversion gives 5.299 and the improved one 4.729.
crumbs: 29  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests

title: 29  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
29.2 When you meet it
Use these conversions when comparing RDP results from different sources. Opacus 1.6.0 and dp_accounting 0.6.0 use the improved conversion; older papers and code often use Mironov’s. In this part’s running example, 10,000 steps of private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) each sample 1% of the data and use noise multiplier 1. Mironov’s conversion gives 7.43, compared with 6.71 for the improved conversion.
The difference depends only on the order. Two RDP accountants reporting values about 0.36 apart for the same run, with a best order near 10, likely use different conversions. Recompute both with one library before comparing them.
crumbs: 29  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests

title: 29  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
29.3 How to use it
In dp_accounting, get_epsilon_and_optimal_order converts at the best grid order and returns both values. The same curve supports multiple \(\delta\) values, so get_epsilon can report several pairs without additional privacy cost. The snippet converts the Gaussian release above.
from dp_accounting import GaussianDpEvent
from dp_accounting.rdp import RdpAccountant

accountant = RdpAccountant()
accountant.compose(GaussianDpEvent(1.0))  # one release, noise multiplier 1
eps, order = accountant.get_epsilon_and_optimal_order(1e-5)
print(f"{eps:.4f} {order:g}")  # 4.7285 5.4
print(f"{accountant.get_epsilon(1e-8):.4f}")  # 6.0864
Reducing \(\delta\) by a factor of 1,000 raises \(\varepsilon\) from 4.7285 to 6.0864 because the conversion depends logarithmically on \(\delta\). The best order is selected from a fixed grid. Short, high-noise runs may require orders above 63, beyond Opacus’s default grid. If the returned order is at a grid endpoint, extend the grid and convert again (Rényi differential privacy).
crumbs: 29  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests

title: 29  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
29.4 What goes wrong
No conversion reaches the exact value because the curve is only a summary. Other mechanisms with the same curve may have a larger exact \(\varepsilon\), so the conversion must cover them too. For the plain Gaussian mechanism, the improved conversion is 5–10% above the exact value, and the gap is larger for subsampled DP-SGD steps. A privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant tracks the full distribution and returns the exact 4.377 for the single release (Numerical accounting).
Conversion is one-way: an \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) guarantee with \(\delta>0\) does not determine an RDP curve. For example, a mechanism that publishes a record with probability \(\delta\) is \((0,\delta)\)-DP but has infinite Rényi divergence. Do not enter an \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) pair into an RDP accountant; obtain the curve from the mechanism.
A conversion also loses what the curve says about attacks. Take a membership attack on the single release above, at a false-positive rate of \(10^{-3}\). The curve limits the attack’s true-positive rate to \(2.4910 \times 10^{-2}\). But the pair at \(\varepsilon = 4.729\) limits it only to 0.1131 (f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy).

title: 30  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
30.1 What it is
A privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant numerically computes the privacy level \(\varepsilon\) of a complete differential privacy (DP) run. Compare a dataset with a neighbour differing in one record. The privacy loss \(L\) is the logarithm of the output likelihood ratio between these datasets. Because the output is random, \(L\) has a distribution called the PLD. Outputs with loss above \(\varepsilon\) contribute to slack \(\delta\); the minimum slack is given below, where \((\cdot)_+\) sets negative values to 0: \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \mathbb E\big[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\big]. \tag{30.1}\]
With independent noise, step losses add, so the run’s PLD is the convolution of the step PLDs. Numerical error comes from representing losses on a grid with spacing \(h\). Rounding losses up can only increase \(\delta\), so the resulting \(\varepsilon\) is an upper bound, the pessimistic value. Rounding down gives the optimistic lower bound. Each step’s loss shifts by at most \(h\), so after \(T\) steps the two bounds differ by at most \(Th\).
crumbs: 30  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions

title: 30  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
30.2 When you meet it
Opacus uses a PLD accountant by default for training: "prv" is the privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant of Gopi, Lee and Wutschitz (2021). It rounds each loss to a grid point, adds a proven error bound and reports the upper value. Google’s dp_accounting provides PLDAccountant; its default connect the dots method gives the tightest pessimistic rounding on a grid.
Table 30.1 compares PLD accounting with Rényi differential privacy (RDP) and the central limit theorem (CLT) estimate of Gaussian differential privacy (GDP). title: 30  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
30.3 How to use it
In dp_accounting, compose the run as an event and request \(\varepsilon\) at the desired \(\delta\). The get_delta method instead returns a bound on \(\delta\) for a chosen \(\varepsilon\).
from dp_accounting import GaussianDpEvent, PoissonSampledDpEvent, SelfComposedDpEvent
from dp_accounting.pld import PLDAccountant
from opacus.accountants import PRVAccountant

run = SelfComposedDpEvent(PoissonSampledDpEvent(0.01, GaussianDpEvent(1.0)), 10_000)
pld = PLDAccountant(value_discretization_interval=1e-4).compose(run)  # h, 10x the table's
print(f"{pld.get_epsilon(1e-5):.4f}")  # 6.1877
print(f"{pld.get_delta(6.24):.1e}")  # 8.5e-06

prv = PRVAccountant()
prv.history = [(1.0, 0.01, 10_000)]  # (noise multiplier, sample rate, steps)
print(f"{prv.get_epsilon(delta=1e-5):.4f}")  # 6.1980
Both answers are upper bounds within Table 30.1’s bracket. A reviewer can use get_delta to verify the \((6.24,10^{-5})\) claim: it bounds the run’s slack at that \(\varepsilon\) by \(8.5\times10^{-6}\).
Each library exposes one accuracy setting. In dp_accounting, value_discretization_interval sets grid spacing; making the grid ten times finer narrows the bracket tenfold and uses about ten times more memory. In Opacus, eps_error sets the allowed error in \(\varepsilon\). Since error grows with the number of steps, configure either setting for the longest planned run.
crumbs: 30  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions

title: 30  Numerical accounting with privacy loss distributions
text:
30.4 What goes wrong
The main reporting error is to use the wrong side of the bracket. Only the pessimistic value, or the PRV accountant’s upper value, is a guarantee; the optimistic value and midpoint are estimates.
Under add/remove adjacency, a subsampled step has separate PLDs for adding and removing a record; neither direction is always larger. An accountant must compose both and report the larger, as dp_accounting does by default. Opacus’s PRV accountant models removal only, which is the larger direction in this example. Both libraries assume Poisson sampling; shuffled or fixed-size batches violate that assumption (Amplification by subsampling).
For a run that adapts its steps or noise to earlier outputs, use a filter (Adaptive composition).

title: 31  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
31.1 What it is
Every differential privacy (DP) guarantee limits an attacker’s ability to determine whether a target’s record was in the data. The attacker performs a hypothesis test, so the most complete guarantee is a trade-off curve: the minimum false negative rate at each false positive rate. A mechanism is \(f\)-DP if its curve is nowhere below a specified curve \(f\) (Dong, Roth and Su 2022). A privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and slack \(\delta\) summarize this curve.
For Gaussian noise, the curve has one parameter. Let \(\sigma\) be the noise multiplier, the noise standard deviation in units of the query’s \(\ell_2\) sensitivity. The attacker must distinguish a standard normal draw from one shifted by \(\mu = 1/\sigma\). The mechanism therefore satisfies Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) with parameter \(\mu\), or \(\mu\)-GDP. Let \(\Phi\) be the standard normal distribution function. At false positive rate \(\alpha\), no membership attack achieves a true positive rate above \[1 - \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \alpha) - \mu\big). \tag{31.1}\]
crumbs: 31  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy

title: 31  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
31.2 When you meet it
Use GDP to assess whether a guarantee is sufficient; Opacus also exposes it as a potentially unsafe option (Section 31.4). Table 31.1 gives the maximum true positive rate (TPR) at each false positive rate (FPR), regardless of the attacker’s other information. The same representation can account for stochastic gradient descent (SGD) runs without subsampling.

title: 31  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
31.3 How to use it
Gaussian releases compose exactly in GDP, including adaptive releases. Let \(\mu_i\) be the parameter of release \(i\). The full run is \(\mu\)-GDP, where \[\mu = \sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \mu_2^2 + \dots + \mu_k^2}, \tag{31.2}\] Thus, \(\mu^2\) composes additively. For whole-dataset releases, such as analytics queries and full-batch noisy gradient descent, no accountant gives a tighter bound. Track \(\mu^2\) and convert once after composition. Four 1-GDP releases compose to 2-GDP, or \((9.9973,10^{-5})\)-DP. Converting each release separately using one quarter of the slack gives a summed \(\varepsilon\) of 18.7607, almost twice as large.
The snippet computes the attack ceiling and converts between GDP and \((\varepsilon,\delta)\). The dp_accounting functions accept a noise multiplier, so pass \(1/\mu\) for \(\mu\)-GDP.
from statistics import NormalDist

import dp_accounting

N = NormalDist()


def attack_power(mu: float, fpr: float) -> float:
    """Best true positive rate of any membership attack on mu-GDP at a false positive rate."""
    return 1 - N.cdf(N.inv_cdf(1 - fpr) - mu)


print(" ".join(f"{attack_power(mu, 0.001):.4f}" for mu in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0)))  # 0.0048 0.0183 0.1378
print(f"{dp_accounting.get_epsilon_gaussian(1.0, 1e-5):.4f}")  # 4.3772
print(f"{dp_accounting.get_sigma_gaussian(1.0, 1e-5):.4f}")  # 3.7306
The final line returns the noise multiplier for one \((1,10^{-5})\)-DP release. It uses the exact curve, which requires less noise than the classical formula in the Gaussian mechanism.
crumbs: 31  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy

title: 31  f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy
text:
31.4 What goes wrong
Opacus supports accountant="gdp" for DP-SGD. It estimates \(\mu\) using the central limit theorem (CLT) of Bu et al. (2020), which approximates many small privacy losses by a Gaussian curve. This is an approximation, not a bound, and its error can be unsafe. Small \(\delta\) depends on rare, large losses that the CLT models poorly. For this part’s 10,000-step example, the CLT gives 6.0071, while a numerical accountant establishes that true \(\varepsilon\) is at least 6.1377. Use Opacus’s default numerical accountant, "prv", for reporting.
Mixed Laplace and Gaussian releases require a numerical accountant because their composition is not Gaussian. For Gaussian pipelines without subsampling, GDP is the tightest accountant. Even the best conversion from a Rényi DP curve is looser: for 1-GDP at \(\varepsilon = 1\), it gives \(\delta = 0.2149\) instead of the exact 0.1269.

title: 32  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
32.1 What it is
Differential privacy (DP) composition theorems assume that each step’s privacy parameter and the total step count are fixed before the run (Composition). Adaptive runs violate this assumption when later choices depend on earlier outputs; for example, training may stop based on validation loss. The fixed-parameter theorems do not cover the realized values (Rogers et al. 2016). This plug-in mistake can make the bound fail about three times as often as its stated \(\delta\).
A privacy filter fixes a total budget and rejects any step that would exceed it, preserving the guarantee under any stopping rule. A privacy odometer reports cumulative spend for open-ended analyses. Its anytime guarantee has a higher \(\varepsilon\).
crumbs: 32  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 32  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
32.2 When you meet it
Early stopping with a fixed maximum needs neither tool. Set noise, sampling rate and maximum steps in advance. You can then stop when validation loss stops improving, because the executed steps are a prefix of the plan. Report the planned maximum’s \(\varepsilon\), not the value for the steps actually run. The plan’s guarantee is \((5.299, 10^{-5})\)-DP. It covers 100 full-batch Gaussian steps at noise multiplier 10. Training may stop at step 60 and still use that guarantee.
The stop signal must use released models or held-out data, so the decision is post-processing. To exceed the maximum, create a new plan and account for the run from its first step. When resuming, restore the accountant state (the calibration workflow).
Use filters when training changes noise in response to outputs. Analytics services also provide them, including OpenDP’s make_privacy_filter and Tumult Analytics’ Session.
crumbs: 32  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 32  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
32.3 How to use it
Feldman and Zrnic’s (2021) Rényi filter uses one Rényi divergence order \(\alpha\), the order parameter fixed in advance. It charges each step’s Rényi differential privacy (RDP) spend at that order (Rényi DP). A step’s spend may depend on earlier outputs, but must be known before that step runs. The filter rejects any step that would exceed budget \(B\). Let \(\varepsilon_g\) denote the target privacy level and \(\delta\) the slack. Invert the RDP conversion to set \[B = \varepsilon_g - \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{32.1}\]
Let \(\sigma\) denote the Gaussian noise multiplier, the standard deviation relative to sensitivity. A Gaussian step then spends \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\) at order \(\alpha\). For this target, the best order is 5.8 and the budget is \(B = 2.900\). This allows 100 full-batch steps at noise multiplier 10. If validation loss stops improving at step 60, halving the noise makes each later step cost four times as much. The remaining budget covers 10 more steps and preserves the target.
OpenDP’s filter uses zero-concentrated DP (zCDP). Its budget \(\rho\) bounds RDP spend at every order (Concentrated DP).
import opendp.prelude as dp

dp.enable_features("contrib")
domain, metric = dp.atom_domain(T=float, nan=False), dp.absolute_distance(T=float)
odometer = dp.c.make_fully_adaptive_composition(domain, metric, dp.zero_concentrated_divergence())
queryable = dp.c.make_privacy_filter(odometer, d_in=1.0, d_out=0.5)(0.0)  # rho = 0.5, i.e. 2.9 at order 5.8

answered = 0
try:
    for _ in range(1000):  # sigma = 10: rho = 1 / (2 sigma^2) = 0.005 each
        queryable(dp.m.make_gaussian(domain, metric, scale=10.0))
        answered += 1
except dp.OpenDPException:  # the release that would exceed the budget
    pass
print(answered)  # 99
OpenDP permits 99 releases rather than 100 because it rounds each charge up for floating-point safety. For pure-DP queries, the Whitehouse filter (Whitehouse et al. 2023) allows more small queries than basic summation of \(\varepsilon\).
crumbs: 32  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting

title: 32  Adaptive composition: filters, odometers and individual accounting
text:
32.4 What goes wrong
An odometer gives a looser bound than a filter. The Ville odometer converts RDP spend at the best order on a grid fixed in advance. It accounts for this later choice by dividing \(\delta\) by the grid size. For the 100-step run above, this raises \(\varepsilon\) from 5.299 to 6.253.
Individual accounting charges each record according to its clipped gradient norm, since smaller gradients move the model less. It excludes a record when its spend would exceed the budget. In the full edition’s simulation, median individual \(\varepsilon\) is 3.17, compared with worst-case 5.299. Because this accounting uses observed norms, it is an estimate rather than a guarantee. It also reveals which records the model fits well. High-gradient records are excluded first and may be the records the model serves worst (Disparate impact).

title: 33  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
33.1 What it is
Zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) represents a differential privacy (DP) budget by one composable number. It uses the curve of Rényi differential privacy (RDP), which bounds divergence between outputs on neighbouring datasets at each order \(\alpha\), where \(\alpha\) denotes the order parameter. A mechanism is \(\rho\)-zCDP when its curve lies below the line \(\rho\alpha\). Composition adds these slopes, including for adaptive steps.
The Gaussian mechanism has a linear RDP curve. Let \(f\) denote the query. Let \(\Delta_2 f\) denote its \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, the largest Euclidean change caused by replacing one record. Let \(\sigma\) denote the standard deviation of the added noise. A release costs \[\rho = \frac{(\Delta_2 f)^2}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{33.1}\] With noise multiplier 1, \(\sigma = \Delta_2 f\) and \(\rho = 0.5\). Doubling the noise reduces \(\rho\) to one quarter.

title: 33  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
33.2 When you meet it
Use zCDP for whole-dataset releases with Gaussian noise, such as noisy counts or the marginals used to generate synthetic data. The 2020 United States Census used zCDP with the discrete Gaussian mechanism (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms). Tumult Analytics and OpenDP also represent budgets with \(\rho\). For stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with differential privacy, use RDP or numerical accounting instead.

title: 33  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
33.3 How to use it
Track releases in a ledger and charge each according to Table 33.1.



Table 33.1: What each kind of step costs in a zCDP ledger.










Step
Charge in \(\rho\)
Notes




Gaussian, sensitivity \(\Delta_2 f\), noise \(\sigma\)
\((\Delta_2 f)^2/(2\sigma^2)\)
Exact


Any pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP step
\(\varepsilon^2/2\), or \(\varepsilon^2/8\) for an exponential mechanism
Above the plain \(\varepsilon\) once \(\varepsilon \ge 2\): keep such a step in RDP


An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP step
\(\varepsilon^2/2\), plus \(\delta\) in a second column that also adds
Approximate zCDP

\((\Delta_2 f)^2/(2\sigma^2)\), as without sampling
No amplification






Add the charges, then convert the total once. Let \(\varepsilon\) denote the resulting privacy level, and let \(\delta\) denote the slack. For an all-Gaussian ledger, total \(\rho\) is equivalent to one Gaussian release with noise multiplier \(1/\sqrt{2\rho}\), so get_epsilon_gaussian converts it exactly. The snippet performs this conversion and calibrates a \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP release.
from math import sqrt

import dp_accounting

rho = 1 / (2 * 1.0**2)  # one Gaussian release, noise multiplier 1
print(f"{rho:.1f} {dp_accounting.get_epsilon_gaussian(1 / sqrt(2 * rho), 1e-5):.4f}")  # 0.5 4.3772
sigma = dp_accounting.get_sigma_gaussian(1.0, 1e-5)  # one release that must be (1, 1e-5)-DP
budget = 1 / (2 * sigma**2)
quarter = budget / 4  # four releases share it
print(f"{budget:.5f} {sigma:.3f} {1 / sqrt(2 * quarter):.3f}")  # 0.03593 3.731 7.461
For a target privacy level of 1 and slack \(10^{-5}\), the required budget is \(\rho = 0.03593\). One query meets it with noise multiplier 3.731. If four queries share this budget equally, each receives one quarter and requires twice the noise. Allocate in \(\rho\), which composes exactly, not in \(\varepsilon\). A histogram with each person in one cell incurs one charge, not one per cell (Parallel composition).
For a ledger containing non-Gaussian steps, conversion is not exact. At \(\rho = 0.5\), Bun and Steinke’s (2016) simple conversion is 21% above the exact Gaussian value. Canonne, Kamath and Steinke’s (2020) improved conversion is 8% above. The RDP accountant in dp_accounting uses this improved conversion. Use it, or the exact conversion for an all-Gaussian ledger, and identify the method in the report.

title: 33  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
33.4 What goes wrong
Do not confuse \(\rho\) with \(\varepsilon\). A Gaussian release at \(\rho = 0.5\) converts to privacy level \(\varepsilon = 4.3772\). This conversion uses slack \(10^{-5}\); it is not privacy level \(\varepsilon = 0.5\). Also, \(\rho\) covers only data processed through the private mechanism. The Census Bureau released some counts exactly; list these invariants separately because they are outside the guarantee.
Do not account for subsampled steps with zCDP because it does not capture subsampling amplification. In this part’s running example, zCDP gives privacy level \(\varepsilon = 5475.8\) at slack \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for DP-SGD. RDP gives 6.719 for the same run. Use RDP or a numerical accountant for DP-SGD pipelines. Add a \(\rho\)-zCDP release without loss as a GaussianDpEvent with noise multiplier \(1/\sqrt{2\rho}\).
Multiple records from one user increase cost: a group of \(m\) records costs \(m^2\rho\). Four records in a 0.1-zCDP release therefore cost \(\rho = 1.6\).
Budgets do not renew automatically: releases about the same people compose across years. Set the accounting period and total in advance (Release and governance). Track long-term budgets in \(\rho\), not diffprivlib’s BudgetAccountant, which adds \(\varepsilon\) by basic composition (Keeping a budget).

title: 33  Concentrated differential privacy
text:
33.5 References

Bun & Steinke, “Concentrated Differential Privacy: Simplifications, Extensions, and Lower Bounds” (TCC 2016): the definition.
Canonne, Kamath & Steinke, “The Discrete Gaussian for Differential Privacy” (NeurIPS 2020): the improved conversion.

Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 34  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
34.1 What it is
In the shuffle model, each of \(n\) users randomizes their data, producing a report that satisfies local differential privacy (DP) at level \(\varepsilon_0\). A shuffler removes identities and randomizes report order. The combined reports then satisfy central DP at a smaller \(\varepsilon\), which scales as \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/n}\) for \(\delta>0\). Results here use replace-one neighbours.
For binary randomized response, the analyst observes only the count of 1-reports, allowing an exact shuffled guarantee. For other local randomizers, use the clone bound of Feldman, McMillan and Talwar (2021). Another user’s report matches a possible target report with probability \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\); these clones conceal the target’s report. The numeric clone bound computes the guarantee directly. The paper’s closed form is looser and requires enough users.
crumbs: 34  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration

title: 34  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
34.2 When you meet it
Shuffling is used in telemetry systems such as Prochlo (Bittau et al. 2017), where you must choose \(\varepsilon_0\). No maintained library supports this accounting, so use shuffling_iteration.py from the full edition.
Two other uses of “shuffle” do not provide this amplification. A data loader that shuffles once per epoch is a sampler (Match the sampler to the accountant). Federated clients that join when available do not pass through a shuffler; account for them without amplification or use matrix mechanisms.

The bound can determine whether a design is feasible. For 100,000 users and a target of 0.2, the closed form permits \(\varepsilon_0\) up to 2, while the numeric bound permits 4. Use the tighter numeric bound.
Verify these assumptions before reporting shuffled \(\varepsilon\). If any fail—for example, if report order leaks—only the local guarantee \(\varepsilon_0\) remains.

The order is uniformly random and hidden, with no metadata such as arrival time or network address.
The shuffler does not collude with the analyst.
Only honest users count in the number of users \(n\), because colluders reveal their reports to the analyst.
The count of users is the number of reports shuffled, so with several batches it is the size of the smallest batch.
Each user sends one report per batch, or the reports compose like any other releases.
crumbs: 34  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration

title: 34  Amplification by shuffling and by iteration
text:
34.4 What goes wrong
Approximations become unreliable with few users or large \(\varepsilon_0\). For 1,000 users at \(\varepsilon_0=4\), a normal approximation to the count of 1-reports gives 0.9667, compared with the exact value 1.6910.
In amplification by iteration, later training noise also protects records used earlier. The result applies to one pass of noisy stochastic gradient descent (SGD) whose weights remain in a fixed convex set (Feldman et al. 2018). It requires releasing only the final model and making every step a contraction, meaning it cannot increase the distance between weight vectors. This requires a convex, smooth loss and a sufficiently small step size.
The privacy gain varies by record. For 10,000 records and noise multiplier 1, the middle record gets \(\varepsilon=0.0707\) at \(\delta=10^{-5}\), while the last record gets 5.2985, the cost of one Gaussian step. Report the worst-case value.
Deep learning typically violates both conditions. Checkpoints, logged models and selecting the best of several checkpoints reveal more than the final model alone. Steps on non-convex losses need not be contractions; Annamalai (2024) constructs a loss where the final model leaks as much as all intermediate models. Claim iteration amplification only for convex models, such as logistic regression, when releasing only final weights.
