title: Differential privacy in machine learning
text:
This part covers model training, deployment and review under differential privacy (DP). It builds on the Gaussian mechanism and composition in Part 3, the accountants in Part 4 and the membership-inference audits in Part 2.
Private training produces a privacy guarantee and a model. An accountant computes \(\varepsilon\); evaluation measures utility, such as accuracy. The main algorithm is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipped per-example gradients and Gaussian noise (DP-SGD). Its accountant depends on the noise multiplier, sampling rate and step count. The chapters assess both the validity of \(\varepsilon\) and model utility at that level.
Three pages present end-to-end workflows using real libraries and public data. Train a model with DP-SGD trains an Adult classifier with Opacus. Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA adapts a small public model to private text and tests for memorized information. Release and governance recomputes and documents the guarantee, relates it to law, and gives pre-release checks.
The other chapters explain workflow decisions. Private empirical risk minimization covers convex models, followed by DP-SGD, hyperparameter tuning, user-level differential privacy and choosing ε. Public data and private fine-tuning covers public starting models. Disparate impact and Auditing private training address pre-release checks. Reference pages cover private prediction, correlated noise across steps and adaptive data analysis.
Scripts check every reported number.

title: 35  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
35.1 What it is
Empirical risk minimization (ERM) selects weights \(\theta\) that minimize average loss on a training set. Let \(D\) be the training set and \(n\) its record count. Let \(\lambda\) be the strength of the ridge penalty. Training minimizes \[\mathcal L(\theta; D) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\theta; z_i) + \frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2, \tag{35.1}\] where \(\ell(\theta; z)\) is the loss of the weights on one record \(z\). Differential privacy (DP) requires that replacing one record has limited effect on released weights. Add noise to the final weights, the objective or each gradient step.
Output perturbation trains normally, then adds Gaussian noise to the final weights, with slack \(\delta\). Calibrate noise to the maximum change in trained weights \(\theta^*\) between neighbouring datasets \(D\) and \(D'\). For a convex loss, ridge regularization bounds that change: \[\|\theta^*(D) - \theta^*(D')\| \le \frac{2L}{\lambda n}. \tag{35.2}\] Here, \(L\) bounds the maximum norm of one record’s loss gradient. For logistic regression, labels are \(\pm1\) and feature norms are at most 1. These conditions give L of 1.
Objective perturbation adds a random linear term to the objective and minimizes it exactly. Part of privacy budget \(\varepsilon\) accounts for loss curvature, bounded by constant \(c\) (one quarter for logistic loss). The remaining budget is \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon - 2\ln\Big(1 + \frac{c}{n\lambda}\Big). \tag{35.3}\] As \(n\lambda\) decreases, the subtracted term increases. With little data, increase the ridge strength to keep \(\varepsilon'\) positive.
Gradient perturbation adds noise at every gradient step. With random batches and clipped per-record gradients, this is noisy stochastic gradient descent (SGD), or DP-SGD, which also applies to non-convex models.

title: 35  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
35.2 When you meet it
Use these methods for linear models, such as a linear probe on features from a public pretrained network (Public data and private fine-tuning). Objective perturbation often gives higher accuracy because the objective’s full curvature reduces its noise; output perturbation relies only on ridge curvature. Use output perturbation when training is a black box.
Required data depends on \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\). In the training objective, they enter through their product, so halving \(\varepsilon\) has the same effect as halving the sample size. On new data with \(d\) features, privacy adds less error than sampling once \(n\) is much larger than \(d\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon^2\).

title: 35  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
35.3 How to use it
IBM’s diffprivlib offers objective perturbation as LogisticRegression(epsilon=..., data_norm=...), with data_norm bounding each row’s length. Its version 0.6.6 fails with scikit-learn 1.8, so the snippet calls the mechanism it wraps, mechanisms.Vector, with the curvature bound \(c\) as function_sensitivity. The breast-cancer data has no public data dictionary for feature bounds. So the snippet treats 500 rows as private and 69 as a public stand-in. It clips the private rows to the stand-in’s log-transformed ranges and maps them to \([-1, 1]\). A constant 1 replaces the intercept, and dividing by \(\sqrt{31}\) keeps each row’s length at most 1.
import numpy as np
from diffprivlib.mechanisms import Vector
from scipy.optimize import minimize
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
data = load_breast_cancer()
public, private = np.log1p(data.data[:69]), np.log1p(data.data[69:])  # 69 stand-in rows fix the bounds
lo, hi = public.min(axis=0), public.max(axis=0)
X = np.hstack([2 * (np.clip(private, lo, hi) - lo) / (hi - lo) - 1, np.ones((500, 1))]) / np.sqrt(31)
y = 2 * data.target[69:] - 1
Xt, yt, n = X[::2], y[::2], 250  # even rows train, odd rows test
lam = 1 / n  # diffprivlib's default ridge, fixed in advance

def objective(w):  # J(w) and its gradient
    m = yt * (Xt @ w)
    return np.logaddexp(0, -m).mean() + lam / 2 * w @ w, lam * w - Xt.T @ (yt / (1 + np.exp(m))) / n

def accuracy(eps, seed):  # eps = inf adds no noise
    vector = Vector(epsilon=eps, function_sensitivity=0.25, dimension=31, alpha=n * lam, n=n, random_state=seed)
    w = minimize(vector.randomise(objective), np.zeros(31), jac=True, options={"gtol": 1e-9}).x
    return np.mean(np.sign(X[1::2] @ w) == y[1::2])

print(" ".join(f"{np.mean([accuracy(e, s) for s in range(20)]):.3f}" for e in [1, 4, np.inf]))  # 0.783 0.946 0.964
Across 20 noise draws, test accuracy is 0.783 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 0.946 at \(\varepsilon = 4\). Without noise, it is 0.964. With 250 training records, accuracy is close to the non-private result only at \(\varepsilon = 4\). No parameter was tuned on the private rows, so the guarantee is pure DP for the 250 training rows under replace-one adjacency. The 69 stand-in rows receive no protection.

title: 35  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
35.4 What goes wrong
The common failure is deriving a bound from private data. If omitted, data_norm is calculated from training rows and raises PrivacyLeakWarning; the guarantee is then invalid. A range table computed from those rows also leaks through its minima and maxima. Set bounds from public knowledge or public rows, then clip private rows to them.
The solver can also violate assumptions: output and objective perturbation require the exact minimizer. If optimization stops with gradient norm \(g\), sensitivity increases by \(2g/\lambda\). This increase is negligible relative to exact sensitivity \(2L/(\lambda n)\) only when \(g\) is much less than \(L/n\). Set a corresponding tolerance and inspect the final gradient norm, not just the iteration count.
The sensitivity bound also requires ridge curvature in every direction. Scikit-learn’s loss, reused by diffprivlib, leaves the intercept unpenalized, so the snippet adds a constant feature. Set \(\lambda\) by a fixed rule or public data; private-data tuning must be accounted for (Hyperparameter tuning). These guarantees use replace-one neighbours, unlike later add/remove accounting, and the bounds are not directly interchangeable. State the relation with every \(\varepsilon\).
Derivations. Every result here is derived step by step in the full edition’s chapter.

title: 36  DP-SGD
text:
36.1 Why this matters
Nearly every deep-learning system with differential privacy (DP) uses the differentially private version of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD: it clips per-record gradients and adds Gaussian noise at each step (Abadi et al. 2016). Clipping bounds each record’s effect on the model; noise obscures that effect. An accountant composes step costs into privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and slack \(\delta\).
The accountant uses only the noise, sampling rate and number of steps; it does not inspect the model. These parameters determine \(\varepsilon\), while clipping norm and learning rate can be tuned for accuracy. Most failures arise when code violates a proof assumption, so implementation checks are as important as parameter choices. Train a model with DP-SGD demonstrates the full Opacus workflow.

title: 36  DP-SGD
text:
36.2 The algorithm and its guarantee
A training set holds \(n\) records. The gradient of one record’s loss is its per-example gradient, written \(g_i\) for record \(i\). Each step of DP-SGD does five things.

Sample a batch. Each record enters independently with probability \(q\), the sampling rate, which is called Poisson sampling.
Compute the per-example gradient of each record in the batch.
Clip each gradient longer than the clipping norm \(C\) to length \(C\).
Sum the clipped gradients, and add Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(\sigma C\) to each coordinate, where the noise multiplier \(\sigma\) measures the noise in units of \(C\).
Divide the noisy sum by the expected batch size \(B = qn\), a fixed public number, and step against it, scaled by the learning rate \(\eta\).

Write \(\theta_t\) for the weights at step \(t\) and \(S_t\) for its batch. With Gaussian noise \(\xi_t\) drawn afresh on each coordinate, the update is \[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \frac{\eta}{B}\Big(\sum_{i\in S_t}g_i\min\Big(1, \frac{C}{\|g_i\|}\Big) + \xi_t\Big), \qquad \xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2I). \tag{36.1}\] Releasing every intermediate set of weights then satisfies \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for add/remove neighbours, datasets that differ by one record (Amplification by subsampling).
This part’s running example (Section 36.7) is the run of Train a model with DP-SGD. A network with one hidden layer of 64 units learns from 30,000 people of the Adult census survey whether a person’s income exceeds $50K. It runs 300 steps with \(\sigma = 0.973\), and each person joins a batch with probability \(q = 1/30\), so a batch holds about 1,000 people. At the \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) of the book’s rule (How small δ must be), the accountant Opacus uses gives \(\varepsilon = 3.99\) for this run. The Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant, a standard and slightly loose upper bound, gives 4.50. To pick \(\sigma\) for a target \(\varepsilon\), let the accountant you will report solve for it (Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run).

title: 36  DP-SGD
text:
36.3 The implementation checklist
The guarantee requires four implementation properties. Violating one does not necessarily stop training or reporting.
First, one record may change the clipped sum by at most \(C\). Batch normalization violates this condition because its statistics let one record affect other records’ gradients. Use group or layer normalization instead; these operate on each record separately. With strict=False, Opacus’s validator lists incompatible layers rather than raising an error.
from opacus.validators import ModuleValidator
from torchvision.models import resnet18

model = resnet18(weights=None)
print(len(ModuleValidator.validate(model, strict=False)))  # 20
model = ModuleValidator.fix(model)
print(len(ModuleValidator.validate(model, strict=False)))  # 0
Set \(C\) in advance using public data or a private estimate. Estimating \(C\) from the current batch makes the noise data-dependent.
Second, match the accountant to the implemented sampler (Amplification by subsampling). Poisson accounting benefits from the chance that each record is absent from a batch. A loader that shuffles once per epoch and divides data into fixed batches includes every record exactly once per epoch, eliminating that amplification. Its true \(\varepsilon\) may greatly exceed the Poisson estimate.
Fresh fixed-size batches can be accounted with a Poisson accountant using the batch’s sampling rate and half the noise multiplier. A sampled record replaces another, so the sum can change by \(2C\). In the running example, dp_accounting’s numerical accountant gives \(\varepsilon=23.03\), compared with 3.98 for Poisson sampling; this bound uses add/remove neighbours.
Third, divide the noisy sum by the public expected batch size \(B\), not the realized size. The realized size is one larger when the protected record is included, so dividing by it reveals that inclusion.
Fourth, account for every step that accessed the data, including discarded runs during tuning.
State the neighbouring relation with each \(\varepsilon\), and make data-dependent preprocessing private. Use user-level privacy when one person contributes multiple records. For released models, enable Opacus’s secure_mode=True; floating-point sampling does not produce the exact Gaussian noise assumed by the proof (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms).

title: 36  DP-SGD
text:
36.4 Clipping and the learning rate
Clip each record’s gradient separately. PyTorch’s torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_ clips the batch gradient, which does not bound any single record’s contribution and provides no privacy guarantee.
The clipping norm \(C\) does not change \(\varepsilon\), but it affects accuracy. Small \(C\) clips more gradients, reducing the contribution of high-gradient records, which may be rare (Disparate impact). Large \(C\) increases noise because its standard deviation is \(\sigma C\).
When all gradients are clipped to length \(C\), the noise also scales with \(C\). The update therefore depends on the product \(\eta C\), where \(\eta\) is the learning rate. If clipping is aggressive, tune this product. In the running example at \(\varepsilon=4\), fixing \(\eta C=2\) keeps test accuracy between 0.8446 and 0.8464 for \(C\) from 0.1 to 10. Fixing \(\eta=2\) instead gives accuracy 0.7869 at \(C=10\).
Noise and clipping both affect the optimal learning rate. Noise lowers it (Optimization); clipping raises it because gradients become shorter. Their effects do not cancel predictably. Retune the learning rate when \(\sigma\) or \(C\) changes, and include all search runs in the privacy cost.
Gradient norms change during training. In the running example, the median per-example norm on public rows falls from 1.444 to 0.044 over 300 steps. Thus, \(C=1\) clips every row initially but only one quarter at the end. Adaptive clipping adjusts \(C\) toward a gradient-norm quantile using a private count; Opacus enables it with clipping="adaptive". This count consumes budget, increasing gradient noise at the same \(\sigma\).

title: 36  DP-SGD
section: 36.5 Batch size at a fixed budget
text:
36.5 Batch size at a fixed budget
Averaging the noisy sum over \(B\) records divides the added noise by \(B\), so larger batches dilute it. At a fixed budget and number of epochs, a larger batch also means fewer steps. So the noise multiplier must rise to keep \(\varepsilon\), but more slowly than \(B\) does. For a small sampling rate \(q\) and a \(\sigma\) well above 1, the accountant’s cost over a fixed number of epochs depends on \(q/\sigma^2\). So \(\sigma\) only has to grow like \(\sqrt q\). Since \(q = B/n\), with \(n\) the number of records, the noise on the averaged gradient falls with the batch size, \[\sigma \propto \sqrt{\frac Bn}, \qquad \frac{\sigma C}{B} \propto \frac{C}{\sqrt{Bn}}. \tag{36.2}\]
So choose the largest batch your hardware allows, with a larger learning rate for the fewer steps. When it does not fit in memory, Opacus’s BatchMemoryManager splits the sampled batch into physical batches that fit, and still steps once per sampled batch.

title: 36  DP-SGD
text:
36.6 Making it fast
Computed one record at a time, DP-SGD can run tens or hundreds of times slower than ordinary training. Two fixes cost no accuracy. Vectorized per-example gradients, from torch.func.vmap or Opacus’s hooks, compute the same clipped sum in parallel. Ghost clipping also saves memory, because it gets each record’s gradient norm from each layer’s inputs and errors without the gradient itself. Opacus turns it on with grad_sample_mode="ghost".
The third fix, microbatching, costs accuracy. It clips the average gradient of each group of \(m\) records. One record can change its group’s clipped average by up to \(2C\), so the noise doubles. The update then averages over \(B/m\) groups rather than \(B\) records, so the noise on each coordinate of the averaged update becomes \[2m\cdot\frac{\sigma C}{B}. \tag{36.3}\] On the running example at \(\sigma = 0.973\), groups of 4 cut test accuracy from 0.8444 to 0.8206, more than a quarter of the way down to always predicting the larger class. So use microbatching only as a last resort.

title: 37  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
37.1 Why this matters
You have a PyTorch training loop on sensitive data, and it must become private. The algorithm is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with differential privacy (DP), called DP-SGD, which clips each record’s gradient and adds noise at every step (DP-SGD). Opacus does it with one call that wraps the model. The hard part is the decisions around that call. A mistake in one of them leaves code that trains as before but reports a false privacy level \(\varepsilon\).
This chapter trains on Adult, a census survey of 48,842 people from the UCI Machine Learning Repository, to predict whether a person earns more than $50,000 a year. Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run plans the privacy side of this run, and this chapter keeps training, tuning and utility. The script practitioner_dp_sgd.py runs every step except tuning, which practitioner_tuning.py does. Each runs in one to two minutes without a GPU.

title: 37  Train a model with DP-SGD
section: 37.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
text:
37.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
The guarantee protects exactly one record, so first decide what a record is (User-level differential privacy). Adult has no person identifier, so one row counts as one person because of how the survey was collected. When your data has an identifier, count distinct identifiers, not rows.
The script splits the rows with seed 0 into 30,000 private training rows and 16,842 test rows. The other 2,000, the stand-in rows from here on, play the part of public data. The script chooses settings on them but never trains on them. They come from the same survey, so this is an assumption for the demonstration. In production the role belongs to public data, and without any, tuning costs privacy (Section 37.10).
The slack \(\delta\) depends on the number of people \(n\) in the training set, not in the whole dataset. The book’s rule (How small δ must be) gives \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for \(n = 30{,}000\).
crumbs: 37  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 37  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
37.3 Preprocess from public facts
Every statistic computed from the private rows is a release that the accountant does not count. A scaler fitted on the training set leaks each column’s mean and spread. An encoder fitted on it leaks which categories occur, even a country that only one person comes from. So the script takes its category lists from the dataset’s documentation, and scales each number by bounds the survey publishes, such as ages from 17 to 90. Capital gains and losses go on a log scale first, and a missing value becomes its own category.
def features(rows: pl.DataFrame) -> Array:
    """One-hot categories from the documented lists, numbers scaled by public bounds."""
    rows = rows.with_columns(pl.col("capital-gain", "capital-loss").log1p())
    numeric = [
        np.clip((rows[name].to_numpy() - low) / (high - low), 0.0, 1.0) for name, (low, high) in NUMERIC_BOUNDS.items()
    ]
    encoder = OneHotEncoder(categories=list(CATEGORIES.values()), sparse_output=False)
    text = rows.select(pl.col(list(CATEGORIES)).fill_null("?")).to_numpy()
    encoder.fit(text[:1])  # the categories are given, so fitting learns nothing from the rows
    return np.hstack([np.column_stack(numeric), encoder.transform(text)])
This gives 91 features for a network with one hidden layer of 64 units and 6,018 weights. To check this step in other code, find every fit call and ask what data it sees.

title: 37  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
37.4 Train the baselines
A private accuracy means little on its own, so train three baselines with the same model, batch size, epochs and optimizer. The non-private model shows the best you can expect. A model with clipping and no noise separates the cost of clipping from the cost of noise. The majority class shows the floor, where a collapsed private model lands.
non-private: test accuracy 0.847
clip only (C=1, no noise): test accuracy 0.845
always '<=50K': test accuracy 0.759
Clipping alone costs little here. If clip-only accuracy were far below non-private, no budget would fix it, because the problem would be the clipping norm or the learning rate.

title: 37  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
37.5 Check the model
Opacus computes one gradient per record, and some layers break that. Batch normalization is the common case, because its statistics let one record change every other record’s gradient. The validator lists such layers before you train.
errors = ModuleValidator.validate(model, strict=False)
print(f"validator errors: {len(errors)}")
Here it finds none. For a model with such layers, ModuleValidator.fix replaces batch normalization with group normalization (DP-SGD shows it on a ResNet).

title: 37  Train a model with DP-SGD
section: 37.6 Choose the clipping norm, batch and epochs
text:
37.6 Choose the clipping norm, batch and epochs
Fix these settings before you touch the private data, because choosing them on it costs privacy. The usual guide for the clipping norm \(C\), the length each record’s gradient is cut to, is the typical gradient norm on public data. So the script measures it on the stand-in rows.
wrapped = GradSampleModule(model)  # adds hooks that keep one gradient per row
wrapped.train()
logits: torch.Tensor = wrapped(split.x)
nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(logits, split.y).backward()  # fills p.grad_sample for every weight p
norms = stacked_norms(wrapped)
at initialisation: median norm 1.444  90th percentile 1.538
fraction clipped at C=1: 1.000
The median rule would give a \(C\) of about 1.4. The script keeps the usual default \(C = 1\), just below the median, so every gradient is clipped at the start. That costs nothing, because when every gradient is clipped, only the learning rate times \(C\) matters (DP-SGD).
Make the batch as large as you can afford. The reason is that the noise on the averaged gradient is \(\sigma C/B\), where \(B\) is the expected batch size and the noise multiplier \(\sigma\) is the noise’s standard deviation in units of \(C\). With \(B = 1{,}000\), Opacus sets the sampling rate \(q\), the chance that a row joins a batch, to \(1/30 = 0.0333\). Ten epochs then make 300 steps. Fix the epochs now, because the noise is calibrated to them.
The optimizer is SGD with momentum 0.9. The script picks its learning rate on the stand-in rows too. It trains a non-private model on 1,500 of them at six rates and scores each on the other 500.
  lr=0.05: 0.814  lr=0.1: 0.816  lr=0.2: 0.826  lr=0.5: 0.792  lr=1: 0.812  lr=2: 0.768
non-private learning rate 0.2; DP-SGD learning rate 2 (x10)
DP-SGD then uses ten times the winning rate, a rule of thumb rather than a measurement. Private runs usually need a larger step, because clipped gradients are shorter (DP-SGD). No private row was used, so this choice costs no privacy.
crumbs: 37  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 37  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
37.7 Calibrate the noise
The target is a privacy level of \(\varepsilon = 4\) at the slack \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) of Section 37.2. For this \(q\) and these epochs, Opacus’s get_noise_multiplier finds the smallest \(\sigma\) that meets it. With its privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant it gives \(\sigma = 0.973\), and Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run shows the call. That \(\sigma\) holds only for those epochs and that \(q\), so recompute it if you change either.
crumbs: 37  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 37  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
37.8 Train
The privacy engine wraps the model, optimizer and data loader. Its optimizer clips per-record gradients and adds noise. Its loader draws Poisson batches, independently including each row with probability \(q\), matching the accountant. Because the script initially uses fixed batches, make_private must replace its loader.
engine = PrivacyEngine(accountant="prv")
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=lr, momentum=0.9)
model, optimizer, data_loader = engine.make_private(
    module=model,
    optimizer=optimizer,
    data_loader=data_loader,
    noise_multiplier=sigma,
    max_grad_norm=clip,
)  # Poisson sampling is the default: each row joins each batch with probability q
The training loop runs inside BatchMemoryManager, which splits each logical batch of about 1,000 rows into physical batches of at most 500. The optimizer still steps once per logical batch, so the accounting does not change.
with BatchMemoryManager(
    data_loader=data_loader, max_physical_batch_size=PHYSICAL_BATCH, optimizer=optimizer
) as batches:
    for x, y in batches:  # Opacus splits each logical batch; it steps once per logical batch
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = criterion(model(x), y)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
steps=300  q=0.0333
epsilon (Opacus PRV) = 3.99
test accuracy at epsilon=4: 0.846
The script disables secure_mode to seed noise and reproduce results; the run record documents this. For production releases, set secure_mode=True in PrivacyEngine. It uses a secure generator and addresses floating-point weaknesses in ordinary Gaussian sampling (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms).

title: 37  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
37.9 Cross-check ε
An \(\varepsilon\) depends on an accountant’s implementation. The script independently recomputes it with Google’s dp_accounting: the privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant gives 3.98, compared with Opacus’s 3.99. The looser Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant gives 4.50. Name the accountant in every statement. Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run explains this check and potential discrepancies.
crumbs: 37  Train a model with DP-SGD

title: 37  Train a model with DP-SGD
text:
37.10 Tune honestly
This run selected all hyperparameters using public stand-in data, so tuning incurred no privacy cost. Without public data, every private run that affects the release consumes privacy, including discarded runs (Hyperparameter tuning).
The tuning script compares six learning rates under total \(\varepsilon=4\). A grid evaluates all six and composes their costs. Random search draws a Poisson number of models with mean 4, selects each rate from the six candidates, and releases only the best. Since only RDP supports a random run count, the script uses it throughout; its single-run \(\sigma\) exceeds the PRV value above.
def random_search(sigma: float) -> dp_accounting.DpEvent:
    """A Poisson number of runs with mean 4 (shape=inf selects the Poisson case); only the best is released."""
    return dp_accounting.dp_event.RepeatAndSelectDpEvent(one_run(sigma), mean=MEAN_RUNS, shape=math.inf)


def sigma_for(strategy: Callable[[float], dp_accounting.DpEvent], epsilon: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """The smallest noise multiplier per run that keeps the whole strategy within (epsilon, delta).

    The search starts at 0.1 and tries 1 first.
    """
    return dp_accounting.calibrate_dp_mechanism(
        dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant, strategy, epsilon, delta, dp_accounting.LowerEndpointAndGuess(0.1, 1.0)
    )
one run, no tuning: sigma=1.029
grid of 6, all runs counted: sigma=1.816
random search, Poisson mean 4 runs: sigma=1.256
naive grid of 6 at sigma=1.029: reports epsilon=4.00
naive grid, true epsilon of all 6 runs = 9.84
The naive grid illustrates a common error: it trains six models at single-run noise, reports one model’s \(\varepsilon\), but spends 9.84. Random search requires only a moderate increase in \(\sigma\), from 1.029 to 1.256.
With seed 0, the search draws two runs, both at learning rate 0.05, and reaches test accuracy 0.828, compared with 0.846 for the publicly tuned run. Do not rerun the search until a preferred result appears; the guarantee depends on the draw. Use private-data tuning only when public data cannot provide a suitable substitute.

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
38.1 Why this matters
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipped gradients and Gaussian noise satisfies differential privacy (DP) at the accountant’s reported level for one run; this is DP-SGD. Hyperparameter search trains and evaluates multiple models on private data, then selects one. The reported privacy level \(\varepsilon\) must account for the entire search.
Selecting only the best of a fixed number of runs can cost as much as releasing every model. On Adult, six runs each at \(\varepsilon=4\) cost 9.84 in total. If the run count is drawn from a distribution fixed in advance, the search can cost only slightly more than one run.
crumbs: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
38.2 The procedure and the report
The least costly tuning uses no private data. Runs on public or proxy data and published settings for similar tasks incur no privacy cost. Fix a large batch, epoch count and small clipping norm in advance. When the norm is below typical gradient size, accuracy often depends mainly on the product of clipping norm and learning rate, so search only that product (DP-SGD).
If private-data tuning is necessary, specify the complete search in advance: candidate set, distribution for the number of runs (Section 38.4), private score (Section 38.5) and validation set. Extending or restarting the search after seeing results makes it data-dependent and invalidates the stated accounting.
Account for all runs. For two or three candidates, compose the cost of each run (Section 38.3). For larger searches, use random search with a random run count (Section 38.4). Include runs that crashed or were used for debugging, and evaluations used for early stopping.
Log the candidate set, sampled run count, and each run’s settings and score. Report both the released run’s \(\varepsilon\), which assumes public hyperparameters, and the whole procedure’s \(\varepsilon\), which is the release guarantee. An audit tests only the released model and cannot verify the search cost. At \(\delta=10^{-5}\), the book’s rule for 30,000 records (How small δ must be), the Adult search in Section 38.6 reports:

DP-SGD ran for 300 steps with Poisson sampling at rate 1/30. It clipped gradients to norm 1 and added noise with multiplier 1.256, so one run satisfies \((2.73, 10^{-5})\)-DP. The learning rate was chosen by random search over \(\{0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2\}\). The number of runs was drawn from a Poisson distribution with mean 4, and each run was scored on 2,000 validation records treated as public. The whole procedure satisfies \((4.00, 10^{-5})\)-DP for add/remove neighbours, datasets that differ by one record. It was computed with dp_accounting from the Rényi bound of Papernot & Steinke (2022).
crumbs: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
38.3 Paying for every run
Choosing among eight learning rates does not limit leakage to three bits. The selected model depends on all run outcomes. Even if each run is labelled only “good” or “bad”, a bad selected run implies that all candidates were bad, revealing information about every run. Tuning without privacy and then training once privately can also leak: outliers may change the selected regularization weight, revealing their presence (Membership inference).
The safe approach charges for every run because selection uses all run outputs (Composition). For DP-SGD, \(k\) runs of \(T\) steps cost the same as one run of \(kT\) steps. One run of Part 4’s example—10,000 steps, sampling rate 0.01 and noise multiplier 1—costs \(\varepsilon=6.71\) at \(\delta=10^{-5}\). Ten runs cost 27.23, about four times the single-run cost rather than ten times, because conversion to \(\varepsilon\) incurs the \(\delta\) cost once.
crumbs: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
38.4 A random number of runs
The way out is to draw the number of runs \(K\) at random, independently of the data. A search whose runs all came out bad then most likely drew few runs, which says little about the data. So the whole search costs about one run, plus a term that grows with the logarithm of the expected number of runs. For DP-SGD, use the version of Papernot & Steinke (2022), which works with the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) that DP-SGD’s accountants already compute (Rényi DP).
To use it, fix the candidate set and the distribution of \(K\), either Poisson or a truncated negative binomial with a shape parameter \(\nu\). That family includes the geometric distribution, \(\nu = 1\), which is the random stopping of Liu & Talwar, and the logarithmic one, \(\nu = 0\). Then draw \(K\), run that many candidates drawn at random from the set, and release the best one by a private score. To get the cost from Google’s dp_accounting, wrap the event of one run in a RepeatAndSelectDpEvent. Give it \(\nu\) as its shape (infinite for Poisson), and compose it in an RdpAccountant.
NumPy draws \(K\) with rng.poisson(mean), rng.geometric(1 / mean) or rng.logseries(p). The last takes \(p\) rather than a mean, so solve its mean, \(-p/((1 - p)\ln(1 - p))\), for \(p\).

In Table 38.1, the geometric and logarithmic searches barely grow from 10 to 1,000 runs, while composition grows almost linearly. A smaller \(\nu\) gives a cheaper bound, but the search also stops after one run more often. The Poisson bound needs runs that are already very private, which a run at \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) is not, so here it grows almost like composition. A random number of runs may also miss the best candidate. With eight candidates and a geometric number of runs with mean eight, it never tries the best one with probability 0.4667.
The theorems have three conditions, and each is easy to break. First, each run must draw its candidate independently from a fixed distribution, as random search does. Bayesian optimization picks each candidate from earlier scores, so it is not covered and needs adaptive composition. Second, the number of runs must be drawn independently of the data. Third, the score that ranks the runs must be private and counted in each run’s cost.

title: 38  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 38.5 Selecting by a noisy validation score
text:
38.5 Selecting by a noisy validation score
Sometimes the candidates are fixed in advance, such as public pretrained checkpoints, and only the choice among them uses private data. That is a selection problem, which Selection solves with the exponential mechanism, a random choice weighted toward high scores. Score each candidate by its number of correct predictions, which one record changes by at most 1, not by an accuracy, which divides by a private set size. The mechanism’s shortfall from the best count then grows only with the logarithm of the number of candidates.
For the random-number bounds, add Gaussian noise to each run’s count of correct predictions, since an exact validation accuracy leaves the validation records unprotected. With noise of standard deviation 20, one noisy count costs \(\varepsilon = 0.182\). If the validation set is disjoint from the training set, each record pays only one of the two costs. So the event for one run is the costlier of its training and its count, not their sum. Otherwise compose both into one event. On the running example the counts are the cheaper, so they add nothing to the total.

import dp_accounting


def one_run(sigma: float) -> dp_accounting.DpEvent:
    step = dp_accounting.PoissonSampledDpEvent(1 / 30, dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(sigma))

def epsilon(event: dp_accounting.DpEvent) -> float:
    return dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant().compose(event).get_epsilon(1e-5)

print(f"{epsilon(search):.2f}")  # 4.00
print(f"{epsilon(naive_grid):.2f}")  # 9.84

title: 39  User-level differential privacy
text:
39.1 Why this matters
The differential privacy (DP) guarantees described so far protect one record. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with DP is called DP-SGD. In this part’s DP-SGD Adult run, record-level privacy loss is \(\varepsilon=3.98\). A messaging user may contribute hundreds of messages, whose combined information can exceed the protection for any one message.
A DP guarantee protects the changes defined by neighbouring datasets, so the neighbouring relation determines the privacy unit. Adult has no household identifier. To illustrate larger units, this chapter assigns its 30,000 training rows to 3,000 synthetic households, each containing similar rows. The median household has 4 rows and the largest has 359. Here a household is the user and a row is a record.

title: 39  User-level differential privacy
text:
39.2 The privacy unit and δ
Take a mechanism \(M\), and call two datasets neighbours, \(D\) and \(D'\), when they differ by adding or removing all the records of one user. The mechanism is user-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, with a small slack \(\delta\), if every such pair and every set \(S\) of outputs satisfy \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta. \tag{39.1}\] Example-level DP is the same inequality for datasets that differ in one record. So every property and accountant of Part 4 holds for user-level DP unchanged. What changes is the sensitivity, because one user can move the computation with all of their records at once.
Choose the privacy unit—record, user, household or device—to specify whose participation is protected. Report it with each \(\varepsilon\) (Release and governance). It also determines \(\delta\): the book’s rule (How small δ must be) counts users. For 3,000 households it gives \(10^{-4}\) (Section 39.8), so this chapter’s \(10^{-5}\) is stricter.
The general guarantee for a user with \(k\) records is group privacy (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). An example-level \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-DP mechanism also protects users with at most \(k\) records at privacy level \(k\varepsilon\) and slack \[\delta_k = \delta\,\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}. \tag{39.2}\] The slack grows roughly as \(e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\); a record-level \(\delta\) is not a user-level \(\delta\). To keep user-level slack at \(10^{-5}\), per-record \(\delta\) must be much smaller, which increases per-record \(\varepsilon\). The full edition’s Rényi accountant gives the Adult run \(\varepsilon=4.50\) per row. A two-row household therefore has \(\varepsilon=12.43\), not twice 4.50; for ten rows, no sufficiently small per-row \(\delta\) is available.

title: 39  User-level differential privacy
section: 39.3 What an example-level model gives a user
text:
39.3 What an example-level model gives a user
Group privacy treats DP-SGD as a black box, but its sampling process is known. Each record is independently included with probability \(q\), so a user with \(k\) records is represented in a step with probability about \(kq\). When \(kq\) is small, multiple records from that user rarely share a batch. Thus, a user with \(k\) records can be approximated as one record sampled at rate \(kq\). Screen exposure by rerunning the record-level accountant at rate \(kq\) (Section 39.8). Charles et al. (2024) give an exact user accountant.



Table 39.1: The household-level \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) of the Adult run’s example-level DP-SGD (\(q = 1/30\), \(\sigma = 0.973\), 300 steps) for a household with \(k\) rows, from the full edition’s Rényi accountant (4.59 at one record comes from its coarser grid of orders).

The rate-\(kq\) screen underestimates the exact cost by 8% for two rows and 23% for ten. It ignores steps that sample multiple household rows, which are common at \(q=1/30\). Report an exact value when an implementation is available. The libraries used here provide only the screen; report it with this limitation and keep \(kq\) small. It is not a conservative bound because similar records can move gradients in the same direction.

title: 39  User-level differential privacy
text:
39.4 User-level DP-SGD
The better route makes the user the unit that DP-SGD samples, clips and accounts for (McMahan et al. 2018). Starting from weights chosen without looking at the data, each step does five things.

Sample users. Put each user in the batch independently with probability \(q\), now the user sampling rate.
Compute one vector per user. From that user’s records alone, compute their average gradient, or the change in weights after a few training steps on their records.
Clip per user. Rescale that vector to length at most the clipping norm \(C\).
Add noise. Sum the clipped vectors and add Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\), for a noise multiplier \(\sigma\).
Step. Divide by the expected number of sampled users and take a gradient step.

One user moves the sum by at most \(C\), however many records they have. So the guarantee is user-level DP with exactly the accountant of example-level DP-SGD, run at the user sampling rate.
That has two consequences. First, you pay for having fewer units. With 300 steps and about 100 units per batch, sampling rows needs \(\sigma = 0.581\) for \(\varepsilon = 4\). The same batch drawn from ten times fewer households needs a ten times higher rate, and so \(\sigma = 1.03\). Second, records inside a user are free, since you can average them, train on them for several steps or subsample them without changing \(\varepsilon\).
Carry a user identifier through the pipeline, and split training and test data by user. Opacus clips each row of a batch, so write a data loader that yields users and clip each user’s vector yourself. Three things break the guarantee:

A user’s vector depends on other users’ data, for example through normalization statistics computed over all users.
One person is spread over several accounts, so the unit is the account and the person is again a group.
Users are iterated in a fixed shuffled order instead of Poisson-sampled, which is a different mechanism that this accountant does not cover (Matrix factorization).

title: 39  User-level differential privacy
text:
39.5 Contribution bounding
A pipeline built around records can still protect users. Contribution bounding keeps at most \(k\) records of each user, the cap, and runs example-level DP-SGD on what remains. The result is user-level DP with the \(\varepsilon\) the user accountant gives for \(k\) records. The condition is that each user’s kept records are chosen without looking at other users’ data, for example at random. Otherwise adding one user could change which records other users keep, and neighbours would differ by more than one user’s records. To calibrate the noise for a cap, solve for \(\sigma\) with dp_accounting.calibrate_dp_mechanism at rate \(kq\) (Train a model with DP-SGD).
import polars as pl

rows = pl.DataFrame({"user": ["a", "a", "a", "a", "b", "c", "c"], "x": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]})
k = 2  # the cap, fixed from public knowledge of the population
capped = rows.sample(fraction=1.0, shuffle=True, seed=0).group_by("user").head(k)
print(capped.height)  # 5
print(capped.group_by("user").len()["len"].max())  # 2
Choosing the cap trades noise against bias (Amin et al. 2019). A larger cap keeps more data but needs more noise, while a smaller cap discards records and reweights the data toward light users. On Adult’s households at a household-level \(\varepsilon = 4\), a cap of fifty rows instead of one multiplies the noise by 4.2, and accuracy falls from 0.8362 to 0.7943.
So take the cap from public knowledge of the population, or choose it privately and count the cost, for example with a private quantile of records per user (Beyond global sensitivity). Trying caps on test accuracy spends privacy that the accountant does not see.

title: 39  User-level differential privacy
text:
39.6 Heterogeneous users
User-level training also changes the objective. Averaging per user weights users equally, while example-level training weights them by their number of records (Disparate impact). If heavy users should count for more, sum a user’s gradients before clipping. Their influence then rises with their records until clipping caps the sum at \(C\), and \(\varepsilon\) does not change.

title: 39  User-level differential privacy
text:
39.8 Code
The rate-\(kq\) screen needs only a record-level accountant, such as Google’s dp_accounting. This snippet screens households with one and two rows, and computes the book’s \(\delta\) for 3,000 households.
import math

import dp_accounting


def screen(k: int, q: float = 1 / 30, sigma: float = 0.973, steps: int = 300) -> float:
    """The epsilon of a user with k records, screened as one record sampled at rate k * q."""
    step = dp_accounting.PoissonSampledDpEvent(k * q, dp_accounting.GaussianDpEvent(sigma))
    accountant = dp_accounting.rdp.RdpAccountant()
    accountant.compose(dp_accounting.SelfComposedDpEvent(step, steps))
    return accountant.get_epsilon(1e-5)


print(f"{screen(1):.2f}")  # 4.50
print(f"{screen(2):.2f}")  # 9.25
print(10 ** math.floor(math.log10(3_000**-1.1)))  # 0.0001
Its 9.25 matches the table’s screen, but two Rényi accountants with different orders can differ in the last digits, so quote the value you ran and name its accountant. With \(k = 1\) and \(q\) the user sampling rate, the same code accounts for user-level DP-SGD.

title: 40  Choosing ε
text:
40.1 Why this matters
Every model protected by differential privacy (DP) has a privacy budget \(\varepsilon\). The differentially private version of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD, shows how this budget affects accuracy. This chapter relates \(\varepsilon\) to risks for people in the data, providing a basis for choosing it rather than following convention.
Membership tests assess whether a record appeared in training. Their true positive rate (TPR) measures correctly identified members; their false positive rate (FPR) measures non-members incorrectly flagged. The guarantee \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) bounds TPR in terms of FPR (The definition of differential privacy). Each run also has a tighter trade-off curve of achievable rates. Compute that curve, evaluate it at the threat’s FPR and compare it with accuracy at each budget.

title: 40  Choosing ε
text:
40.2 Justifying a choice
A defensible choice specifies what the budget protects before selecting its value.

Unit and period. Say whether one unit is a record, a user or a device, and whether neighbouring datasets differ by adding or removing one unit or by replacing one. Say which runs the budget covers, since every tuning run spends budget too (Hyperparameter tuning).
Threat. Say whether the concern is membership, reconstruction or attribute inference, and what the attacker knows and sees. This sets the false positive rate at which you read the curve, a low one for an attacker who must rarely accuse a non-member.
Whole guarantee. Choose \(\delta\) by the book’s rule (Section 40.5), then compute the trade-off curve (Section 40.3) and read it there.
Evidence. The curve is a theorem about an algorithm, not about your code, so run an audit that could refute it (Auditing private training).
Utility. Put accuracy against \(\varepsilon\) next to the risk, and pick the smallest budget past the bend, where accuracy stops improving. Draw it on public or proxy data, because private runs that choose \(\varepsilon\) are a search whose cost the reported \(\varepsilon\) leaves out.
Comparison. Only now compare with deployments (Section 40.6) and with the tiers in the rules of thumb.

The Adult public census survey illustrates step 5. Train a model with DP-SGD trains a small network on 30,000 people at five privacy budgets, each with \(\delta=10^{-5}\). Table 40.1 compares test accuracy with the maximum membership-test TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\), computed from Section 40.3.

title: 40  Choosing ε
section: 40.3 The pair and the whole curve
text:
40.3 The pair and the whole curve
A membership test says “member” or “non-member” about one target record. Its TPR is the chance that it says “member” when the target was in the training set, and its FPR the chance when it was not. Every test against an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} \le \min\big\{1,\ e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta,\ 1 - e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - \mathrm{FPR})\big\}. \tag{40.1}\] The middle term is the one that binds at low FPR, and the last applies the same cap to the members a test misses. Attacks are judged at a low FPR, because an attack that rarely flags a non-member identifies people with confidence (Membership inference). Yet at \(\varepsilon = 8\) and an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), the pair caps the TPR at 0.9997, which constrains almost nothing.
A real training run satisfies DP for a whole range of pairs, one \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) for each \(\varepsilon\), because its accountant can trade \(\varepsilon\) for \(\delta\). Each pair gives a line, the middle term of Equation 40.1, and every test must stay under all of these lines at once. The best test reaches the lowest line exactly, which is called the trade-off curve: \[\mathrm{TPR}^*(\mathrm{FPR}) = \min_{\varepsilon}\big(e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta(\varepsilon)\big). \tag{40.2}\] For DP-SGD, a privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant computes this curve. It can round the privacy loss up or down, and the two curves it gets bracket the true one (Numerical accounting).
Table 40.2 compares the pair with the curve for two of the Adult runs of Table 40.1, each sampled at rate 1/30 for 300 steps.

To compute the curve with Google’s dp_accounting, build the run’s PLD, ask it for \(\delta\) on a grid of \(\varepsilon\), and take the lowest line. The snippet’s first print is the upper end of a bracket in Table 40.2, and its second gives the last column of Table 40.1.
import numpy as np
from dp_accounting.pld import privacy_loss_distribution as pld

EPS_GRID = np.linspace(0.0, 20.0, 2001)


def tpr_at(sigma: float, q: float, steps: int, fpr: float) -> float:
    run = pld.from_gaussian_mechanism(sigma, sampling_prob=q).self_compose(steps)
    deltas = np.array(run.get_delta_for_epsilon(EPS_GRID))
    return float(np.min(np.exp(EPS_GRID) * fpr + deltas))


print(f"{tpr_at(0.722, 1 / 30, 300, 1e-2):.4f}")  # 0.1563
adult = [tpr_at(sigma, 1 / 30, 300, 1e-3) for sigma in (8.125, 2.383, 1.431, 0.973, 0.722)]
print(" ".join(f"{tpr:.4f}" for tpr in adult))  # 0.0013 0.0023 0.0046 0.0123 0.0445
The library’s default PLD rounds the loss up, so its curve is a valid upper bound. A Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant gives a valid but looser curve. The Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) approximation is quick but not a bound, so use it to explain and the PLD to certify.
The curve is a worst case, for an attacker who sees every intermediate model, so a typical record attacked through the final model alone is much safer. The curve bounds reconstruction too, since a guess among \(m\) equally likely records is a membership test at an FPR of \(1/m\) (Reconstruction attacks).

title: 40  Choosing ε
text:
40.4 What an attacker can believe
Most people ask how sure an attacker can become that a person was in the data. Write \(p\) for the attacker’s prior, its probability of “member” before it sees the model. A privacy loss of at most \(\varepsilon\) means that no output is more than \(e^\varepsilon\) times as likely with the person’s record as without it. So the attacker’s belief afterwards is at most \[\Pr[\text{member} \mid \text{output}] \le \frac{p\,e^\varepsilon}{p\,e^\varepsilon + 1 - p}. \tag{40.3}\] So DP bounds the change of belief, not the belief itself.
For example, an attacker who starts at 1% can end at 35.55% when \(\varepsilon = 4\). That is for the worst output, and in DP-SGD the privacy loss of the released model is usually far below \(\varepsilon\).
Base rates matter as much as the loss. An attacker who accuses every person its test flags as a member is right with probability \[\Pr[\text{member} \mid \text{flag}] = \frac{p\,\mathrm{TPR}}{p\,\mathrm{TPR} + (1 - p)\,\mathrm{FPR}}. \tag{40.4}\] Take the Adult run at \(\varepsilon = 8\) and an attacker with a 1% prior who flags at an FPR of \(10^{-2}\). The curve caps its TPR there at 0.1563 (Table 40.2), so at most 0.1363 of its flags are right, and more than six out of seven are false. An insider with a prior of 0.5 would be right far more often, so a statement about beliefs must name the attacker.

title: 40  Choosing ε
text:
40.5 How small δ must be
For \(n\) privacy units, the book’s rule sets \(\delta \le 1/n^{1.1}\), rounded down to a power of ten (How small δ must be). The units are people when one person has many records (User-level differential privacy). For Adult’s 30,000 people it gives \(10^{-5}\). That is not far below \(1/n\), as always when \(n\) is just above a power of ten. NIST SP 800-226, the US guidelines for evaluating DP claims, calls a \(\delta\) above \(10^{-5}\) suspicious unless justified.
For DP-SGD a smaller \(\delta\) is cheap. Take the Adult run at \(\varepsilon = 4\). When \(\delta\) falls to \(10^{-8}\), the PLD accountant puts it at only 5.763. So report \(\varepsilon\) at a second, smaller \(\delta\) too, and never quote a \(\delta\) as large as one over the number of units.

title: 40  Choosing ε
text:
40.6 Comparing with deployed values
“Industry uses \(\varepsilon\) between 1 and 10” hides what every \(\varepsilon\) needs, its privacy unit and the period over which it is spent. The Census Bureau’s 2020 redistricting data used zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), which states the guarantee as one number, written \(\rho\), that converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pairs. Its unit was one person’s record under the replace-one relation, and persons got \(\rho = 2.56\), reported as \(\varepsilon = 17.14\) at \(\delta = 10^{-10}\).
So before you compare, convert both budgets to the same unit, neighbouring relation and \(\delta\). A zCDP parameter \(\rho\) converts to a pair by \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}. \tag{40.5}\] For the Census figures this formula gives 17.92, and the Bureau’s 17.14 comes from a tighter conversion. Since a replacement is a removal followed by an addition, an add/remove guarantee \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) implies only the replace-one guarantee \((2\varepsilon, (1 + e^\varepsilon)\delta)\) (The definition of differential privacy). And a budget stated per day adds up over time by composition, to 365 a year at \(\varepsilon = 1\) per day.
So it would be wrong to call the Adult run at \(\varepsilon = 8\) “less than half the Census budget”. At the Census’s \(\delta = 10^{-10}\) it is at 13.812, and under the Census’s replace-one relation that can double.

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
41.1 Why this matters
Differential privacy (DP) applied to stochastic gradient descent (SGD), or DP-SGD (DP-SGD), can cause substantial accuracy loss when training from random initialization, especially at privacy loss \(\varepsilon \le 1\). More accurate private models often start from weights pretrained without privacy on a large public dataset, then fine-tune them on sensitive data (Tramèr & Boneh 2021).
Fine-tuning fewer weights can further improve accuracy. DP-SGD adds noise to every trained weight, while the useful signal does not grow with the number of weights. Training fewer weights therefore reduces noise relative to signal. Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA demonstrates this workflow.
crumbs: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
41.2 How many weights to train
The trainable weights do not change \(\varepsilon\): DP-SGD requires only that one record changes the clipped sum by at most clipping norm \(C\). The choice affects the noise added to the model. Other computations based only on public data are also free, provided they do not depend on private data. Examples include initial weights, tokenizers and normalization statistics.
Noise magnitude grows with the number \(d\) of trainable weights. Let \(\sigma\) be the noise multiplier and \(B\) the expected batch size; Poisson sampling gives variable batch sizes. The averaged-gradient noise has length about \[\text{noise length} \approx \frac{\sigma C\sqrt d}{B}. \tag{41.1}\] The average clipped-gradient signal has length at most \(C\), independent of \(d\). Training fewer weights omits gradient components for frozen weights, although clipping may then reduce the remaining components less.
Consider the Adult network in DP-SGD, with 6,018 weights. Pretrain it without privacy on the 1,500 public stand-in rows used by Train a model with DP-SGD, then fine-tune on 30,000 private rows. At \(\varepsilon=1\), noise is 1.6 times the signal when all weights train, but 0.4 times the signal when only the 130 last-layer weights train. This difference is smaller than the formula’s factor of 6.8 because the last-layer signal is also shorter (0.0726 rather than 0.1137).
Parameter count overstates the cost of full fine-tuning. Noise affects loss mainly along directions with curvature; steps along flat directions have little effect. Near a pretrained model, few directions are curved (Li, Liu et al. 2022). In the running example, full fine-tuning uses 46 times as many weights as last-layer training, but its noise should increase loss only 16 times as much. Larger learning rates expose more nearly flat directions to noise, so private fine-tuning often needs smaller steps than training from scratch.
Training fewer weights has its own cost, a bias, because no private data can move the model along a frozen direction that the task needs.
crumbs: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
41.3 Linear probing first
The simplest option freezes all but the last layer and trains a linear classifier on the fixed features, a method called linear probing. Its loss is convex, so it reduces private deep learning to Private empirical risk minimization and provides a useful baseline.
A private probe has two error sources. Privacy error for convex empirical risk minimization (ERM) grows with feature count \(d\). The feature gap is the difference between the best linear model on the features and the best model of any type; more data or a larger \(\varepsilon\) cannot remove it. In this example, the non-private probe reaches test accuracy 0.8431, while a non-private network trained from scratch reaches 0.8498. Across budgets in Section 41.5, private-probe accuracy stays within 0.002 of its ceiling, comparable to run-to-run variation.
Measure the probe’s ceiling by fitting it without privacy on labelled public data similar to the task. If it meets the target, use the probe. For private training, pass frozen features to diffprivlib’s LogisticRegression (Private empirical risk minimization) or run DP-SGD on the final layer.
crumbs: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
41.4 Low-rank adapters and full fine-tuning
When the probe’s ceiling is below your target, only changing the earlier layers can lift it. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022) freezes each pretrained matrix and learns a small correction to it. The correction is the product of two thin matrices that each have \(r\) columns, where \(r\) is the rank. A matrix with \(d_{\text{in}}\) inputs and \(d_{\text{out}}\) outputs has \(d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}\) weights, while its adapter has only \[d = r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}}). \tag{41.2}\]
The adapter comes from Hugging Face’s peft library. This snippet puts a rank-4 adapter on the first layer of the running example’s network, and trains its last layer in full.
import torch
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model

model = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(91, 64), torch.nn.ReLU(), torch.nn.Linear(64, 2))
print(sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()))  # 6018
config = LoraConfig(r=4, lora_alpha=8, target_modules=["0"], modules_to_save=["2"], lora_dropout=0.0)
adapted = get_peft_model(model, config)  # freezes every pretrained weight
print(sum(p.numel() for p in adapted.parameters() if p.requires_grad))  # 750
In the snippet, target_modules and modules_to_save name layers by their index in the Sequential, and lora_alpha scales the correction. It trains 750 weights, the adapter’s \(4 \times (91 + 64) = 620\) and the last layer’s 130. Opacus’s PrivacyEngine computes per-example gradients only for the parameters that require them, so the frozen weights cost nothing. Call model.train() before make_private, because Opacus rejects a model in evaluation mode, as a pretrained model often is after you measure it.
The adapter’s second factor starts at zero, so training begins exactly at the pretrained model. The first factor starts random, and that draw must not depend on the private data.
Yu et al. (2022) showed that private fine-tuning of language models with LoRA matches or beats private full fine-tuning, at a fraction of the compute and memory. Each adapter factor is an ordinary linear layer, so the ghost clipping of DP-SGD applies to it. Still, Li, Tramèr et al. (2022) matched the adapters with full fine-tuning, using large batches and a learning rate tuned for private training.

41.5 Which method at which budget
The script practitioner_adult_studies.py pretrains the running example on the public stand-in rows, then fine-tunes it with Opacus on the private rows, for the workflow’s 300 steps. DP-SGD fine-tunes the last layer, a rank-4 adapter plus the last layer, or all weights, against a model trained privately from scratch. Each method’s learning rate was chosen at \(\varepsilon = 1\) from 0.1, 0.3, 1 and 3, on half of the test rows, and accuracy comes from the other half. That choice looked at private data without paying, so the table shows each method at its best, not what a real run could claim (Hyperparameter tuning).

Adult is an easy task, so every gap here is under two points, but the pattern is the one larger tasks show. Pretraining is worth about a factor of eight in \(\varepsilon\), since the adapter at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) matches training from scratch at \(\varepsilon = 4\).
At \(\varepsilon = 0.25\) the last layer is best, because its noise is 6.8 times shorter than full fine-tuning’s, and its ceiling does not yet bind. From \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) on it stays near its ceiling, while first the adapter and then full fine-tuning pass it. The adapter is never more than 0.0023 below the best method, so it is the robust middle choice here. But a public task further from the private one can reverse the ranking even when the probe’s ceiling looks fine, so rerun the comparison on a public stand-in for your task.
The learning rate matters as much as the method, since a step three times too large costs full fine-tuning 1.1 percentage points of accuracy at \(\varepsilon = 1\). The adapter’s rank matters little, since at \(\varepsilon = 1\) ranks 1, 4 and 16 differ by about the run-to-run spread.

title: 41  Public data and private fine-tuning
section: 41.6 What public data does not buy
text:
41.6 What public data does not buy
Whatever the public data are, training on the private data is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, where \(\delta\) is the small additive slack the guarantee allows. The public data get no guarantee of any kind. Non-private pretraining can memorize individual records (Memorization and training-data extraction), and the fine-tuned model inherits whatever the pretrained weights encode (Tramèr, Kamath & Carlini 2024).
So a person in both datasets has protection only in the private copy. A membership attack against the pretrained model (Membership inference) has no bound at all. Web-scale “public” datasets contain posts, profiles and leaked documents, so private notes or emails may well overlap with them. For text, also mind the privacy unit, because one person’s documents span many training sequences (User-level differential privacy).
Check three things before you train and when you report.

Check that the public data resemble the private task, and deduplicate the private set against them. Deduplication protects copies, not people, since exact matching misses paraphrases.
Choose the public model and the hyperparameters on public data. Otherwise every private run costs privacy (Hyperparameter tuning).
Name the public data and the overlap check, and state that the guarantee covers the private data given the pretrained model.

title: 42  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
42.1 Why this matters
Fine-tune a pretrained language model on private text, such as support tickets or clinical notes, without exposing training examples. Non-private fine-tuning can reproduce frequent phone numbers or passwords (Memorization and training-data extraction). Differential privacy (DP) applied through stochastic gradient descent (SGD), or DP-SGD, limits this risk. Training a small adapter on frozen weights can retain accuracy while reducing noise cost (Public data and private fine-tuning). This workflow uses Hugging Face’s low-rank adaptation (LoRA) in peft and Opacus.
The model is EleutherAI’s public Pythia-14m, with 14 million parameters. The private text is Tiny Shakespeare, about one million characters of plays. The script fine-tunes the model with and without privacy. The private run has privacy loss \(\varepsilon\) of 8 per training sequence. It inserts synthetic secrets, called canaries, to test memorization. practitioner_lora.py runs in a few minutes without a GPU.

title: 42  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
section: 42.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
text:
42.2 Fix the privacy unit, n and δ
Define the privacy unit before training. Language models process fixed-length sequences of tokens, or word pieces produced by a tokenizer. This script uses 32-token sequences, roughly one or two lines of verse, as units. It trains on the first 1,024 sequences and holds out the last 128 to limit runtime.
sequences of 32 tokens: 10,632  training n=1,024  held out 128
delta=1e-04 (privacy unit: one training sequence)
For \(n = 1{,}024\) sequences, the book’s rule for the slack \(\delta\) gives \(10^{-4}\) (How small δ must be).
A sequence is suitable for this demonstration but rarely for production. A person’s document may span many sequences, and one user may contribute several documents. Sequence-level privacy therefore provides weaker person-level protection. For production, use a document or user as the unit, bound each contribution, and set \(\delta\) from the user count (User-level differential privacy).
crumbs: 42  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 42  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
42.3 Plant canaries
The script writes canaries into the training text so their memorization can be measured. Each canary is a sentence such as “the pin of Alice is 8 6 5 2 3”; its last five digits are the secret. The script inserts three canaries 1, 4, 16 and 64 times each. It draws three controls in the same way but never inserts them. The controls show how an unseen secret scores in the audit of Section 42.9.
def insert_canaries(
    train: torch.Tensor, canaries: list[Canary], tokenizer: PreTrainedTokenizerBase, rng: np.random.Generator
) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Write each copy of each canary over the start of a different training sequence."""
    train = train.clone()
    total = sum(c.copies for c in canaries)
    rows = iter(rng.choice(len(train), size=total, replace=False).tolist())
    for canary in canaries:
        tokens = torch.tensor(tokenizer(canary.text)["input_ids"])
        for _ in range(canary.copies):
            train[next(rows), : len(tokens)] = tokens
    return train
The 255 copies take up a quarter of the training set, far more than secrets occupy in real data. This deliberate density lets a small model memorize them during a short run and provides a positive control for the audit.
canary sequences: 255 (3 canaries each at (1, 4, 16, 64) copies)
tokens per secret: [5]
candidates: 2,000  exposure cap 10.97 bits  (full space 16.61)
Spaces separate the digits so every possible secret has exactly five tokens. The second line confirms this for 1,000 random secrets.
crumbs: 42  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 42  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
section: 42.4 Load a public model and tokenizer
text:
42.4 Load a public model and tokenizer
All components not trained privately must come from outside the private data. This includes the tokenizer: a vocabulary built from private text could expose rare words. The script loads the weights and tokenizer from the same pinned public checkpoint, Pythia-14m. It loads the model in float32 because transformers loads some checkpoints in float16, which runs far more slowly on a CPU.
The guarantee then covers the private text given the pretrained model, and says nothing about the model’s own training data. Pythia was pretrained on the Pile, which includes Project Gutenberg’s books and so very likely Shakespeare’s plays. That is harmless here, but with real data, check for overlap with the public model’s training data (Public data and private fine-tuning).
crumbs: 42  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 42  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
42.5 Choose what to train
DP-SGD adds noise to every trained weight. The noise on the averaged gradient grows with the square root of the number of trained weights, but the clipped signal does not (Public data and private fine-tuning). The number of trainable weights and the learning rate therefore affect accuracy. LoRA freezes each pretrained matrix and learns a correction formed by multiplying two thin factors; their width is the rank.
attention_and_mlp = ["query_key_value", "dense", "dense_h_to_4h", "dense_4h_to_h"]  # every linear layer
config = LoraConfig(r=rank, lora_alpha=2 * rank, target_modules=attention_and_mlp, lora_dropout=0.0)
lora_model = get_peft_model(model, config)  # freezes the pretrained weights
trainable_count = sum(p.numel() for p in lora_model.parameters() if p.requires_grad)
total_count = sum(p.numel() for p in lora_model.parameters())
print(f"trainable parameters: LoRA {trainable_count:,}  full fine-tuning {total_count - trainable_count:,}")
full model parameters: 14,067,712
trainable parameters: LoRA 98,304  full fine-tuning 14,067,712
By default, the adapters have rank 8 and cover every linear layer in attention and the feed-forward blocks. They train 98,304 weights, compared with about 14 million for full fine-tuning. lora_alpha scales the correction and is set to twice the rank. For a real task, choose the rank and layers using public data. Choices based on private runs cost privacy (Hyperparameter tuning).
crumbs: 42  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 42  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
42.6 Make the model Opacus-compatible
Opacus needs one gradient per sequence. Layers that mix records within a batch, such as batch normalization, prevent this calculation. Opacus’s ModuleValidator.validate lists such layers before training.
validator errors: 0
Pythia has none, and the script trains only the adapters. These are ordinary linear layers handled by Opacus’s default hooks, so the script sets grad_sample_mode="hooks". Opacus computes per-sequence gradients only for trainable weights; the 14 million frozen weights add no cost. Call model.train() before wrapping a model that has been evaluated, because Opacus rejects evaluation mode. After training, the hooks remain attached and slow later operations. The script calls remove_hooks() before evaluating the private model.
crumbs: 42  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 42  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
42.7 Calibrate and train
The accountant finds the noise for a fixed target, here \(\varepsilon = 8\) over 3 epochs with an expected batch of 32 sequences. The sampling rate \(q\) is the share of the data in an average batch, or \(32/1{,}024\). The run therefore takes 96 steps. The accountant is the privacy loss random variable (PRV) accountant, which computes \(\varepsilon\) almost exactly (Choosing an accountant).
privacy_engine = PrivacyEngine(accountant="prv")
private_model, optimizer, loader = privacy_engine.make_private_with_epsilon(
    module=model,
    optimizer=optimizer,
    data_loader=loader,  # replaced by Poisson sampling with rate BATCH / n
    target_epsilon=epsilon,
    target_delta=delta,
    epochs=EPOCHS,
    max_grad_norm=MAX_GRAD_NORM,
    grad_sample_mode="hooks",
)
print(f"noise multiplier: {optimizer.noise_multiplier:.3f}")
The training loop is an ordinary one, with Poisson batches, in which each sequence joins each batch independently with probability \(q\).
for (batch,) in loader:  # each batch holds a random number of sequences
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = private_model(input_ids=batch, labels=batch).loss
    loss.backward()  # Opacus's hooks keep one gradient per sequence
    optimizer.step()  # clips each one to MAX_GRAD_NORM, sums, adds noise
    steps += 1
noise multiplier: 0.553
sample rate q=0.03125  steps=96  noise multiplier=0.553
epsilon (Opacus PRV)=7.99  epsilon (dp_accounting PLD)=7.98  at delta=1e-04
The noise multiplier gives the noise’s standard deviation in units of the clipping norm, MAX_GRAD_NORM, which the script sets to 1. The last line cross-checks \(\varepsilon\) with the privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant in Google’s dp_accounting, as in Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run. The accountants agree.
Both runs use AdamW at a learning rate of \(10^{-3}\). The private run differs only in clipping, noise and Poisson sampling. The learning rate, rank and epochs were chosen in non-private trials on the same text. A real run must choose them using similar public text, such as other public-domain plays, or account for the trials in \(\varepsilon\) (Hyperparameter tuning).
For a real run, use batches in the thousands when the dataset is larger. Opacus’s BatchMemoryManager can split them into physical batches that fit in memory (Train a model with DP-SGD). Set secure_mode=True in PrivacyEngine for a released model. Secure noise cannot be seeded, so the script leaves this option off.
