title: 42  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
42.8 Evaluate
Language-model quality can be measured by predictions on held-out text. The script measures mean cross-entropy per token on the 128 held-out sequences and reports its exponential, the perplexity. A perplexity of 159.3 corresponds to uncertainty similar to choosing among about 159 equally likely tokens. Lower perplexity is better.
held-out loss pretrained: 5.306 nats/token  perplexity 201.6
held-out loss LoRA non-private: 5.071 nats/token  perplexity 159.3
held-out loss LoRA DP eps=8: 5.044 nats/token  perplexity 155.1
Both fine-tuned models improve on the pretrained model. On this seed, the private model’s slightly lower perplexity shows only that DP has no measurable cost in this run. Both gains are modest because canaries, rather than Shakespeare, begin a quarter of the training sequences.
This result does not imply that privacy has little cost on other tasks. This run is short, trains few weights, and uses text likely to appear in the pretraining data. For a harder task or smaller \(\varepsilon\), compare the private model with both baselines at several budgets, as in Train a model with DP-SGD.
crumbs: 42  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA

title: 42  Fine-tune a language model privately with LoRA
text:
42.9 Check memorization
The canaries show what perplexity cannot, whether the model will repeat a secret. The script measures each canary in two ways. The first is extraction. It gives the model the prefix “the pin of Alice is”, lets it write the likeliest next token five times, and checks whether the result is the secret.
@torch.no_grad()
def greedy_completion(model: PeftModel, tokenizer: PreTrainedTokenizerBase, prefix: str) -> str:
    """The five tokens the model writes after the prefix when it always picks the likeliest one."""
    ids = tokenizer(prefix, return_tensors="pt")["input_ids"]
    for _ in range(5):
        next_token = model(input_ids=ids).logits[:, -1].argmax(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
        ids = torch.cat([ids, next_token], dim=1)
    return tokenizer.batch_decode(ids[:, -5:])[0].strip()
The second is the exposure of Memorization and training-data extraction. It ranks the canary’s secret among random secrets of the same format by how likely the model finds each, and turns the rank into bits. The script’s likelihood is the summed log-probability of the five digits. Each bit halves the number of guesses an attacker needs.
@torch.no_grad()
def secret_scores(model: PeftModel, tokenizer: PreTrainedTokenizerBase, prefix: str, secrets: list[str]) -> Scores:
    """Summed log-probability of each secret's five digit tokens after the prefix."""
    prefix_ids = tokenizer(prefix)["input_ids"]
    rows = [prefix_ids + tokenizer(" " + s)["input_ids"] for s in secrets]
    ids = torch.tensor(rows)  # every secret is five tokens, so the rows have equal length
    logits = model(input_ids=ids[:, :-1], logits_to_keep=5).logits  # the predictions of the five digits
    logprobs = logits.log_softmax(dim=-1).gather(-1, ids[:, -5:, None])
    return logprobs.sum(dim=(1, 2)).double().numpy()


def canary_exposure(
    model: PeftModel, tokenizer: PreTrainedTokenizerBase, canary: Canary, candidates: list[str]
) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """The exposure of the canary's secret among the candidates, measured and extrapolated past the cap."""
    candidate_scores = scores_batched(model, tokenizer, canary.prefix, candidates)
    score = float(scores_batched(model, tokenizer, canary.prefix, [canary.secret])[0])
    return exposure(score, candidate_scores), extrapolated_exposure(score, candidate_scores, SECRET_SPACE)
No library installed with this book computes exposure, so exposure and extrapolated_exposure come from the book’s helper module practitioner_privacy_tests.py, after TensorFlow Privacy’s versions. With 2,000 random candidates, a canary that beats them all reaches a cap of 10.97 bits. A secret the model has never seen has a random rank and averages about 1.44 bits (\(\log_2 e\)). Each line below gives a group’s mean exposure, the same past the cap, and how many of its three secrets greedy decoding wrote out.
non-private 1 copies: mean exposure 2.0 bits  extrapolated 2.0  extracted 0/3
non-private 4 copies: mean exposure 5.9 bits  extrapolated 5.7  extracted 0/3
non-private 16 copies: mean exposure 10.0 bits  extrapolated 13.0  extracted 0/3
non-private 64 copies: mean exposure 11.0 bits  extrapolated 16.3  extracted 3/3
non-private controls: mean exposure 1.4 bits  extrapolated 1.5  extracted 0/3
DP 1 copies: mean exposure 0.9 bits  extrapolated 0.9  extracted 0/3
DP 4 copies: mean exposure 0.6 bits  extrapolated 0.6  extracted 0/3
DP 16 copies: mean exposure 4.2 bits  extrapolated 4.3  extracted 0/3
DP 64 copies: mean exposure 4.0 bits  extrapolated 3.9  extracted 0/3
DP controls: mean exposure 2.2 bits  extrapolated 2.2  extracted 0/3
The non-private model, the positive control, leaks. Exposure rises with the number of copies, from 2.0 bits for one copy to the cap for 64, and the model writes out all three 64-copy secrets. The extrapolated column sees past the cap by fitting a skew-normal distribution, a normal with one heavier tail, to the candidates’ scores. It puts the 64-copy secrets near the 16.61 bits of the whole space.
The 4-copy canaries are the instructive case. Two of the three reach 6.9 and 8.2 bits, yet none is extracted, so exposure detects memorization that extraction alone would miss.
Greedy decoding extracts nothing from the private model, and its canaries with 1 or 4 copies score no higher than its controls. The controls’ 2.2 bits are within the scatter of a mean over three secrets. Still, DP limits the effect without erasing it, since the canaries with 16 and 64 copies still average about 4 bits.
The guarantee allows that, because \(\varepsilon = 8\) protects one sequence, while a canary with many copies is many sequences. Group privacy bounds a group of units at about their number times \(\varepsilon\). So 16 copies get \(16 \times 8\), far too much to promise anything (User-level differential privacy). A secret that a user repeats across many documents is the same case, one more reason to make the unit the user.
Two cautions apply. Because the canaries are so dense, a real non-private model may leak less than this one, and a real audit should plant fewer copies. And three canaries per group is a small sample. For a fuller assessment before release, run the attacks of Pre-release privacy risk assessment. For a statistical lower bound on \(\varepsilon\), run the one-run audit of Auditing private training.

42.10 Variants
Three variants matter for real models. The block below shows ghost clipping, LoRA on GPT-2, and packages that wrap the whole loop, with pinned versions. It was not run.
# opacus==1.6.0: ghost clipping, when per-sequence gradients do not fit in memory
model, optimizer, criterion, loader = privacy_engine.make_private_with_epsilon(
    module=model, optimizer=optimizer, data_loader=loader, criterion=torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss(),
    target_epsilon=8.0, target_delta=1e-4, epochs=3, max_grad_norm=1.0, grad_sample_mode="ghost",
)
logits = model(input_ids=batch).logits[:, :-1]                 # predict each next token
loss = criterion(logits.flatten(0, 1), batch[:, 1:].flatten(), shape=logits.shape)
loss.backward()                                                # norms first, then the clipped sum

# peft==0.21.2: GPT-2 stores its attention as Conv1D, with the weight transposed
LoraConfig(r=8, lora_alpha=16, target_modules=["c_attn"], fan_in_fan_out=True)

# dp-transformers==1.0.0 (Microsoft): Opacus inside the Hugging Face Trainer
# private-transformers (Li et al.): install from its GitHub repository, pinned to a commit
Ghost clipping gets each sequence’s gradient norm without storing the gradient, so memory no longer holds one gradient per sequence (DP-SGD).

Release and governance builds the statement from the run’s record. For this run, it adds three things. The guarantee covers the private text given the pretrained model, named with its revision. The hyperparameters came from non-private trials on the private text, which a real release could not claim for free. And the canary audit is attached as evidence, with its caveats.
What ships is the adapter. With --save-adapter FOLDER, the script saves it after remove_hooks() and loads it back onto the same pinned checkpoint.
private.save_pretrained(path)  # only the adapter weights and config, after Opacus's hooks are removed
base_model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(folder, dtype=torch.float32)  # the same pinned checkpoint
reloaded = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base_model, path)
The folder holds only the adapter, so the statement names the base checkpoint and revision it fits. The guarantee covers the adapter and anything computed from it.

title: 43  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
43.1 What it is
Private prediction applies differential privacy (DP) to each answer rather than to stochastic gradient descent (SGD) training. Split private records into disjoint shards and train an ordinary teacher model on each. Keep teachers private. For each query, add noise to vote counts and release the winning label. The privacy level is \(\varepsilon\), and \(\delta\) is the failure-probability allowance. Each record belongs to one shard and can change one vote from one label to another, changing the count vector by at most \(\sqrt2\) in Euclidean norm.
Let \(\sigma\) denote the standard deviation of the added Gaussian noise. GNMax adds this noise to each count and releases the label with the largest noisy count. In Rényi differential privacy (RDP), each answer costs a line with slope \(1/\sigma^2\) at order \(\alpha\), the Rényi order parameter. Slopes compose additively (Rényi DP). Let \(\rho(\varepsilon,\delta)\) be the largest slope that converts to the target guarantee. For a fixed number \(Q\) of answers, including adaptively chosen queries, the required noise is \[\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{Q}{\rho(\varepsilon, \delta)}}. \tag{43.1}\] For example, set target privacy level \(\varepsilon = 1\) and slack \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). The allowed slope is 0.0306. Then 1,000 answers require \(\sigma = 181\).
crumbs: 43  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning

title: 43  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
43.2 When you meet it
Use private prediction when private model training is impractical. One example is a large language model (LLM) interface whose answers could expose records in prompts. Split records into disjoint groups, query the model once per group, and release a GNMax label (Duan et al. 2023). Wu et al. (2024) answered 10,000 sentiment queries with accuracy matching one non-private prompt. Their privacy level was \(\varepsilon=1\).
The alternative is a private model with fixed accuracy. Vote noise grows as \(\sqrt Q\), so private answers are preferable only up to a break-even query count. On the full edition’s synthetic task, the data contains 10,000 records. Voting outperforms private SGD (DP-SGD) only for the first 18 queries at privacy level \(\varepsilon=1\). Compare both approaches at the expected query count and budget, using Train a model with DP-SGD as the baseline.
PATE (private aggregation of teacher ensembles) labels public, unlabelled inputs with GNMax and trains a student model on those labels. Only the student is released, at the privacy cost of its labels. PATE therefore requires public inputs from the private data distribution. Papernot et al.’s MNIST student comes within one percentage point of non-private accuracy, but its \(\varepsilon\) is data-dependent (Section 43.4). On the synthetic task, DP-SGD outperforms the best student at every budget.
crumbs: 43  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning

title: 43  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
43.3 How to use it
dp_accounting accounts for the vote. One GNMax answer is a GaussianDpEvent whose noise multiplier, the noise over the sensitivity, is \(\sigma/\sqrt2\).
import numpy as np
from dp_accounting import GaussianDpEvent, SelfComposedDpEvent
from dp_accounting.pld import PLDAccountant
from dp_accounting.rdp import RdpAccountant

sigma, queries = 181.0, 1000  # noise per count, answers to release
event = SelfComposedDpEvent(GaussianDpEvent(sigma / np.sqrt(2)), queries)  # sensitivity sqrt(2)
rdp = RdpAccountant().compose(event).get_epsilon(1e-5)
pld = PLDAccountant().compose(event).get_epsilon(1e-5)
print(f"{rdp:.3f} {pld:.3f}")  # 0.999 0.914
The RDP accountant confirms \(\varepsilon = 0.999\). The privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant, exact for Gaussian noise, gives 0.914, so solving for \(\sigma\) with it gives less noise. To solve, pass a function from \(\sigma\) to this event to dp_accounting.calibrate_dp_mechanism. For many answers the PLD is much slower, so RDP is the fallback. When each query draws a fresh Poisson sample of records, as in Wu et al., wrap each event in a PoissonSampledDpEvent.
crumbs: 43  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning

title: 43  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
43.4 What goes wrong
The guarantee needs each record in exactly one shard. So assign shards by a hash of the record’s or the user’s identifier, never by position in a file, where one inserted record shifts every later shard. Release the label only, and fix \(Q\) in advance.
Noise this large wipes out close votes. With two labels and a gap \(g\) between the counts, the vote returns the plurality with probability \(\Phi(g/(\sqrt2\sigma))\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function.
For example, 1,000 answers at privacy level \(\varepsilon = 4\) require noise \(\sigma = 51.8\). With that noise, a vote of 98 to 2 is correct with probability 0.9051. For a close vote of 52 to 48, accuracy is only about one half. Measure the noiseless vote first, because no privacy budget can improve it. Adding teachers widens vote gaps because \(\sigma\) does not depend on the teacher count. This helps only until the shards become too small to train on.
Finally, beware of a data-dependent \(\varepsilon\). When teachers agree, a sharper analysis charges less, but that smaller \(\varepsilon\) is computed from the votes and leaks them. Until it is released with noise, it is a measurement, not a guarantee.
Confident-GNMax answers only queries on which a noisy check finds agreement, the cheap and accurate ones.

title: 44  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
44.1 What it is
Gradient descent without momentum accumulates clipped gradients, so weights after each step depend on their prefix sum. Differential privacy (DP) applied to stochastic gradient descent (SGD) yields DP-SGD, which adds fresh noise at every step. Prefix-sum noise then grows like a random walk. Matrix mechanisms correlate noise across steps so some noise cancels in later sums.
Place the step gradients in the rows of matrix \(x\). Their prefix sums are \(Ax\), where \(A\) has ones on and below its diagonal. The matrix factorization mechanism factors \(A\) into decoder \(L\) and encoder \(R\), adds Gaussian noise \(z\) to the encoded gradients, then decodes: \[\hat S = L(Rx + z) = Ax + Lz. \tag{44.1}\] Each record affects only the encoder column for its step, so privacy depends on the encoder’s largest column norm. Accuracy depends on the decoder: row \(t\) determines how noise affects prefix sum \(t\).
The first method applied follow the regularized leader (FTRL) to binary-tree sums and is called DP-FTRL (Kairouz et al. 2021). The common square-root factorization uses the lower-triangular square root of \(A\) for both factors. At equal privacy over 100 steps, its final-sum noise standard deviation is about one quarter that of independent noise.

title: 44  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
44.2 When you meet it
Use matrix mechanisms when the pipeline cannot use the Poisson sampler assumed by DP-SGD accounting. Examples include fixed batches from a shuffled dataset, data processed in arrival order and federated devices that report when available. Treating these as Poisson understates \(\varepsilon\) (Amplification by subsampling); matrix mechanisms do not require subsampling.
Without sampling, independent noise can sharply reduce accuracy; correlated noise can recover much of it. On the full edition’s synthetic task, ten fixed-order epochs at \(\varepsilon=2\) give test accuracy 0.8641 with independent noise, 0.9491 with the banded square root of Section 44.4 and 0.9493 with Poisson-sampled DP-SGD. Use Opacus with Poisson sampling when possible; otherwise consider a banded matrix mechanism, as Google did for Gboard models (Xu et al. 2023).

title: 44  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
44.3 How to use it
Google’s JAX Privacy implements banded matrix factorization. The block below was not run, because JAX is not in this book’s environment. It cycles through 100 fixed groups of records, one per step, so each record takes part once every 100 steps.
# jax-privacy==2.0.0 (not run)
from jax_privacy.experimental.execution_plan import BandMFExecutionPlanConfig

config = BandMFExecutionPlanConfig.default(
    num_bands=100,       # at most the 100 steps between a record's turns
    iterations=1000,     # ten epochs of 100 steps
    epsilon=2.0,
    delta=1e-5,
    sampling_prob=1.0,   # all of the step's group joins: no amplification claimed
    l2_clip_norm=1.0,
)
plan = config.plan       # calibrates the noise multiplier with dp_accounting
The training loop samples batches with plan.batch_selection_strategy, clips and sums gradients with plan.clipped_grad, and adds noise with plan.noise_addition_transform. Use dp_accounting on plan.dp_event to calculate reported \(\varepsilon\). The module is experimental; pin its version.

title: 44  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
44.4 What goes wrong
Repeated participation creates the main risk. Across \(E\) epochs, one record affects \(E\) encoder columns. Nearby square-root columns overlap, increasing sensitivity faster than \(\sqrt E\). Banding retains \(b\) encoder diagonals: the main diagonal and \(b-1\) below it. It requires each pair of a record’s participations to be separated by at least \(b\) steps (\(b\)-min-separation). The columns then share no rows, bounding sensitivity by \(\sqrt E\) times the longest column, as with independent noise.
Data order is part of the mechanism. Fix it independently of private data and reuse the same permutation every epoch. Reshuffling can place a record at the end of one epoch and the start of the next, violating the separation condition.
The neighbouring relation also affects sensitivity. This analysis leaves a neighbour’s slot empty, so one step changes by at most the clipping norm. Replacing a record with another doubles sensitivity; report the relation with each \(\varepsilon\).
dp_accounting 0.6.0 enforces this restriction. Its tree-aggregation event is supported only by a Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant using NeighboringRelation.REPLACE_SPECIAL, where a record is replaced by an empty slot. Under DP-SGD’s default add/remove relation, it raises UnsupportedEventError; the privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant also rejects it. Therefore, DP-FTRL and DP-SGD runs cannot share an add/remove ledger.

text:
44.5 References

Choquette-Choo et al., “(Amplified) Banded Matrix Factorizations: A Unified Approach to Private Training” (NeurIPS 2023): banding, min-separation and amplification.

title: 45  Disparate impact
text:
45.1 Why this matters
Average test accuracy can hide groups that bear more of privacy’s accuracy cost. Differential privacy (DP) applied to stochastic gradient descent (SGD), called DP-SGD (DP-SGD), can disproportionately reduce accuracy for under-represented groups. Bagdasaryan, Poursaeed & Shmatikov (2019) called this the disparate impact of DP.
A one-point average loss can conceal a ten-point loss for a small group. Before release, compare each group’s private-model accuracy with a non-private baseline and report confidence intervals.

title: 45  Disparate impact
section: 45.2 Evaluating a private model per group
text:
45.2 Evaluating a private model per group
Specify relevant groups before examining results to avoid selecting groups based on outcomes. Train a non-private baseline with the same data and procedure; group differences may exist without privacy. Measure DP’s cost as each group’s accuracy change under private training.
Let \(\mathrm{acc}_g\) be model accuracy on test records from group \(g\). Since private training is random, average accuracy over multiple runs, denoted \(\mathbb E\). The group’s privacy cost \(\pi_g\) is its accuracy loss under private rather than non-private training with the same data and hyperparameters: \[\pi_g = \mathrm{acc}_g(\text{non-private}) - \mathbb E\big[\mathrm{acc}_g(\text{private})\big]. \tag{45.1}\] DP has disparate impact when groups have different privacy costs.
Report an interval for each accuracy. Correct classifications are binomial outcomes, so the exact Clopper–Pearson interval covers the true group accuracy in at least 95% of samples (Hypothesis testing).
Compute a separate interval for differences between groups. Let \(\hat p_g\) be measured accuracy for group \(g\), and let \(m_g\) be the number of its test records. For disjoint test sets, the variances add. This gives the following approximate 95% interval when counts are sufficiently large: \[(\hat p_a - \hat p_b) \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_a(1 - \hat p_a)}{m_a} + \frac{\hat p_b(1 - \hat p_b)}{m_b}}. \tag{45.2}\]
Small test groups produce wide intervals. For example, suppose 88 of 100 minority-group records are classified correctly. The majority group has 1,812 correct predictions among 1,900 records, or accuracy 0.954; the measured gap is 0.074. SciPy gives the minority interval, and Equation 45.2 gives the gap interval.
from math import sqrt

from scipy.stats import binomtest

minority = binomtest(88, 100).proportion_ci(confidence_level=0.95, method="exact")
print(f"{minority.low:.3f} {minority.high:.3f}")  # 0.800 0.936

gap, se = 0.954 - 0.880, sqrt(0.954 * 0.046 / 1_900 + 0.880 * 0.120 / 100)
print(f"{gap - 1.96 * se:.3f} {gap + 1.96 * se:.3f}")  # 0.010 0.138
The gap’s interval excludes zero, but its value could range from one to fourteen points. Distinguishing a five-point gap from zero requires hundreds of group test records; a one-point gap requires thousands.
Privacy cost needs a paired interval because both models use the same test records, so their accuracies are dependent and Equation 45.2 does not apply. For group \(g\), let \(u\) count records only the non-private model classifies correctly. Let \(v\) count records only the private model gets right, and let \(m_g\) be the test-record count. One run’s cost is \((u-v)/m_g\). For large counts, an approximate 95% interval is \[\frac{u - v}{m_g} \pm \frac{1.96}{m_g}\sqrt{u + v - \frac{(u - v)^2}{m_g}}. \tag{45.3}\]
Training introduces additional variation that a larger test set cannot remove. Small-group accuracy varies more across training runs, so a one-run comparison can reverse. Train each procedure with multiple seeds and report mean cost and its spread.
Per-group accuracy on a private test set is itself a statistic of private data. To publish it, add noise to each group’s correct-prediction count and allocate a separate privacy budget (Release statistics with a library).

text:

It trains once without privacy and once with DP-SGD at a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) of 4 and a slack \(\delta\) of \(10^{-5}\). title: 45  Disparate impact
section: 45.4 Why small groups pay: clipping and noise
text:
45.4 Why small groups pay: clipping and noise
DP-SGD can lose accuracy through clipping and noise, and both steps treat every record alike. The clipping-only column of Table 45.2 adds no noise and gives no privacy. Clipping alone costs the Asian-Pac-Islander group 0.57 points and the Other group 1.18 points. The White group gains 0.08 points, so clipping can affect groups unequally.
Clipping caps every record’s pull on the update at the clipping norm \(C\), so it cuts back the groups with long gradients hardest. A group’s gradients are long where the model fits it badly, as it does a rare pattern the rest of the data does not teach. So training gives such a group less weight than its share of the records.
The noise is the same for every group, while a group’s signal grows with its size. A small group therefore has a weaker signal relative to the noise. When that group needs a rule of its own, its privacy cost can grow inversely with its share of the training records.
On Adult, reducing the Asian-Pac-Islander share from 3.1% to 1% leaves its cost at \(\varepsilon = 1\) within the spread of three runs. The measured cost is 3.13 points. Measure the cost rather than predicting it from group size. Clipping and noise compound because noise acts on the update after clipping has reduced it. If clipping halves a group’s gradients, its signal is like that of a group half its size.
To see which cause hurts your model, measure per-example gradient norms by group. Opacus’s GradSampleModule, the wrapper DP-SGD training already uses, keeps one gradient per row in each parameter’s grad_sample, so one backward pass gives the norms.
wrapped = GradSampleModule(model)  # adds hooks that keep one gradient per row
wrapped.train()
logits: torch.Tensor = wrapped(split.x)
nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(logits, split.y).backward()  # fills p.grad_sample for every weight p
norms = stacked_norms(wrapped)
Group the norms by each row’s group label, kept beside the batch but not fed to the model. Log each group’s median norm and fraction clipped as training goes on, because the groups can separate late. At initialization on Adult, the median norm is 1.444, so \(C = 1\) clips every row, whatever its group.

title: 45  Disparate impact
text:
45.5 Mitigations and what they cost
At a fixed budget, a change to the training recipe only moves the cost between the groups or between clipping and noise (Table 45.3). Only the last row, which changes the data, the starting model or the budget, reduces it.

The fixes that work






Oversampling costs the group’s privacy because a record’s guarantee depends on its chance of being sampled (Amplification by subsampling). Run the accountant at the oversampled rate. On Adult, sampling the Asian-Pac-Islander rows four times as often at \(\varepsilon = 1\) raises the noise multiplier from 2.383 to 8.828.
Every group then loses accuracy, with the largest loss in the oversampled group. Its accuracy falls from 0.8145 to 0.7657; the White group’s falls from 0.8310 to 0.7860. These comparisons use the same DP-SGD at the ordinary sampling rate. This is levelling down with no gain for anyone.
No algorithm avoids some privacy cost. A model that learns a small group’s rule must estimate it privately from that group’s records. With few records, private estimation has an error floor that no mechanism can beat (Lower bounds).

title: 45  Disparate impact

title: 46  Auditing private training
text:
46.1 Why this matters
For differential privacy (DP), an accountant maps the training configuration to privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and slack \(\delta\). This proves a property of the algorithm, but deployed systems run code. Bugs in noise, clipping or sampling can weaken privacy without noticeably changing accuracy, which often remains stable across a wide range of noise levels (the training workflow). Standard accuracy tests may not detect these bugs.
An audit tests implementation privacy by attack. It inserts canaries, trains with and without them, then measures membership-test success. DP limits every test’s success rate, so a rate above the limit disproves the claimed guarantee. A low rate proves nothing: a weak attack may fail even against a non-private model.

title: 46  Auditing private training
section: 46.2 Known bugs, and which audit catches them
text:
46.2 Known bugs, and which audit catches them
The following implementation errors can invalidate stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with differential privacy, DP-SGD.

The variance passed where the standard deviation is expected, or noise scaled for the mean but added to the sum, which adds the batch size times too little noise. A unit test in continuous integration (CI) catches both (Section 46.3).
Clipping applied after averaging, or noise from a weak seed. Nasr et al. (2023) found both in real code with per-step audits like the CI test.
The accountant told the wrong numbers, such as a record count that includes augmented copies, which makes \(\varepsilon\) look smaller than it is. Only an end-to-end audit can catch it, and only if the error is large.
Batches shuffled but accounted as Poisson sampling, which can make the true \(\varepsilon\) several times the reported one (Amplification by subsampling). No audit here exercises the sampling, so check the loader itself.

Audits detect only privacy loss beyond the claim; code that adds excess noise will pass.

title: 46  Auditing private training
section: 46.3 A CI test for the noise and the clipping
text:
46.3 A CI test for the noise and the clipping
An efficient strong audit repeatedly tests one optimizer step. A Dirac canary has a nonzero per-example gradient only in one coordinate; all other records have zero gradient there. Include it at every step in one run and omit it in another. Let \(x_t\) be the noisy gradient sum in that coordinate at step \(t\), divided by clipping norm \(C\). A canary longer than \(C\) is clipped to length \(C\), contributing exactly 1. The optimizer adds noise with standard deviation \(\sigma C\), where \(\sigma\) is the noise multiplier, so each reading follows \[x_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) \text{ without the canary}, \qquad x_t \sim \mathcal N(1, \sigma^2) \text{ with it}. \tag{46.1}\]
A threshold test reports “canary in” when a reading exceeds a threshold. Its true positive rate (TPR) is the detection frequency with the canary present; its false positive rate (FPR) is the frequency without it.
For two normal distributions separated by \(\mu\), every threshold satisfies \(\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{TPR})-\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})=\mu\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function. Measured rates therefore bound the separation \(\mu\), which a correct optimizer limits to \(1/\sigma\): \[\mu \ge \Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{TPR}) - \Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}). \tag{46.2}\] The test plugs in the low end of the TPR’s Clopper–Pearson interval and the high end of the FPR’s. Each end is taken at level \(\beta/2\), so the bound holds with probability \(1 - \beta\) (Hypothesis testing). If this bound exceeds \(1/\sigma\), the code adds less noise than it claims.
The script practitioner_audit.py runs the test on Opacus’s own DPOptimizer. It writes per-example gradients into grad_sample by hand, as Opacus’s hooks would, and reads the noisy sum that optimizer.step() leaves in grad.
def canary_coordinate(sigma: float, planted_bug: str, with_canary: bool, steps: int) -> Array:
    """Run the optimizer for `steps` steps; return the canary coordinate of each noisy sum, in units of C."""
    layer = torch.nn.Linear(DIM_CI, 1, bias=False)
    optimizer = make_optimizer(layer, sigma, planted_bug)
    observations = np.empty(steps)
    for t in range(steps):
        setattr(layer.weight, "grad_sample", batch_grad_samples(with_canary))  # as Opacus's hooks would
        optimizer.step()  # clip each row to C, sum, add N(0, σ²C²)
        assert layer.weight.grad is not None
        observations[t] = layer.weight.grad[0, CANARY_COORD].item() / CLIP_CI
        optimizer.zero_grad()
    return observations
The canary’s gradient is ten times \(C\), so the test also exercises clipping. The script chooses the threshold on the first half of the steps and counts the rates on the second half. It also checks that the canary-free readings have a standard deviation within 10% of \(\sigma\), since with no noise every reading is 0. The command uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/practitioner_audit.py tests three optimizers at \(\sigma = 0.7\) and a batch of \(B = 64\) records, the correct one, one with the variance bug and one with no noise. The variance bug removes noise only because \(\sigma^2 < \sigma\) when \(\sigma\) is below 1, and above 1 it would pass.
sigma=0.7  C=1.0  B=64  steps per run=2000  claim mu=1/sigma=1.429
correct: noise std 0.687 (claim 0.7)  FP 206/1000  TP 710/1000
correct: mu_lo=1.201  pass
variance for std: noise std 0.481 (claim 0.7)  FP 206/1000  TP 862/1000
variance for std: mu_lo=1.722  FAIL
no noise: noise std 0.000 (claim 0.7)  FP 0/1000  TP 1000/1000
no noise: mu_lo=5.360  FAIL
The correct optimizer’s bound on \(\mu\) is 1.201, below its claimed 1.429, so it passes. The variance bug’s bound is 1.722 and the missing noise’s is 5.360, so both fail. The test takes seconds, so run it on every commit.
Three things go wrong in practice.
First, a correct optimizer still fails with probability \(\beta\), here 5%, so an unseeded test fails one build in twenty. Fix the seed, or use a \(\beta\) of \(10^{-3}\) with more steps. Second, the script builds its own optimizer, so it tests Opacus, not your call to it. To test your code, have your setup function return the optimizer it makes, and drive that one. Third, the test never draws a batch or calls the accountant. So the same suite should assert that the loader is Opacus’s DPDataLoader and that a second library’s \(\varepsilon\) matches yours (Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run).

title: 46  Auditing private training
section: 46.4 From an attack to a lower bound
text:
46.4 From an attack to a lower bound
For a whole training run, the attack is a membership test on a planted canary. A trial is one training run, with or without the canary. Under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, every such test satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta, \qquad 1 - \mathrm{FPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,(1 - \mathrm{TPR}) + \delta. \tag{46.3}\]
Solving these for \(\varepsilon\) turns measured rates into a lower bound on it. Write \(\overline{\mathrm{FPR}}\) for the one-sided Clopper–Pearson upper bound on the FPR at level \(\beta/2\), and \(\underline{\mathrm{TPR}}\) for the TPR’s lower bound. With probability at least \(1 - \beta\), the code is then not \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, at the claimed \(\delta\), for any \(\varepsilon\) below \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}} = \max\Big\{\ln\frac{\underline{\mathrm{TPR}} - \delta}{\overline{\mathrm{FPR}}},\ \ln\frac{1 - \overline{\mathrm{FPR}} - \delta}{1 - \underline{\mathrm{TPR}}}\Big\}. \tag{46.4}\] The bound needs independent trials, and a threshold chosen on other trials than those it counts, because a threshold tuned on them inflates it.
No library installed with this book computes the bound, so the script imports eps_lower_bound from the book’s helper module, practitioner_privacy_tests.py. Suppose an attack catches the canary in 500 of 1,000 runs that include it, and raises one false alarm in 1,000 runs without it.
for false_pos, true_pos in ((1, 500), (0, 1_000)):  # out of 1,000 runs without and with the canary
    eps_lo = eps_lower_bound(false_pos, true_pos, 1_000, DELTA)
    print(f"FP {false_pos}/1000  TP {true_pos}/1000: certified eps lower bound {eps_lo:.2f}")
FP 1/1000  TP 500/1000: certified eps lower bound 4.43
FP 0/1000  TP 1000/1000: certified eps lower bound 5.60
The raw rates alone would suggest 6.21, but the certified bound is only 4.43, and even a perfect attack certifies only 5.60 from 1,000 trials per hypothesis. So do not expect an end-to-end audit to certify all of a large claim.

title: 46  Auditing private training
section: 46.5 A one-run audit of the trained model
text:
46.5 A one-run audit of the trained model
Thousands of runs are out of reach for a real model, so Steinke, Nasr & Jagielski (2023) get many trials from one run. Plant a number \(m\) of canaries, include each one by its own fair coin, train once and score every canary. Then fix a list length \(r\). Guess “in” for the \(r/2\) highest scores and “out” for the \(r/2\) lowest, and make no guess about the rest. Write \(W\) for the number of correct guesses.
Under \(\varepsilon\)-DP, no attack guesses one canary’s coin right with a probability above the limit \(p_\varepsilon\) given below. So the count \(W\) is no more likely to reach any value \(v\) than a binomial count with that success rate is: \[\Pr[W \ge v] \le \Pr\big[\mathrm{Bin}(r, p_\varepsilon) \ge v\big], \qquad p_\varepsilon = \frac{e^\varepsilon}{1 + e^\varepsilon}. \tag{46.5}\] An observed count that this binomial reaches with probability below \(\beta\) rules out that \(\varepsilon\), and the certified bound is the largest \(\varepsilon\) ruled out. Under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, the paper adds at most \(2m\delta\) to that probability. The coins must be independent and fair, and several list lengths need a Bonferroni correction, which runs each test at \(\beta\) divided by their number.
The script runs it on the released pipeline of Train a model with DP-SGD on the Adult census data. It adds only the canaries, 1,000 held-out rows with flipped labels. The coins put 537 of them in the training set, and the release’s noise multiplier gives \(\varepsilon = 3.91\) for this larger set at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). A non-private model uses the release’s baseline recipe, and a memorizing control runs non-private Adam for 60 epochs with small batches. Each canary is scored by minus its loss, and Table 46.1 gives each model’s best of six list lengths from 20 to 1,000.



Table 46.1: One-run audit of the released pipeline on Adult with 1,000 mislabeled canaries, at 95% overall confidence and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).

Both release-recipe models certify nothing, and the reason is the recipe, not privacy. Ten epochs with large batches barely fit the flipped labels, so included canaries have the same loss as excluded ones, with or without noise. Only the memorizing control separates its canaries. Even it certifies just 0.53 for a model with no finite \(\varepsilon\), because each canary is a single trial. A perfect list of all 1,000 guesses would certify at most 5.27.
So use the one-run audit to expose a bug, when a DP model certifies more than its claim, never as evidence of privacy. Report it with its threat model, a black-box attacker who sees only the final model, and with a control that shows the attack can detect leakage on your data.
Stronger black-box attacks, such as the likelihood ratio attack (LiRA) of Pre-release privacy risk assessment, train shadow models. These are copies of the model, trained with its exact recipe on similar data. Run them before release and keep their results with the evidence (Release and governance). LiRA’s TPR at a low FPR shows what a realistic attacker learns. But its (model, record) pairs share models, so they are not independent trials and give no certified bound.

title: 47  Adaptive data analysis
text:
47.1 What it is
Tuning on a held-out validation set uses scores to choose later settings. This adaptive reuse overfits the holdout, making its scores overstate performance on new data.
Each question is a statistical query: the average of a per-record value in \([0,1]\) over \(n\) held-out records, where \(n\) is the holdout size. Classifier accuracy is one example; its population value is the corresponding average on new data. If records are independent and \(k\) denotes the number of queries fixed before any answers, the expected largest gap between empirical and population values is at most \[\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2k)}{2n}}. \tag{47.1}\] The query count affects this bound only logarithmically.
Adaptive queries invalidate this fixed-query bound because later queries can fit the sample’s noise. Blum & Hardt’s boosting attack demonstrates this on a leaderboard with coin-flip labels, where population accuracy cannot exceed 0.5. After 1,000 submissions, the leaderboard reports 0.7182. This score uses 1,000 holdout records.
Differential privacy (DP) limits how much answers reveal about each record, reducing their ability to overfit the sample.
Let \(\alpha\) be the average distance between answers and their empirical values. Let \(\varepsilon\) denote the privacy level and \(\delta\) the slack. Suppose the complete exchange is differentially private under replace-one neighbours. The transfer theorem bounds expected maximum error against population values by \[\alpha + e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta, \tag{47.2}\] regardless of how the analyst uses the answers. For small \(\varepsilon\), the middle term is approximately \(\varepsilon\), so the bound is useful mainly when \(\varepsilon\ll1\). It protects answer accuracy, not the people represented in the holdout.

title: 47  Adaptive data analysis
text:
47.2 When you meet it
Adaptivity arises when a validation set, test set or leaderboard answers questions in multiple rounds, as in hyperparameter search. A round is a batch fixed before receiving its answers. The bounds below depend on the round count; Table 47.1 summarizes the options.



Table 47.1: How to reuse a holdout set, by situation.









Situation
What to do




A final evaluation
Keep a test set and use it once


Few adaptive rounds, plenty of data
Give each round its own slice of data


Many adaptive rounds, scarce data
Answer through noise, or use Thresholdout


A search that is private in the holdout set
Nothing more, since the transfer theorem covers the winner


A public leaderboard
Show a new score only when it beats the best by a margin (Blum & Hardt’s Ladder)

title: 47  Adaptive data analysis
text:
47.3 How to use it
The simplest method is sample splitting: assign each of \(r\) rounds its own \(n/r\) records. For \(k\) total queries, expected maximum error is at most \(\sqrt{r\ln(2k)/(2n)}\), so required data grow proportionally with \(r\). Suppose 1,000 rounds evaluate 1,000 adaptively selected configurations. The holdout has 10,000 validation records, and the bound is 0.6165. Accuracy scores lie in \([0,1]\), so that bound is too large. To reduce error to 0.05, sample splitting would require 1,520,181 records. Fixed queries require 1,521 records for the same error.
The transfer theorem implies that Gaussian-noisy answers require data growing only as \(\sqrt{k}\). Its constants are large, however, so sample splitting remains cheaper for up to a few hundred adaptive queries.
Thresholdout (Dwork et al. 2015) answers using training-set values while they agree with holdout values; these answers reveal nothing about the holdout. When the difference exceeds a noisy threshold, it records a detection and returns a noisy holdout value. Privacy cost depends on detections rather than total queries. However, the full edition’s experiment gives \(\varepsilon\approx29\). No mainstream library implements the method, so treat it as a practical limit on reuse rather than a strong guarantee.

title: 47  Adaptive data analysis
text:
47.4 What goes wrong
The common failure is a long search that selects each setting from earlier validation scores. A fixed grid evaluated once, as in scikit-learn’s GridSearchCV, is one round, so Equation 47.1 bounds the selected score’s overstatement. Count and report the rounds of validation reuse. Typical overfitting may be smaller than the worst-case bound, but risk remains high with few records and many rounds.

title: 48  Release and governance
text:
48.1 Why this matters
A model trained with differential privacy (DP) is not ready to ship when training ends. A privacy reviewer or data protection officer must determine what the guarantee covers, whether its value is correct and how it relates to law. They may not be able to rerun training, so provide the evidence needed to verify the claim. This chapter defines the privacy statement and review process.
The example model is a small stochastic gradient descent (SGD) network trained under this guarantee on 30,000 Adult records, with target privacy level \(\varepsilon=4\). It is produced by Train a model with DP-SGD. The script practitioner_release.py runs in seconds and reads the training run record supplied with --record PATH, or a built-in example record.

title: 48  Release and governance
text: uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/practitioner_release.py

title: 48  Release and governance
text:
48.2 Assemble the run record
The run record must include the inputs to the accountant, which converts settings to \(\varepsilon\) (Choosing an accountant): noise multiplier \(\sigma\), sampling rate \(q\), step count and slack \(\delta\). It must also document assumptions: privacy unit (one person here), neighbouring relation, batch sampler and whether any other use of private data was excluded.
Also record \(n\), the number of units, the random seed, Opacus’s secure_mode, library versions, hyperparameter selection and any preprocessing on private data. In the excerpt, data is the training record and RELEASE_CONTEXT contains release-owner additions.
merged = RELEASE_CONTEXT | data  # the training record, plus what the release owner adds
rec = load_record(merged)
for key, value in asdict(rec).items():
    print(f"{key}: {value}")
problems = record_problems(merged)  # missing fields, sampler not Poisson, delta above 1/n^1.1, tuning
limitations = record_limitations(merged)  # stated, so not a problem, but the statement must disclose them
print(f"record problems: {len(problems)}")
for problem in problems:
    print(f"  - {problem}")
print(f"record limitations: {len(limitations)}")
for limitation in limitations:
    print(f"  - {limitation}")
unit: person (one row of Adult)
neighbours: add/remove
n: 30000
delta: 1e-05
sigma: 0.972900390625
sample_rate: 0.03333333333333333
sampler: poisson
secure_mode: False
seed: 0
steps: 300
...
record problems: 0
record limitations: 1
  - secure_mode=False: Opacus drew the noise from a seeded, non-cryptographic generator so the numbers reproduce; floating-point attacks on the noise are not excluded. Retrain with secure_mode=True to ship
The record’s \(\delta=10^{-5}\) follows the book’s rule (How small δ must be). Its \(\varepsilon\) values come from the independent check in Calibrate and account a DP-SGD run.
The tuning record is essential because the final run’s \(\varepsilon\) excludes runs used to select hyperparameters. Here, non-private runs selected the learning rate on 2,000 held-out Adult rows treated as public, and \(\varepsilon=4\) was fixed before private training. The training run’s \(\varepsilon\) therefore equals the procedure’s cost. The 2,000 people receive no guarantee and must be named in the statement. For private-data tuning, report both costs (Hyperparameter tuning).
Stop release for a record problem such as missing fields, a non-Poisson sampler, excessive \(\delta\) or undocumented tuning. Here, secure_mode is disabled to keep example numbers reproducible. Disclose this limitation and enable secure mode when retraining a production model.

title: 48  Release and governance
text:
48.3 Recompute the guarantee
The release owner recomputes \(\varepsilon\) from \(\sigma\), \(q\) and the steps alone, with a library other than the one that trained. A recomputation inside the training code would reuse any wrong number. Compare the result only with a budget from the same kind of accountant, because a looser accountant gives a larger \(\varepsilon\) for the same run. The script uses the privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant of dp_accounting, as in the cross-check, and compares it with the looser Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant. It also reads \(\varepsilon\) at a \(\delta\) a hundred times smaller, and the trade-off curve. That curve gives the largest true positive rate (TPR) that any membership test can reach at each false positive rate (FPR) (Choosing ε).
pld = privacy_loss_distribution.from_gaussian_mechanism(sigma, sampling_prob=sample_rate).self_compose(steps)
eps_pld = pld.get_epsilon_for_delta(delta)
eps_pld_small = pld.get_epsilon_for_delta(delta / 100)
eps_rdp = rdp_epsilon(sigma, sample_rate, steps, delta)
eps_rdp_small = rdp_epsilon(sigma, sample_rate, steps, delta / 100)
tpr = {fpr: tpr_bound(pld, fpr) for fpr in FPRS}  # largest TPR of any membership test
eps PLD at delta=1e-05: 3.981
eps RDP at delta=1e-05: 4.503
eps PLD at delta=1e-07: 5.191
eps RDP at delta=1e-07: 5.736
TPR bound at FPR 1e-03: 0.0123 (PLD curve)  0.0536 (pair eps, delta only)
TPR bound at FPR 1e-02: 0.0652 (PLD curve)  0.5355 (pair eps, delta only)
record's PRV eps: reported 3.99, recomputed 3.98: consistent
The PLD value, 3.981, agrees with the reported 3.99. The curve gives a number a non-specialist can use. At an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), no membership test can reach a TPR above 0.0123, while the pair \((3.98, 10^{-5})\) on its own would allow 0.0536.
The script flags a reported \(\varepsilon\) more than 0.05 below the recomputation. The subtler failure is a recomputation that agrees on wrong inputs, such as code that shuffles the data into fixed batches while the accountant assumes Poisson sampling (Amplification by subsampling). No number shows that, so the record’s sampler, read from the loader, is what catches it.

text:
48.4 Attach the evidence
An accountant proves a theorem about an algorithm, not about the code that runs it, so the release also needs evidence about the code and the model. title: 48  Release and governance
text:
48.5 Write the statement
The statement goes in the model card’s privacy section. The script’s format_statement builds it from the record, so no number is typed by hand. The block omits lines that repeat the record.
Guarantee: (3.98, 1e-05)-DP per person (one row of Adult), add/remove neighbours,
  for the whole training run on Adult (UCI 2), 30,000 training rows (n = 30,000).
  Also (5.19, 1e-07)-DP. Any membership test has TPR at most 0.0123 at FPR 1e-3.
Mechanism: DP-SGD, poisson sampling q = 0.0333, noise multiplier 0.9729,
  clipping norm 1, 300 steps (10 epochs).
Accounting: prv, Opacus 1.6.0; recomputed with dp_accounting PLD (RDP gives 4.50).
...
Noise generator: Opacus secure_mode=False, seed 0.
...
Not covered: data outside the training set, API outputs that use other private data, other releases.
Below the statement, add the evidence of Table 48.1. The last line needs the most care. The guarantee covers the weights and anything computed from them alone, such as the logits that the deployed application programming interface (API) returns, because post-processing cannot weaken DP. An output that also uses other private data, such as a retrieval index, is a new release, and so is a second model trained on the same people.

title: 48  Release and governance
text:
48.6 Map the claim to regulation
This section is not legal advice, since every answer depends on facts beyond the model. In the European Union, Recital 26 of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) exempts anonymous information. It asks about the means of identification “reasonably likely to be used”. Pseudonymised data, which only information kept separately links to a person, remain personal data under Article 4(5).
For AI models, Opinion 28/2024 of the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) sets a test, assessed case by case. A model is anonymous only if the likelihood of extracting personal data about its training set is insignificant. The opinion names DP and attack tests, such as membership inference, as measures to weigh, and warns that a test shows resistance only to the attacks tested. The trade-off curve speaks to extraction as well as membership, because it caps reconstruction too (Choosing ε).



Table 48.2: What DP evidence answers, and leaves open, for the legal questions a release meets.










Legal question
What DP evidence supports
What DP does not answer




Is the model anonymous (GDPR Recital 26; EDPB Opinion 28/2024)?
A bound on what any attacker can learn about one person’s presence or record: the TPR cap and the audits
Whether the bound is “insignificant”; the training data stay personal data


Is this only pseudonymisation (GDPR Art. 4(5))?
DP relies on no separately kept key that could re-link the data to people
Removing identifiers before training is pseudonymisation at most

Necessity and proportionality (Art. 35(7)(b)), and the lawful basis (Art. 6)


Is the risk of identification very small (HIPAA §164.514(b)(1))?
A quantitative bound that an expert can cite, with documented methods
Whether it is “very small”; the expert’s determination itself


Is the information deidentified (California Consumer Privacy Act, Cal. Civ. Code §1798.140(m))?
A bound on how much one person’s record can change what is inferred
Whether that meets the standard, since DP does not stop inferences from population patterns; the business’s own duties


Does the data governance meet the EU AI Act (Art. 10)?
Documented data handling and per-group evaluation
Data quality, representativeness and bias, which DP can worsen






Training still processes personal data, so the GDPR applies to it, lawful basis included. Article 35 requires a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) before processing likely to result in a high risk. The DPIA is the natural home for the statement. In the United States, the safe harbor route of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) removes listed identifiers (§164.514(b)(2)), which DP does not do. Its expert determination route can cite DP evidence but not be replaced by it. California’s law, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act, adds duties against re-identification for the business.
None of these texts says that DP makes a model anonymous by itself. A DPIA entry built from this chapter’s evidence can read as follows, and the controller and counsel fill in the bracketed parts.

The model was trained on personal data under [lawful basis, Art. 6]. Training used DP-SGD with a guarantee of \((3.98, 10^{-5})\)-DP per person, add/remove neighbours, for the whole training run. No membership test against the released weights can exceed a TPR of 0.0123 at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\), and the same curve caps reconstruction. The code passed a CI test of its noise and clipping. A one-run audit of the released pipeline found nothing, while a memorizing control certified 0.53. [A shadow-model attack was / was not run.] These tests show resistance only to the attacks run. DP does not remove identifiers and is not pseudonymisation. Whether the bound makes the model anonymous is for [counsel], and we make no claim of automatic anonymity. Not covered: the 2,000 stand-in rows, the test rows, outputs that use other private data, and later model versions.

title: 48  Release and governance
text:
48.7 Review someone else’s claim
When someone else hands you a model, run the same steps in reverse. Ask for the record of Section 48.2, and refuse a claim that cannot be recomputed. Recompute \(\varepsilon\) from the claim’s own parameters, and check its \(\delta\) against the number of units. Matching the accountant to the code gives the checks on the accountant and the sampler.
The script reviews a claim made up for this book, with every flaw a review should catch. It claims \(\varepsilon = 1\) at \(\delta = 10^{-3}\) for a model trained on 50,000 records, over 5,000 steps with noise multiplier 0.8. Its batches of 256 were shuffled and of fixed size but are accounted as Poisson sampling. The claim states no unit, no clipping norm and no tuning.
def review(claim: dict[str, Any]) -> list[str]:
    """Recompute a claim from its own parameters and list what does not hold up."""
    findings = record_problems(claim)  # includes a sampler that is missing or not Poisson
    sigma, q, steps, delta = claim["sigma"], claim["sample_rate"], claim["steps"], claim["delta"]
    pld = privacy_loss_distribution.from_gaussian_mechanism(sigma, sampling_prob=q).self_compose(steps)
    recomputed = {"PLD": pld.get_epsilon_for_delta(delta)}
    if "rdp" in str(claim.get("accountant")).lower():  # also the accountant the claim names
        recomputed["RDP, the accountant named,"] = rdp_epsilon(sigma, q, steps, delta)
    for name, eps in recomputed.items():
        if eps > claim["epsilon"] + 0.05:
            findings.append(f"eps={claim['epsilon']} does not follow: {name} gives {eps:.2f} at its delta")
    delta_ok = delta_for(claim["n"])
    findings.append(f"at delta={delta_ok:.0e} (1/n^1.1) PLD gives eps={pld.get_epsilon_for_delta(delta_ok):.2f}")
    return findings
claim: Our model is trained with differential privacy, epsilon = 1.
findings: 10
  - missing field: unit
  - missing field: neighbours
  - missing field: max_grad_norm
  - missing field: secure_mode
  - sampler 'shuffled fixed-size batches' is not Poisson subsampling: Poisson-subsampled accounting does not apply
  - delta=1e-03 is above 1/n^1.1 (use 1e-06)
  - tuning not reported: the cost of choosing hyperparameters is unknown
  - eps=1.0 does not follow: PLD gives 2.17 at its delta
  - eps=1.0 does not follow: RDP, the accountant named, gives 2.55 at its delta
  - at delta=1e-06 (1/n^1.1) PLD gives eps=3.75
By the vendor’s own parameters the claimed 1 is 2.17, and the RDP accountant it names gives 2.55. At a \(\delta\) the book accepts it is 3.75. Even that is too low, because shuffled fixed-size batches get no amplification by Poisson subsampling, so the true \(\varepsilon\) can be far above all these numbers.
The script takes \(n\) as given, so it cannot see a wrong unit. If the records are messages and a customer sends many, screen the per-customer \(\varepsilon\) yourself with User-level differential privacy. Send the findings back with a request for a corrected record.

title: 48  Release and governance
text:
48.8 After release
Every retraining on the same people is a new release that composes with the old ones. For identical runs, compose the PLD of one run with itself once per version, pld.self_compose(steps * versions). State the budget per model version and in total over a fixed period. If the total over a schedule is too large, calibrate each version to a share of it.
Deletion requests need their own answer, because DP deletes nothing. The model is about as likely as one trained without the person, but their row is still in the data. So honour a request by removing the row, from the stand-in and test rows too, and retraining on a fixed schedule. Whether that is fast enough for the GDPR’s Article 17 is a question for counsel.
Give each model version its own record and statement, and name in advance the incidents that reopen a release. A failing CI test, an audit bound above the claim, or a bug in the sampler or the accountant needs a corrected statement or a retrained model.
